stem: A 17-year-old girl who is a soccer player is brought to the emergency department after a posterior dislocation of her right knee during a soccer game. On physical examination, there is significant swelling of the knee and significant bruising on the posterior aspect. The dislocation is reduced, but the pulses distal to the site of injury are not easily palpable. Angiograms of the lower extremities are shown. Which of the following vascular structures, indicated by arrows in the image, is most likely damaged in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery as the femoral artery exits the adductor hiatus. The popliteal artery descends posterior to the knee joint and divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries at the lower border of the popliteus muscle. Because the popliteal artery is the most anterior neurovascular structure in the popliteal fossa and closest to the femur, it is most likely to be injured with a posterior dislocation of the knee. The fibular artery is a branch of the posterior tibial artery in the upper leg.

Any loss of pulses distal to the site of injury should prompt an angiographic evaluation.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect: anterior tibial artery branches distal to the knee; the source arrows mark the vessel at the knee joint.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect: fibular artery is a distal branch and is not the vessel indicated at the knee.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: popliteal artery is vulnerable to injury in knee dislocation.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect: posterior tibial artery is distal to the popliteal artery bifurcation.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect: femoral artery is proximal to the knee and not the vessel marked by the arrows.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. Two hours after arrival, he dies despite appropriate lifesaving measures. Three days after the patient's death, his younger brother begins to wear the patient's jacket all of the time, no matter how warm the weather. This is most likely an example of which of the following defense mechanisms?
explanation: Identification is the unconscious adoption of another person's characteristics or activities, and may help reduce the pain of separation or loss. The brother adopts his deceased sibling's behavior. Denial acts as if a threatening fact is not known; rationalization supplies a plausible but false explanation; reaction formation expresses behavior opposite to the person's underlying feelings; sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially acceptable activity.

choice_explanations.A: Denial refuses to acknowledge a painful reality.
choice_explanations.B: Identification adopts characteristics or behavior of another person.
choice_explanations.C: Rationalization gives a plausible but inaccurate justification.
choice_explanations.D: Reaction formation expresses the opposite of an unacceptable impulse.
choice_explanations.E: Sublimation redirects an unacceptable impulse into a socially acceptable activity.

stem: A neonate develops a yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae two days after birth. The condition worsens the following day. Appropriate therapy and vitamin supplementation are begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate vitamin therapy for this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Neonatal jaundice is a very common condition that may require medical attention in newborns. Accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin (UCB) causes the yellow coloration (jaundice or icterus) of the skin and sclera. In many cases, this is a physiologic rather than a pathologic occurrence. It is observed in approximately 60% of term neonates and 80% of preterm neonates. There is great cause for concern, however, if serum UCB levels increase too much (for example, with Rh incompatibility) because UCB is neurotoxic. It can cause kernicterus (deposition of lipid-soluble UCB in the basal ganglia), which can produce lifelong neurologic complications in neonates who survive. Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia occurs more frequently in boys and those of East Asian and Native American descent. Breast milk jaundice is a type of neonatal jaundice associated with breastfeeding.
Neonatal jaundice develops for two reasons. First, bilirubin production is increased because of hemolysis of fetal red blood cells (RBCs) as they are replaced with newly formed hemoglobin A-containing RBCs. The porphyrin ring of the heme prosthetic group of hemoglobin liberated by hemolysis is converted by NADPH-requiring heme oxygenase to linear biliverdin as carbon monoxide and iron are released. Biliverdin is reduced to bilirubin by NADPH-requiring biliverdin reductase. Bilirubin is conjugated with two molecules of glucuronic acid by bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyl transferase (bilirubin UGT), a hepatic enzyme, and ultimately secreted into the bile. If more bilirubin is made than can be conjugated, UCB accumulates. Second, the hepatic excretory capacity for bilirubin is low at birth, in part because of low bilirubin UGT levels in the perinatal period. Genetic deficiencies in bilirubin UGT are the cause of Gilbert syndrome and Crigler–Najjar syndrome.
Treatment is with phototherapy, but this can also destroy riboflavin, so this vitamin should be supplemented in neonates receiving the treatment. Phototherapy is routinely used to treat neonatal jaundice because light converts bilirubin into water-soluble isomers that are excreted into urine. Another molecule that absorbs light is the water-soluble vitamin riboflavin (vitamin B₂), which degrades with phototherapy (but not heat). Riboflavin supplementation is required to prevent deficiency of the vitamin. Ascorbate (choice A), folate (choice B), and niacin (choice C) are water-soluble vitamins that do not appreciably degrade under the conditions of phototherapy and do not have to be supplemented. Vitamin D is not typically depleted by phototherapy.

choice_explanations.A: Vitamin C is not the light-sensitive vitamin depleted by phototherapy.
choice_explanations.B: Folate is not specifically degraded by phototherapy.
choice_explanations.C: Niacin is not the vitamin classically lost during phototherapy.
choice_explanations.D: Riboflavin is light-sensitive and should be supplemented during phototherapy.
choice_explanations.E: Vitamin D is not the relevant phototherapy-associated depletion.

A.text: Vitamin C is not the light-sensitive vitamin depleted by phototherapy.

B.text: Folate is not specifically degraded by phototherapy.

C.text: Niacin is not the vitamin classically lost during phototherapy.

fa_summary: Riboflavin (B2) is light-sensitive and may be degraded during neonatal phototherapy; supplement it while treating jaundice.

stem: A study is conducted to determine the relationship between the amount of time spent studying for the USMLE, in weeks, and the score that the person makes on the exam. Which of the following methods will most likely be used to evaluate the findings of the study?
explanation: Pearson correlation assesses the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two interval/continuous variables measured in one study. Study duration and exam score are both continuous variables. A positive correlation would mean that more weeks of study tend to accompany higher scores; this does not by itself prove that study time caused the higher score. ANOVA compares group means, chi-square analyzes categorical variables, meta-analysis combines results across studies, and odds ratios/relative risks quantify associations for categorical exposure and outcome data.

choice_explanations.A: ANOVA compares means across groups, rather than continuous-variable association.
choice_explanations.B: Chi-square tests associations between categorical variables.
choice_explanations.C: Meta-analysis combines results from multiple studies.
choice_explanations.D: Odds ratios summarize associations for categorical exposure/outcome data.
choice_explanations.E: Pearson correlation assesses linear association between two continuous variables.
choice_explanations.F: Relative risk compares outcome risk between categorical exposure groups.

stem: During an investigational study, a researcher finds a marker that is unique to neuroectoderm cells. The marker can be detected using immunofluorescent methods. Which of the following cell types will most likely show positivity for this marker?
explanation: The correct answer is C. Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm cells. Other neuroectoderm cell derivatives include neuroblasts, astrocytes, and ependymal cells. All of the other choices are derived from neural crest cells (choices A, B, D, and E). Other neural crest derivatives include the neurons of the parasympathetic and sympathetic ganglia (including the adrenal medulla), the dorsal root ganglia of the peripheral nervous system, the sensory ganglia of cranial nerves V, VII, IX, and X, and the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid).

choice_explanations.A: Melanocytes are listed among neural crest derivatives.
choice_explanations.B: Odontoblasts are listed among neural crest derivatives.
choice_explanations.C: Oligodendrocytes are CNS glial cells derived from neuroectoderm.
choice_explanations.D: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons derive from neural crest.
choice_explanations.E: Schwann cells derive from neural crest and myelinate peripheral nerves.

B.text: Odontoblasts are listed among neural crest derivatives.

E.text: Schwann cells derive from neural crest and myelinate peripheral nerves.

fa_summary: Neuroectoderm forms the neural tube; CNS glia such as oligodendrocytes arise from neural tube neuroectoderm, while neural crest forms Schwann cells, melanocytes, odontoblasts, and postganglionic sympathetic neurons.

stem: A 43-year-old pregnant woman with a history of gestational diabetes recently gave birth to a male neonate who is now in the first week of life. Upon delivery, the baby was notably cyanotic, macrosomic, and had relatively poor muscle tone. He was started on 100% oxygen, which improved his oxygen saturation only slightly. After a week of poor feeding and gradually worsening symptoms, the baby eventually succumbs to his condition. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this baby's death?
explanation: Transposition of the great arteries is strongly associated with maternal diabetes and causes parallel systemic and pulmonary circulations. Survival requires mixing through an ASD, VSD, or patent ductus arteriosus; without adequate mixing, severe cyanosis persists despite supplemental oxygen. AV septal defect more often presents later with heart failure, coarctation causes obstructive/weak-pulse findings rather than this cyanotic pattern, Eisenmenger syndrome develops after a chronic left-to-right shunt, and although tetralogy causes cyanosis, it is not the classic diabetic-mother association described here.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. A high-resolution fetal ultrasound shows a 3 cm by 5 cm sac-like structure that contains neural elements overlying the lumbosacral area. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Failure of absorption of cerebrospinal fluid by the arachnoid villi
Failure of closure of the caudal neuropore
Failure of closure of the rostral neuropore
Persistence of remnants of Rathke's pouch

explanation: A lumbosacral sac containing neural elements is a meningomyelocele, a form of open spina bifida caused by failed closure of the caudal neuropore. His past medical history is remarkable for diabetes, which he manages with subcutaneous insulin injections. He does report frequent travel and is frustrated because he always seems to trigger the metal detector at the airport. Which of the following is the most likely underlying explanation for this patient's condition?
explanation: Hyperpigmentation, diabetes, and iron sufficient to trigger a metal detector point to hereditary hemochromatosis. Increased intestinal iron absorption causes iron deposition in the liver, pancreas, skin, and heart.

stem: A 15-year-old male comes to the physician for a sports physical prior to joining the basketball team at his high school. He states that he occasionally gets chest pain and palpitations with exercise. His family history is significant for his father passing away at age 29 years from an aortic dissection. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 89/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 122/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows he is a tall male with disproportionately long limbs. On auscultation of the heart, there is a mid-systolic click. followed by a late 3/6 systolic murmur. Which of the following is the most likely probability of this patient's offspring also inheriting this syndrome?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The young male is presenting with Marfan syndrome. Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant defect in the gene (FBN1) encoding the connective tissue protein fibrillin-1. The affected structures include cardiac, aortic, skeletal, ocular, and pulmonary. The primary cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with Marfan syndrome is aortic root disease that can lead to aneurysmal dilatation and aortic dissection, as present in this patient's father. Patients also have an increased risk of mitral valve prolapse, which is present in this patient who has a mid-systolic click and systolic murmur. Other clinical manifestations include excessive linear growth of the long bones, excess joint laxity, and an ectopic lens.

Patients with Marfan syndrome should have routine follow-up for mitral valve prolapse, aortic dilation, skeletal and ophthalmologic complications, as well as genetic counseling. Autosomal dominant inheritance means the risk of passing on the defect in the gene is 50%. In a Punnett square where “A” is the mutant allele, the male patient would be Aa and mating with an unrelated female (aa). Thus, a 50% possibility of offspring (2/4) being Aa, displaying the Marfan phenotype. In an autosomal dominant disease, it is possible but highly unlikely that a male, AA (homozygous with the mutant allele), would mate with an AA female. If he did, then the correct answer would be 100% (choice E).

choice_explanations.A: Autosomal recessive transmission requires two pathogenic alleles.
choice_explanations.B: X-linked inheritance is inconsistent with the autosomal dominant pedigree pattern.
choice_explanations.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternally transmitted.
choice_explanations.D: Autosomal dominant heterozygous disease carries a 1-in-2 transmission risk per pregnancy.
choice_explanations.E: A 100% risk is not expected from one affected heterozygous parent.

A.text: Autosomal recessive transmission requires two pathogenic alleles.

B.text: X-linked inheritance is inconsistent with the autosomal dominant pedigree pattern.

C.text: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternally transmitted.

D.text: Autosomal dominant heterozygous disease carries a 1-in-2 transmission risk per pregnancy.

E.text: A 100% risk is not expected from one affected heterozygous parent.

fa_summary: First Aid lists Marfan syndrome among autosomal dominant disorders (p58) and states that each child of an affected heterozygous parent has a 50% risk (p57).

stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of abdominal discomfort and weight loss. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a lower left quadrant mass. Ultrasound reveals an enlarged left ovary. Pelvic examination shows a left-sided ovarian mass. The mass is resected, and histologic examination shows small lymphocytes, interspersed with macrophages surrounded by clear spaces. Which of the following is the most likely genetic abnormality associated with this patient's condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has small noncleaved cell lymphoma (Burkitt lymphoma), as evidenced by the “starry-sky” pattern described in the question. It is a high-grade B-cell lymphoma composed of intermediate-sized lymphoid cells interspersed with numerous reactive “tingible-body macrophages” (phagocytosis of apoptotic tumor cells). The figure shows the typical appearance of Burkitt lymphoma, with a “starry-sky” appearance (dense sheets of tumor cells with interspersed tingible-body macrophages that appear as the “stars”). The low-power view best shows the starry-sky appearance, while the high-power view shows how the arrangement of the tumor cells (small purple cells) and macrophages (areas of clearing) produces this appearance.

Burkitt lymphoma is associated with c-MYC activation due to a t(8;14) translocation that places the c-MYC-containing segment of chromosome 8 near an actively transcribed gene for immunoglobulin heavy chains on chromosome 14.

There are two forms of Burkitt lymphoma, and both largely occur in children and young adults. The American type is nonendemic and sporadic. It commonly involves the pelvis and abdomen (e.g., ovaries, bowel, retroperitoneum) and has a high incidence in patients with AIDS. The African type is endemic, characteristically involves the mandible or maxilla, and is associated with Epstein-Barr virus.

The abl-bcr hybrid (choice A) and t(9;22) (choice D) are associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and can also be seen with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Leukemias are diseases that affect the bone marrow and peripheral blood. They rarely involve organs such as the ovaries. BCL-2 activation (choice B) and t(14;18) (choice E) are associated with follicular lymphomas, not Burkitt lymphoma. On microscopy, follicular lymphomas have a nodular or follicular pattern, are comprised of small- to medium-sized lymphocytes, and are not associated with tingible-body macrophages.

choice_explanations.A: BCL2/t(14;18) distinguishes follicular lymphoma from Burkitt lymphoma.
choice_explanations.B: 该选项（BCL2 activation）不是本题最佳解释。The starry-sky pattern suggests Burkitt lymphoma, driven by MYC activation, classically t(8;14). BCL2 activation/t(14;18) is associated with follicular lymphoma; BCR::ABL1/t(9;22) with CML.
choice_explanations.C: Burkitt lymphoma is listed with MYC t(8;14).
choice_explanations.D: 该选项（t(9;22)）不是本题最佳解释。The starry-sky pattern suggests Burkitt lymphoma, driven by MYC activation, classically t(8;14). BCL2 activation/t(14;18) is associated with follicular lymphoma; BCR::ABL1/t(9;22) with CML.
choice_explanations.E: 该选项（t(14;18)）不是本题最佳解释。The starry-sky pattern suggests Burkitt lymphoma, driven by MYC activation, classically t(8;14). BCL2 activation/t(14;18) is associated with follicular lymphoma; BCR::ABL1/t(9;22) with CML.

B.text: BCL2 activation is associated with follicular lymphoma.

C.text: Burkitt lymphoma is associated with MYC activation, classically t(8;14).

D.text: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) is described in the leukemia section.

E.text: Follicular lymphoma is associated with t(14;18) and BCL2.

fa_summary: Burkitt lymphoma is linked to MYC activation; First Aid also contrasts follicular lymphoma and BCL2.

stem: A 24-year-old man sustains an abrasion that removes the epidermis over a large area of his arm. The dermis remains intact. One month later, the epidermis has regrown. Which mechanism best explains this restoration?

options.text: Growth of epidermis from stem cells in hair follicles and sweat glands in the dermis
Migration of endothelial cells from newly grown capillaries
Transformation of dermal fibrobiasts into epidermal cells
Transformation of macrophages into epidermal cells
Transformation of melanocytes nto epidermal cells

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The dermis contains skin appendages (e.g., hair follicles) that contain epithelial stem cells. In the process of healing a large area where the epidermis has been lost but the dermis is intact, re-epithelialization occurs by ingrowth of epidermal cells from the underlying skin appendages, as well as from the intact epidermis along the wound edges.

Recall that in addition to forming the epithelium of the epidermis, the embryonic ectoderm also forms the skin appendages such as hair follicles and sweat glands. The epithelial cells from these appendages can serve as the source of new epithelial cells for the epidermis. Even though the dermis itself is derived from mesoderm, the ectodermal skin appendages migrate into the dermis during their development. None of the other cell types (choices B, C, D, and E) are known to directly contribute to the regeneration of epidermis over abraded skin.

stem: A 23-year-old man receives a tetanus booster vaccine after stepping on a nail. The physician explains that the immunization may cause swelling and inflammation within 24 hours after injection and so should be administered in the patient's nondominant arm. The reaction that will occur at the injection site is a reflection of which of the following mechanisms?
explanation: A local reaction within about a day after booster vaccination in a previously sensitized person is an Arthus reaction: pre-existing IgG–antigen complexes activate complement and recruit neutrophils.

stem: A 2-week-old girl has vomiting, jaundice, lethargy, hepatomegaly, and poor suck. Northern blot analysis shows a normal amount of GALT mRNA, but enzyme activity is absent. Which mutation best explains these findings?

options.text: Premature transcription termination sequence in the DNA

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) is a key enzyme in the metabolism of galactose. Lack of a functional enzyme causes galactosemia, an autosomal recessive condition characterized by vomiting, hyperbilirubinemia with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts. Northern blot is a technique that studies gene expression by analyzing mRNA. A nonsense mutation is a change in one DNA base pair that leads to a premature stop codon when the mRNA is being translated into protein. The mRNA would be transcribed correctly, but when the protein was being translated, it would be stopped prematurely, leading to a truncated protein, which functions abnormally.
Immediate minimization of dietary galactose is essential. Human milk and formula based on bovine milk should be discontinued and replaced with soy formula. This will decrease the acute toxicity but does not prevent all long-term complications of this disease, and monitoring of these patients throughout their lives is necessary. Patients with this disease require a lactose-restricted diet for life.
A gene deletion (choice A) would result in either the absence of mRNA or mRNA of a different size, both of which would be apparent by Northern blot analysis. A premature transcription termination sequence in the DNA (choice C) might result in premature termination of the mRNA chain, leading to a diminished or absent message. A promoter mutation (choice D) in the DNA, if it caused the gene in question to be less actively transcribed, would result in a diminished amount of message. An RNA splicing mutation (choice E) would result in the production of an mRNA molecule of a different size, which would be apparent on Northern blot.

choice_explanations.A: DNA mutations include deletions and insertions that may alter coding sequence.
choice_explanations.B: A nonsense mutation introduces a premature stop codon.
choice_explanations.C: A transcription-termination signal issue would not be the best fit for normal mRNA abundance.
choice_explanations.D: A promoter mutation commonly reduces transcription and mRNA abundance.
choice_explanations.E: A splice mutation alters RNA processing and often transcript size/composition.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has a 2-year history of joint pain, oral swelling, dry mouth, dysphagia, and new dental caries. She reports adequate hydration and dental hygiene. Her family history is significant for hypertension and rheumatoid arthritis. Physical examination shows slight enlargement of the parotid glands. stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe left hip pain that is worst in the morning when he awakens and improves throughout the day, eye pain and redness. He also has occasional swelling of his hands and fingers. Physical examination shows several 2–3 cm inflamed, erythematous plaques covered by silvery-white scale. X-rays of his lumbar spine and hips show left sacroiliitis. X-rays of his hands show severe erosions of the right distal interphalangeal joints. HLA-B27 is positive. Which diagnostic test should most likely be performed in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Seronegative spondyloarthropathies are a group of joint disorders characterized by a lack of rheumatoid factor, axial skeleton involvement (sacroiliac joint), pathologic changes in the ligament (not synovium), and an HLA-B27 association. Disease examples include ankylosing spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)-associated arthritis.

This patient has psoriatic arthritis, an inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. Psoriatic arthritis affects men and women equally in the third to fourth decade of life. The arthritis tends to develop after the rash in most patients, as in the one described here. The spectrum of arthropathy is quite broad and axial involvement (spine and sacroiliac joints) is common. The etiology of psoriatic arthritis is unknown; however, it certainly has an autoimmune and genetic component.

The patient is describing eye redness and pain, and a work-up to rule out anterior uveitis should be performed. Anterior uveitis can be seen in all forms of seronegative spondyloarthropathies. Blurry vision and sensitivity to light (photophobia) can also occur. Anterior uveitis is an inflammation of the middle layer of the eye, which includes the iris and ciliary body. If untreated, it can lead to permanent damage and loss of vision due to development of glaucoma, cataract, or retinal edema. It occurs in approximately 7% of psoriatic arthritis patients. Anterior uveitis can be diagnosed with a slit-lamp examination. The lamp facilitates an examination of the anterior segment and posterior segment of the eye, including the eyelid, sclera, conjunctiva, iris, lens, and cornea. Anterior uveitis is seen as presence of a haze due to protein accumulation and fibrin exudate. Treatment is with anti-inflammatory drugs.

HLA-B27 is also associated with reactive arthritis, formerly known as Reiter syndrome, which can be remembered as the syndrome in which the patient “can't see” (anterior uveitis/conjunctivitis), “can't pee” (nongonococcal urethritis), and “can't climb a tree” (arthritis). HLA-B27 is also associated with acute anterior uveitis, post-gonococcal arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. Abdominal ultrasound (choice A), brain MRI (choice B), liver function tests (choice C), and renal ultrasound (choice D) are not indicated in a patient with psoriatic arthritis.

choice_explanations.A: 该选项（Abdominal ultrasound）不是本题最佳解释。The plaques and distal interphalangeal erosions indicate psoriatic arthritis, a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. Painful red eye raises concern for anterior uveitis, which can threaten vision and is associated with HLA-B27 disease. A slit-lamp examination evaluates the anterior chamber for inflammatory cells and flare. The other listed tests do not assess the suspected ocular complication.

stem: An 82-year-old woman with chronic dementia dies suddenly of an apparent myocardial infarction. Before death, neurologic examination showed no abnormalities except deficits in cognition and memory. At autopsy, the brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy with relative sparing of primary motor and sensory areas. Which finding is most likely on microscopic examination of brain tissue?
explanation: Progressive memory and cognitive impairment with diffuse association-cortex atrophy is characteristic of Alzheimer disease. Microscopy shows extracellular β-amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles made of hyperphosphorylated tau; therefore E is correct. Lewy bodies and loss of pigmented substantia nigra neurons point to Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia, while caudate degeneration is associated with Huntington disease. Central chromatolysis is a neuronal response to axonal injury.

stem: A 25-year-old man who is a farmer is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of respiratory distress. After work he began to feel sweaty and dizzy. His pulse is 48/min and blood pressure is 110/72 mm Hg. He appears agitated, is drooling and gasping for air, and his pupils are 2 mm and constrict to light. The toxin to which he was most likely exposed directly interferes with which of the following?
explanation: Miosis, bradycardia, sweating, drooling, and respiratory distress after farm work indicate organophosphate poisoning. Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing acetylcholine accumulation and excessive muscarinic and nicotinic activity. Atropine treats muscarinic manifestations; pralidoxime can reactivate acetylcholinesterase before the enzyme-organophosphate complex ages. The toxin acts on the enzyme, not directly on cholinergic receptors.

stem: A 56-year-old man was treated with chemotherapy for a brain tumor. His hemoglobin at the end of chemotherapy was 12.1 g/dL and hematocrit was 35%. Erythropoietin is started; one month later, his hematocrit is 60%. Renal blood flow is unchanged at approximately 1000 mL/min, blood pressure is 125/80 mm Hg, and there is no proteinuria. His glomerular filtration rate has decreased from 50 L/day to 42 L/day. Which is the most likely cause of the decreased GFR?

options.text: Decreased hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule

explanation: Renal plasma flow equals renal blood flow multiplied by (1 − hematocrit). With renal blood flow unchanged, the rise in hematocrit from 35% to 60% lowers plasma flow from about 650 to 400 mL/min. Less plasma water is filtered along the glomerular capillary, so protein concentration and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure rise more steeply. Oncotic pressure opposes filtration, lowering net filtration pressure and GFR; therefore E is correct.

choice_explanations.A: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is one term in the filtration-pressure equation.
choice_explanations.B: Lower capillary oncotic pressure would reduce opposition to filtration.
choice_explanations.C: Bowman-space hydrostatic pressure is a term opposing filtration.
choice_explanations.D: Higher glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure favors filtration.
choice_explanations.E: Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure opposes filtration and lowers GFR when increased.

stem: During an investigational study, 20 male experimental animals are orchiectomized. After 2 weeks of recovery, the effects of castration on hormone secretion are evaluated. The animals are otherwise normal and no experimental disease modifications have been made. Changes in hormone secretion will most likely include which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This question tests the concept of surgical castration. Through orchiectomy, the testicle is unable to respond to LH secretion by the pituitary to produce testosterone and levels of LH will increase. This is actually a treatment for advanced prostate cancer. By surgically removing the testicles, the production of testosterone is inhibited, which will cause regression of hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. In such patients, a successful response to treatment is achieved by having castrate levels of testosterone in the blood (less than 50 mg/dL) and high levels of LH. The same effect can be achieved with LHRH agonist-antagonist agents such as leuprolide.

Castration drastically decreases testosterone levels, removing the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. This is an important treatment for advanced prostate cancer. Consequently, GnRH and pituitary LH and FSH levels will increase.

Decreased prolactin (choice B) would not be an effect of decreased testosterone. The effect of prolactin on male reproduction is not well understood, but it is well known that hyperprolactinemia inhibits gonadotropin secretion and action. Therefore, elevated prolactin acts to decrease testicular steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis, and results in infertility and impotence. Increased activin (choice C) and increased inhibin (choice D) are incorrect, because both of these hormones are made in the testes. Therefore, castration would decrease these hormones.

choice_explanations.A: The testis feedback diagram links GnRH to pituitary gonadotropins; loss of gonadal feedback raises rather than suppresses GnRH.
choice_explanations.B: 该选项（Decreased prolactin）不是本题最佳解释。Orchiectomy removes the testes, sharply reducing testosterone and testicular inhibin. Loss of testosterone's negative feedback increases hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary LH (and FSH). Thus increased LH is expected. Inhibin and activin are testicular products and do not increase after removal of the testes; prolactin is not expected to decrease.

stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine physical examination. He has no significant medical history but has been under stress related to graduate-school examinations. Examination shows mild scleral icterus. Total bilirubin is 1.7 mg/dL and direct bilirubin is 0.2 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Gilbert syndrome is a relatively common hereditary condition that is so mild that a case can be made for classifying it as a normal variant rather than a true disease. It occurs due to a genetic defect in bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT). The jaundice is related to stress, fasting, or infection. It produces asymptomatic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It is important to know about this disease to avoid unnecessary diagnostic procedures. On the wards, look for classmates and residents who appear slightly jaundiced!

Note that the unconjugated bilirubin is not given; rather, it must be quickly recognized as elevated by inferring from the given labs. Total bilirubin = conjugated (direct) bilirubin + unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. If the total bilirubin is elevated and conjugated bilirubin is normal, then the unconjugated bilirubin is elevated. Recall that unconjugated bilirubin is a product of heme metabolism and is elevated in conditions of hemolysis as well.

Crigler-Najjar syndrome (choice A) represents several hereditary diseases characterized by severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Type I has absent UDP-glucuronyltransferase activity and is fatal due to kernicterus (bilirubin accumulation in the brain). Type II has markedly decreased UDP-glucuronyltransferase activity. It is usually diagnosed in newborns.

Dubin-Johnson (choice B) and Rotor (choice D) syndromes are relatively mild hereditary conjugated hyperbilirubinemias. These are both defects in the excretion of conjugated bilirubin. Dubin-Johnson patients have black pigment in their hepatocytes, and thus their livers appear black. In Rotor syndrome, there is no black pigment, and thus the liver appears normal.

Wilson disease (choice E) is a serious disorder of copper metabolism associated with hepatic cirrhosis, movement disorder, and pathognomonic gold-colored rings (Kayser-Fleischer rings) in the iris. Diagnosis is based on reduced serum ceruloplasmin (a copper-binding protein), increased hepatic copper content, and increased urinary copper excretion.

choice_explanations.C: Correct: Gilbert syndrome is a benign inherited reduction in bilirubin conjugation due to decreased UGT activity. It causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that may become apparent with stress, fasting, or illness. A normal direct bilirubin with a mildly increased total bilirubin supports this diagnosis.

stem: A 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis is brought to the physician because of indigestion and abdominal pain, especially after fatty meals. For several years she has had bulky, greasy stools that float on the water. Serum amylase, lactase, and trypsinogen are elevated. Which of the following best explains these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Pancreatitis is an inflammation of the pancreas. The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes into the small intestine that are essential in the digestion of fats, proteins, and carbohydrates. Reduced secretion of fluid into the pancreatic ducts in cystic fibrosis causes these digestive enzymes to accumulate in the ducts. The digestive enzymes then become activated in the pancreatic ducts (which typically would not occur) and can begin to “digest” the pancreas, leading to inflammation and myriad other problems (gallstones, cysts, and internal bleeding).

Enterokinase (choice A) is located at the brush border of intestinal enterocytes, where it normally activates trypsin from its precursor, trypsinogen.

Trypsin inhibitor (choice B) is normally present in the pancreatic ducts, where it prevents trypsin from being activated and thus prevents autodigestion of the pancreas. When the ducts are blocked in cystic fibrosis, the available trypsin inhibitor is insufficient to prevent trypsin from being activated.

Excessive secretion of CCK (choice D) does not occur in cystic fibrosis.

Gallstone obstruction (choice E) can lead to pancreatitis (by autodigestion) when the obstruction prevents pancreatic juice from entering the intestine, but this is unrelated to cystic fibrosis.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a 15-year history of ulcerative colitis is admitted with jaundice. Ultrasound shows no gallstones, and liver biopsy shows concentric periductal fibrosis. Which finding is most likely on ERCP?

options.text: Aftemating constriction and dilatation of intrahepatic bile ducts.
Markedly dilated common bile duct containing irregular radiolucent masses
Mass at the ampulla of Vater
Moderately dilated intrahepatic bile ducts and stricture in the bile duct at the porta hepatis
Severely diated biiary tree terminating in a blunt, nipple-Iike obstruction at the lower end of the common bile duct

explanation:
The correct answer is A. The most likely diagnosis is primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), a disease characterized by progressive inflammation (cholangitis), fibrosis (sclerosing), and stricturing of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Up to 90% of patients with PSC have ulcerative colitis, suggesting an autoimmune process is involved in this disease. As scarring increases, the ducts become blocked, leading to biliary cirrhosis and liver failure.

The most important imaging study is endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). The alternating strictures and dilatations of the bile ducts appear as “beaded” or “pearls on a string” on ERCP. The most common histologic feature is concentric periductal fibrosis (onion-skin fibrosis). Serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) levels are elevated.

Gallstones in the biliary tree produce irregular radiolucent masses (choice B). Choledocholithiasis and cholelithiasis due to cholesterol and/or pigment stones may be present in up to a third of patients with PSC. Ultrasound studies showed no gallstones in this patient.

Choices C, D, and E all involve masses that might obstruct the biliary system, but would not produce the characteristic concentric periductal fibrosis, nor are they strongly associated with ulcerative colitis. Choice C describes the findings associated with carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater. Choice D describes the findings associated with carcinoma of the extrahepatic bile ducts. Choice E describes the findings associated with carcinoma of the pancreas.

stem: A 44-year-old man has multiple intractable duodenal ulcers, markedly increased basal acid output, a 2-cm mass in the pancreatic head, and persistently elevated serum gastrin. Which additional finding is most likely?

options.text: Arise in serum gastrin during somatostatin infusion
HCI secretion increasing excessively after a test meal
Parietal cell hyperplasia in the body of the stomach

explanation:
The correct answer is D. The patient has Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES), in which a duodenal or pancreatic gastrin-secreting endocrine tumor causes hypersecretion of gastric acid. Gastrin is a peptide hormone secreted by G cells located in the pyloric antrum and in the duodenum that stimulates gastric acid secretion by parietal cells (oxyntic cells).

Gastrin is normally released in response to stomach antrum distension or to the presence of amino acids in the stomach. Gastrin release by G cells is normally subject to negative feedback by local somatostatin release from D cells (paracrine signaling). The gastrinomas that cause ZES are typically pancreatic and thus are not subject to this feedback regulation. Gastrin is secreted and circulates continually at high levels as a result, stimulating acid release in amounts that overwhelm the buffering capacity of the duodenum and typically causing one or more ulcers (gastric ulcers are less common because the stomach, unlike the duodenum, has a protective barrier). Chronic increases in circulating gastrin also have a trophic effect on parietal cells, resulting in parietal cell hyperplasia.

One of the peculiarities of gastrinomas is that secretin strongly stimulates gastrin release. Secretin normally stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and inhibits gastric acid production by parietal cells. The secretin stimulation test is used to differentiate between gastrinomas and other causes of increased gastrin secretion.

Somatostatin infusion (choice A) would not increase gastrin secretion, but rather would suppress G cells in the stomach and duodenum.

In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, HCl secretion (choice B) does not increase in response to a test meal because normal stomach gastrin secretion has been suppressed by the excessive gastric acid. The basal level of HCl is high, but it does not increase appropriately after a meal; certainly there is not an excessive response.

Helicobacter pylori infection (choice C) is a leading cause of gastric ulcers. The stomach is endowed with a protective barrier (a thick layer of viscous, bicarbonate-infused mucus) that shields the mucosa against acid, even when acid production is elevated, so gastric ulcers are far less common in ZES than duodenal ulcers. H. pylori erodes this barrier and exposes the mucosa to gastric acid and peptidase, resulting in an ulcer.

Serum antibodies to intrinsic factor (choice E), a product of parietal cells, would result in pernicious anemia, not uncontrolled gastrin secretion.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a 30-year history of alcoholism has scleral icterus, pitting leg edema, and shifting dullness to percussion. A decrease in which of the following is the most likely cause of his edema and ascites?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. The history and physical examination strongly suggest alcoholic liver disease. The plasma colloid osmotic pressure is often low in alcoholic persons with chronic liver disease (cirrhosis). The diseased liver cannot produce adequate amounts of albumin, which leads to a decrease in the concentration of albumin in the plasma, i.e., hypoalbuminemia. Because about 75% of the plasma colloid osmotic pressure can be attributed to the presence of albumin in the plasma, the decrease in plasma albumin concentration that occurs in the latter stages of cirrhosis often leads to peripheral edema.

Cirrhosis also causes excess fluid to accumulate in the peritoneal cavity as ascites. In the case of ascites, the edema results not only from hypoalbuminemia but also from portal vein obstruction (which increases capillary hydrostatic pressure) as well as from obstruction of lymphatic drainage of the liver. In fact, ascites is observed more often than peripheral edema in liver disease.

A decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure (choice A) would tend to decrease fluid loss from the capillaries, and thereby oppose the development of edema.

A decrease in the colloid osmotic pressure of the interstitial fluid (choice B) would decrease fluid loss from the capillaries, thereby opposing the development of edema.

A decrease in interstitial hydrostatic pressure (choice C) would tend to increase fluid loss from the capillaries, but this cannot be considered a primary cause of edema because the interstitial hydrostatic pressure actually increases when a tissue becomes edematous.

A decrease in precapillary arteriolar resistance (choice E), which means arteriolar dilation, would increase capillary hydrostatic pressure and tend to cause edema. However, decreased precapillary arteriolar resistance in the peripheral vasculature is not associated with cirrhosis.

ReKaps: Cirrhotic patients have decreased albumin production. Colloid osmotic pressure is dependent on proteins; therefore, these patients have decreased oncotic pressure, which can cause edema.

choice_explanations.B: This alternative does not account for the key pattern: cirrhosis with reduced hepatic albumin synthesis and low plasma oncotic pressure. The best fit is D (Plasma colloid osmotic pressure), which explains that finding.
choice_explanations.C: This alternative does not account for the key pattern: cirrhosis with reduced hepatic albumin synthesis and low plasma oncotic pressure. The best fit is D (Plasma colloid osmotic pressure), which explains that finding.

stem: A 5-week-old infant has 2 days of persistent nonbilious vomiting after each feed. He is irritable, mildly dehydrated, and has delayed capillary refill. Laboratory findings show hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. What is the next best diagnostic step?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. The infant is presenting with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is characterized by hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, which may lead to gastric outlet obstruction. Infants with pyloric stenosis present with forceful, nonbilious emesis. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency that warrants correction of hydration status and electrolyte abnormalities before surgical intervention (choice C). Electrolyte abnormalities characteristic of pyloric stenosis are hypokalemia, hypochloremia, and metabolic alkalosis, as demonstrated in this patient by low potassium, low chloride, and elevated bicarbonate. The metabolic alkalosis is caused by both loss of HCl in gastric acid and contraction alkalosis. Due to decreased blood volume as a result of dehydration, production of angiotensin II increases. Angiotensin II causes increased Na⁺/H⁺ exchange in the proximal tubule and increased HCO₃⁻ reabsorption in the proximal tubule, leading to metabolic alkalosis. Potassium loss occurs from aldosterone release, which increases urinary potassium loss. Diagnosis of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is made by abdominal ultrasound demonstrating increased pyloric muscle width and length.

CT scan of the abdomen (choice B) is not the preferred method of diagnosis because of unnecessary radiation exposure.

KUB (choice D) may show gaseous distension in the stomach with paucity of gas distally, but it is not diagnostic. It cannot demonstrate hypertrophy of the pylorus and therefore cannot definitively rule in pyloric stenosis.

Stool studies (choice E) would not be useful in a patient without diarrhea or concern for an infectious etiology of the vomiting.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has generalized pruritus and mild jaundice. Laboratory studies show increased conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Liver biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation centered on small portal bile ducts without cirrhosis. Which finding is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Primary biliary cirrhosis is characterized by chronic granulomatous inflammation leading to destruction of medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts. A cholestatic picture develops, with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and increased alkaline phosphatase. Itching is due to elevated levels of circulating bile salts. The disease predominantly affects middle-aged women and progresses to cirrhosis. Ninety percent of patients have circulating antimitochondrial autoantibodies, which may play a pathogenic role. Patients can also present with fatigue, xanthelasmas, xanthomas, and high total cholesterol. However, they are not at increased risk for atherosclerosis.

Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (AATD, choice A) is a genetic disease of decreased alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT). AAT is an antiprotease that normally protects against excess neutrophil elastase-mediated alveolar destruction. AATD results in emphysema, even in the absence of smoking. The Pi (SERPINA1) gene is highly pleomorphic, but homozygous Z alleles (PiZZ) result in AAT that polymerizes and builds up within the endoplasmic reticulum. This is thought to lead to hepatocyte destruction, chronic liver failure, and subsequently the typical sequelae of cirrhosis. PiZZ is the most common form of AATD.

Decreased serum ceruloplasmin (choice C) suggests Wilson disease, an inherited condition characterized by accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, heart, and eye (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Increases in hepatic copper content and urinary copper excretion are diagnostically important findings.

Elevated hematocrit (choice D) increases blood viscosity and slows blood flow through vessels. Thus, one complication of elevated hematocrit is Budd-Chiari syndrome, in which a thrombus in the inferior vena cava and/or hepatic vein obstructs the venous outflow of the liver.

Elevated serum iron (choice E) is seen with hemochromatosis, hereditary or acquired. The hereditary form is a heterogeneous autosomal recessive disorder associated with the HFE gene on chromosome 6. Acquired hemochromatosis can be dietary (ingestion of iron supplements) or from chronic blood transfusions in patients with sickle cell disease and thalassemia.

Hypoalbuminemia (choice F) is caused by liver failure of any etiology and results from decreased hepatocyte protein synthesis.

Prolonged prothrombin time (choice G) is also an effect of liver failure from any cause. Coagulopathy is attributable to impaired synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.

ReKaps: Primary biliary cirrhosis typically presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and increased alkaline phosphatase. Microscopically, chronic granulomatous inflammation around medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts is seen. Primary biliary cirrhosis is strongly associated with antimitochondrial antibodies.

stem: A 30-year-old man has fever and night sweats. CT shows mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy and multiple liver lesions. Lymph-node biopsy shows a nodular pattern with small cleaved lymphocytes. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most likely associated with this disease?

options.text: Kappa immuncglobulin light chain and myc

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The lymphoma described in the question stem is follicular B-cell lymphoma, and its characteristic reciprocal translocation is t(14;18)(q32;q21). The site on chromosome 14 involves the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus (IgH), while that on chromosome 18 involves the BCL-2 oncogene. The translocation produces a hybrid BCL-2/immunoglobulin heavy-chain transcript. BCL-2 inhibits apoptosis, so this translocation promotes cell proliferation. The translocation t(18;14), which forms the hybrid Ig heavy-chain (14)/BCL-2 (18) transcript, is characteristic of follicular B-cell lymphoma.

Translocations occur when chromosomes are broken and the broken elements reattach to other chromosomes. They can be classified into two major types: reciprocal and Robertsonian. Reciprocal translocations occur when genetic material is exchanged between nonhomologous chromosomes. Reciprocal translocations can occur in gametogenesis due to errors in meiosis, or during cellular division of somatic cells due to errors in mitosis. The latter type can lead to the formation of cancers by altering the genetic code controlling cellular proliferation. More than 100 different chromosome rearrangements involving nearly every chromosome have been observed in more than 40 types of cancer. An example of a reciprocal translocation is shown below.

Robertsonian translocations only occur in the acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, and 22) and involve the loss of the short arms of two of the chromosomes and subsequent fusion of the long arms. An example is a cause of Down syndrome, in which the mother carries the Robertsonian translocation and can have more than one child with trisomy 21.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction and epistaxis. He has no hematuria or gastrointestinal bleeding. PTT is 42 seconds, PT is 13 seconds, and bleeding time is 11 minutes. Which function is most likely abnormal?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is an autosomal-dominant bleeding disorder caused by either a deficiency or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a multimeric protein required for platelet adhesion by binding to platelet GPIb. vWF is normally produced by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. Abnormal vWF causes a defect in the initial adhesion of normal platelets to a damaged vessel wall. vWF also carries factor VIII in the blood, so factor VIII levels are consequently low and the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. Defects in platelet adhesion are also seen in Bernard-Soulier disease, which is caused by deficiency of the GPIb platelet receptor.

Clinical features include spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes, prolonged bleeding from wounds, and menorrhagia in young females; bleeding into joints is uncommon. Laboratory studies show a normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time (indicating platelet pathology), normal PT, and often a prolonged PTT (indicating an intrinsic pathway defect). An abnormal platelet aggregation response to ristocetin is an important diagnostic test. Ristocetin will only cause platelet agglutination in the presence of vWF, so if it is added to blood without vWF, aggregation will not occur. Treatment is with desmopressin (DDAVP) in type 1 vWD (deficiency of vWF), which releases vWF from Weibel-Palade bodies of endothelial cells. This patient's increased bleeding time, prolonged PTT, and spontaneous, prolonged bleeding lead to the diagnosis of vWD.

Abnormal platelet morphology (choice B) is not seen in vWD, but may be observed with infiltration of the bone marrow by tumor or fibrosis, after splenectomy, and even with platelet granule disorder (grey platelet syndrome). Platelet dysfunction would cause prolonged bleeding time, but would not cause the prolonged thromboplastin time seen in this patient. Defects in primary platelet aggregation (choice C) are seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which is caused by a deficiency or defect in the glycoprotein GPIIb-IIIa complex. A prolonged bleeding time would be seen, but this would not cause the prolonged thromboplastin time. Defects in release of platelet vesicles (choice D) or secondary aggregation (choice E) are seen in storage pool disease and aspirin use. These conditions would cause a prolonged bleeding time, but neither would cause the prolonged thromboplastin time.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has fever, headache, confusion, jaundice, purpura, bleeding gums, dark urine, and oliguria. Laboratory studies show thrombocytopenia and hemolysis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a rare disorder. It is frequently seen in women and is characterized by a pentad: thrombocytopenia with purpura, fever, neurologic symptoms (altered mental status), microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and acute renal failure. Thrombocytopenia causes bruising, purpura, and prolonged bleeding time. Elevated indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and schistocytes in the blood smear are characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Microthrombi occur within organs, causing renal dysfunction and neurologic symptoms. Treatment is with plasmapheresis (exchange of the patient's plasma with normal plasma) to remove ultralarge von Willebrand factor (ULVWF).

The pathophysiology of TTP is becoming increasingly well understood. Idiopathic cases are due to a defect or deficiency of a metalloprotease that cleaves ULVWF, ADAMTS13. In the vast majority of TTP cases, the functional deficiency in ADAMTS13 is due to antibodies directed against the enzyme. In 5–10% of cases, a genetic-based enzyme deficiency (known as Upshaw-Schulman syndrome) is present. Formation of thrombi composed of uncleaved ULVWF multimers combines with platelets from the circulation without stimulation of the clotting cascade, hence the normal PT and PTT. Secondary cases are due to underlying conditions such as HIV, immunosuppression, cancers, pregnancy, or medications (hormone replacement therapy, immunosuppressants, platelet aggregation inhibitors, antivirals, etc.). In secondary cases, ADAMTS13 is not depressed, and endothelial damage is thought to be the underlying mechanism.

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (choice A) can cause anemia and an elevated indirect bilirubin, but generally produces only mild symptoms, is not associated with thrombocytopenia, and does not cause fragmentation of red blood cells on the peripheral smear. The negative Coombs test argues against an immune-mediated hemolytic anemia. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC; choice B) can be differentiated from TTP by abnormal coagulation tests. In DIC, microangiopathic hemolysis (schistocytes) is present, but PT and PTT are prolonged, fibrinogen levels are reduced, and fibrin split products are elevated.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS; choice C) and TTP are considered manifestations of the same pathogenetic spectrum. However, HUS is mainly seen in children and is associated with enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 verotoxin or Shiga toxin. Children who eat contaminated foods (e.g., hamburgers) present subsequently (5–10 days) with HUS: thrombocytopenia, bruising, purpura, acute renal failure, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. The vascular bed of the central nervous system is not involved in HUS; thus, mental-status changes are not part of its clinical picture. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP; choice D) is an immune disorder caused by autoantibodies to platelet antigens. Systemic illness is not present in ITP, which is characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia without other hematologic abnormalities. There are acute and chronic forms. The acute form is commonly seen in children, is treated with IV immunoglobulin, and has few sequelae. The chronic form is seen in adults, has an autoimmune basis, and can be treated with splenectomy. Ten percent of cases manifest in association with autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Evans syndrome).

stem: A 35-year-old woman has easy bruising and petechiae. CBC shows leukocytes 10,200/mm³, erythrocytes 4.5 million/mm³, hemoglobin 13 g/dL, and platelets 23,000/mm³; creatinine and urea nitrogen are normal. The peripheral smear shows a few large, young platelets, and bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytes. Which condition best explains these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This clinical scenario is most consistent with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), which is an immune-mediated destruction of platelets by the spleen. Antibodies to platelet receptors (GP Ib or GPIIb/IIIa) are formed. There are 2 types of ITP: acute and chronic. The acute form is seen in children and young adults, is preceded by a viral infection, and is self-limited. The chronic type is seen in female adults and may require intravenous immune globulin (IVIG; prevents the spleen from recognizing platelets and platelet destruction), corticosteroid, or splenectomy as therapy. The peripheral smear and bone marrow show the features described. Immature giant platelets and increased megakaryocytes are compensatory mechanisms in the bone marrow in response to the increased platelet destruction. Decreased platelets and normal red blood cells on peripheral smear help establish this diagnosis.

In both Glanzmann thrombasthenia (choice A) and von Willebrand disease (choice F), the platelet count will be normal. Platelet aggregation will be impaired with Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while platelet adhesion will be impaired with von Willebrand disease.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (choice B; HUS) is usually associated with exposure to enterohemorrhagic, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 infection. Shigella, Campylobacter, and viruses (HIV, Coxsackie virus, Echovirus) may also cause this condition. Patients (most commonly children) may have eaten contaminated foods (e.g., hamburgers). Patients present with fever, bloody diarrhea, and subsequent (2–7 days afterwards) thrombocytopenia, bruising, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and acute renal failure (oliguria, elevated renal function tests). Patients may also have irritability, lethargy, and seizures. Histologic changes in the renal glomeruli show presence of microthrombi. Peripheral blood smear reveals decreased platelets and schistocytes.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 37 weeks develops severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding from placental abruption. After emergency cesarean delivery, she develops dyspnea, cyanosis, and diffuse wound bleeding. Platelets are 76,000/mm³, PT 30 seconds, PTT 56 seconds, fibrinogen is decreased, and D-dimer is elevated. Which factor best accounts for the bleeding disorder?

The correct answer is D. The patient most likely experienced placental abruption. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), or consumptive coagulopathy, develops when blood is exposed to large amounts of tissue factor over a brief period of time, with massive generation of thrombin, resulting in the acute triggering of coagulation. DIC is seen in more than 50% of cases of amniotic fluid embolism and abruptio placentae.

The human decidua is immensely abundant in tissue factor, which is the primary initiator of the clotting cascade through thrombin generation. Clinically, there is profound systemic bleeding. Thromboembolism and dysfunction of the kidney, liver, lungs, and central nervous system often develop because of widespread intravascular fibrin deposition. Diagnosis of DIC is confirmed by laboratory studies that reveal decreased platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, decreased fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin degradation products (FDPs) and D-dimers.

The figure shows the coagulation pathway; the extrinsic clotting pathway begins with release of tissue factor after tissue injury.

Symptoms relate to both thrombotic and hemorrhagic events. DIC is distinct from TTP, which results from primary platelet activation instead of tissue-factor exposure. Laboratory studies show decreased platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, decreased fibrinogen, and elevated fibrin degradation products (FDPs) and D-dimers.

stem: A 26-year-old primigravid woman at 37 weeks has placental abruption and undergoes cesarean delivery with multiple transfusions. On hospital day 3 she develops confusion, hypoxemia, petechiae, purpura, bilateral rales, and red-tinged oliguria. Which laboratory tests are the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bleeding time, partial thromboplastin time. and von Willebrand factor levels.
Partial thromboplastin time and factor Vill levels
Partial thromboplastin time and factor Xl levels
Platelet count and platelet aggregation studies with ADP and epinephrine
Platelet count, prothrombin time, and fibrin degradation products

explanation:
The correct answer is E. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is characterized by consumption of platelets, fibrinogen, and clotting factors, bleeding, and organ dysfunction. The best tests to order are platelet count (which will be markedly decreased), prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time (PT/PTT; which will be prolonged), serum fibrinogen level (which will be low), and fibrin degradation products (which will be high).

Causes of DIC include sepsis, trauma, obstetrical complications (placental abruption, as in this patient), acute pancreatitis, malignancy (adenocarcinoma, acute promyelocytic leukemia), nephrotic syndrome, and incompatible transfusion reactions ("STOP Making New Thrombi"). The common underlying mechanism for DIC is endothelial cell damage, which triggers release of tissue factor and stimulation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in consumption of platelets, clotting factors, and fibrinogen as microthrombi form. Concurrent stimulation of the fibrinolytic system occurs to break down clots, resulting in elevated levels of fibrin degradation products, fibrin split products, and D-dimers. This sequence becomes a vicious cycle, which does not stop, and the body cannot adequately produce and replenish clotting factors, platelets, and fibrinogen. Clinically, patients will clot first, then bleed (venipuncture sites, mouth, skin, bladder). Organ dysfunction occurs in the brain (altered mental state), lungs (dyspnea), liver (elevated liver enzymes, jaundice), and kidneys (oliguria, elevated creatinine/urea nitrogen). Schistocytes are present in the peripheral blood smear, reflecting red blood cell damage as cells pass through microthrombi in the circulation (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia).

Treatment is removal of the underlying cause. In this case, IV fluid administration, blood transfusion, fetal monitoring, removal of the placental abruption, delivery via cesarean section, and postpartum care are considered. Administration of platelets and fresh frozen plasma may be needed; this is a sensitive balance since both will try to prevent bleeding but will create more clots. It is assumed that this patient received compatible blood transfusion.

Bleeding time, partial thromboplastin time, and von Willebrand factor levels (choice A) reflect von Willebrand disease, a common autosomal dominant inherited bleeding disorder. Bleeding time and PTT will be prolonged. PTT is prolonged because von Willebrand factor promotes the half-life of clotting factor VIII. Patients present with bleeding after trauma or surgical procedures. It is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi formation, or organ dysfunction.

Partial thromboplastin time and factor VIII levels (choice B) reflect hemophilia A, an X-linked inherited bleeding disorder that presents with hemarthrosis, purpura, and ecchymosis. Clotting factor VIII is present in the intrinsic coagulation cascade pathway. A deficiency is reflected by prolonged PTT. It is not associated with placental abruption, microthrombi formation, or organ dysfunction.

Partial thromboplastin time and factor XII levels (choice C) reflect factor XII (Hageman factor) deficiency. Clotting factor XII is present in the intrinsic coagulation cascade pathway. A deficiency is reflected by prolonged PTT. Patients are usually asymptomatic, but some may present with paradoxical thromboembolism. Spontaneous miscarriages may occur in pregnancy.

Platelet count and platelet aggregation studies with ADP and epinephrine (choice D) reflect platelet aggregation disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a dysfunction or deficiency of platelet receptor glycoprotein IIb/IIIa. Patients would have a normal platelet count and an abnormal platelet aggregation study with ADP and epinephrine (platelet agonists for platelet aggregation). The glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor binds to fibrinogen for platelet aggregation.

stem: A 32-year-old woman undergoes mastectomy for breast cancer. The muscle deep to the breast is involved and removed. Which function is most likely impaired?

options.text: Abduction of the humerus at the shoulder
Adduction of the humerus at the shoulder
External rotation of the humerus at the shoulder

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The muscle deep to the breast is the pectoralis major. Breast cancer can invade this muscle, but usually does not because the relatively thick deep fascial layer serves as a barrier. Formerly, the pectoralis major was removed during radical mastectomy, leaving the patient with a major loss of function of the adjacent arm. The modified radical mastectomy, now more frequently used, spares the pectoralis major. The major actions of the muscle, which attaches to the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus, are to adduct and internally rotate the humerus at the shoulder.

The deltoid muscle and the supraspinatus muscle act to abduct the humerus at the shoulder (choice A). External rotation of the humerus at the shoulder (choice C) is performed by the infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid muscles. stem: A 28-year-old woman has 2 days of acute, painful, warm, erythematous right-knee swelling, fever, and limited motion without trauma. Which history would most support the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. A monoarticular arthritis with an acute onset should raise the suspicion of an acute infectious arthritis. The presence of fever, pain with weight-bearing, and limited range of motion, as well as the acuity of onset, all increase the likelihood of septic arthritis over non-infectious causes. In this regard, the major differential diagnosis is between Staphylococcus and gonococcus. The gonococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is usually obtained through unprotected sexual contact and is now the most common cause of bacterial arthritis in adults. Septic arthritis can generally be divided into gonococcal and nongonococcal arthritis. N. gonorrhoeae appears as gram-negative diplococci found within white blood cells. The organism spreads from infected mucosal surfaces to joints, with the small joints of the hands, wrists, knees, and ankles the most commonly affected. Involvement of the axial skeleton is uncommon. Patients with gonococcal arthritis may have features of a disseminated gonococcal infection with a 5- to 7-day history of fever and shaking chills. Various skin lesions may also be present, including petechiae, papules, pustules, hemorrhagic bullae, and necrotic lesions. A history of migratory arthralgias and tenosynovitis may be present.

Rheumatoid arthritis (choice A) rarely manifests with a monoarticular arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is a progressive form of arthritis that is most common in women 20 to 60 years old. It is an autoimmune reaction with circulating rheumatoid factor antibodies. Although bacterial gastroenteritis (choice B) does not cause monoarticular arthritis, it may cause reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome). Drinking alcohol (choice C) can predispose to gouty arthritis, which often affects the great toe but can also affect the knee joints. Gout typically affects individuals from 30–60 years of age and would be unusual in a woman this young. Hepatitis B (choice D) may be associated with a serum sickness-like illness that affects multiple joints with arthralgias.

stem: A 43-year-old man has difficulty raising his right arm after a heavy object struck his shoulder. The medial border of the scapula protrudes when he presses his hands against a wall. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle. This nerve is derived from branches of the anterior rami of C5, C6, and C7. Paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle weakens upward rotation of the scapula, which is needed for full abduction or flexion at the shoulder. Weakness of this muscle also results in “winged scapula,” in which the medial border of the scapula is pushed away from the chest wall. A downward blow on the shoulder may result in stretching of this nerve. Another common mechanism of injury is damage during axillary surgery, such as during a mastectomy. The long thoracic nerve lies on the medial wall of the axilla.

The axillary nerve (choice A) innervates the teres minor and deltoid muscles. Paralysis of the deltoid will cause weakness in abduction but will not cause a winged scapula. The teres minor is an external rotator of the shoulder. The axillary nerve is a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and is subject to injury from a dislocation of the glenohumeral joint or a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. The dorsal scapular nerve (choice B) innervates the rhomboideus major and rhomboideus minor muscles. These muscles retract the scapula. Their paralysis might cause minor winging of the scapula but will not affect abduction or flexion at the shoulder. The dorsal scapular nerve is a branch of the C5 anterior ramus. The suprascapular nerve (choice D) innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The supraspinatus is used during abduction and the infraspinatus is an external rotator of the shoulder. The suprascapular nerve is a branch of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and contains nerve fibers from the C5 and C6 anterior rami. The thoracodorsal nerve (choice E) innervates the latissimus dorsi muscle, which is an extensor and an internal rotator at the shoulder. The thoracodorsal nerve is a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and contains nerve fibers from the C6, C7, and C8 anterior rami.

stem: A 51-year-old supermarket cashier has weakness and numbness of the right hand, sensory loss over the palmar thumb and first two digits, and thenar atrophy. Which additional muscle is supplied by the affected nerve?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The nerve is the median nerve, which can be damaged by repetitive minor trauma (e.g., typing or using a cash register) as it passes under the flexor retinaculum. Inflammation of the synovial tendon sheaths of the digital flexors causes tissue swelling within the carpal tunnel, producing carpal tunnel syndrome and compressing the nerve. The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb and adjacent two-and-one-half fingers. Prior to entering the carpal tunnel, it supplies motor function to all of the anterior forearm muscles except the flexor carpi ulnaris (supplied by the ulnar nerve) and one-half of the flexor digitorum profundus (supplied by the ulnar nerve). Distal to the carpal tunnel, the median nerve also supplies the thenar muscles and the first and second lumbricals. Note: Palm sensation is not affected by carpal tunnel syndrome; the superficial palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the carpal tunnel.

The abductor pollicis longus (choice A) and the extensor pollicis brevis (choice C) are in the forearm and are supplied by the radial nerve. The adductor pollicis (choice B) and the first dorsal interosseous (choice D) are supplied by the ulnar nerve. The adductor pollicis functions to adduct the thumb, and the first dorsal interosseous functions to abduct the index finger. The extensor pollicis brevis (choice C) is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve, which is a branch of the radial nerve. It causes extension of the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint.

stem: Two 23-year-old identical twins train for different events: one runs marathons and the other sprints. At rest, which muscle characteristic is most likely greater in the marathon runner?

options.text: Little difference because they are identical twins.
The muscles of the marathon runner will have a greater concentration of glycogen
The muscles of the marathon runner will have a greater concentration of myoglobin.
The muscles of the marathon runner will have a greater diameter
The muscles of the marathon runner will have a greater number of fast-twitch fibers.

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Endurance conditioning (long-distance running) and strength conditioning (sprinting) have different effects on muscle. Two types of skeletal muscle fibers can be found in most human muscle tissues. These are called slow-twitch, or type I fibers, and fast-twitch, or type II fibers, and they differ in their anatomic structure, biochemistry, and physiologic functions. Although to some extent the proportion of these two fiber types is determined by genetics, the proportions can be altered by training.

Type I fibers: endurance- and posture-maintaining muscles; designed for endurance; more will develop in individuals training for long-distance running. Greater endurance implies resistance to fatigue, and resistance to fatigue requires a dependable supply of ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation is the most efficient way to produce ATP; as a consequence, type I fibers are designed to obtain the maximum amount of energy from oxidative phosphorylation. Thus, these fibers are particularly rich in mitochondria, the organelle in which oxidative phosphorylation occurs, and they also have a high level of myoglobin (choice C), which serves as an oxygen reservoir, supplying oxygen when a sufficient quantity cannot be obtained via the circulatory system. This myoglobin tints these fibers a deep red color. Type I fibers have less glycogen than type II fibers, smaller-diameter motor units and muscles, and more slow-response fibers.

Type II fibers: more will develop in individuals training for sprints; they fatigue more readily, do not have much myoglobin, and thus make up white muscle; they have a greater amount of glycogen, larger-diameter motor units and muscles, and more fast-response fibers.

Although the fact that they are identical twins (choice A) would determine the initial proportion of the two types of muscle, training will alter it. The person who trains for endurance will develop more type I muscle, whereas the person who trains for a short duration and rapid response will develop type II fibers.

The muscles of the twin who runs the 100-meter dash will have a greater concentration of glycogen (choice B). The immediate consequence of contraction is a decrease in ATP concentration and an increase in ADP and AMP concentrations. This will immediately stimulate glycogenolysis and glycolysis through a series of allosteric reactions and will not require a major input of oxygen from the circulatory system. Thus, ATP levels will be rapidly restored, permitting a fast response, but only for a limited time, because even though glycogen stores are greater than in type I fibers, they are still limited. Moreover, the resultant anaerobic glycolytic conditions will cause lactic acid to accumulate, resulting in pain and muscle fatigue.

Type I motor units are innervated by neurons that have a smaller diameter, and the muscle cells are smaller in diameter than muscles of strength-conditioned athletes. Endurance conditioning causes much less muscle hypertrophy than strength conditioning (sprinting), so muscle diameter (choice D) of the marathon-running twin would be smaller, rather than larger, in the endurance athlete.

Muscle plasticity allows alteration of muscle structure and function with exercise training. The type of exercise training affects the relative population of slow oxidative versus fast-twitch fibers. High-intensity, short-duration exercise favors hypertrophy of fast-glycolytic muscles. Endurance training increases the population and oxidative capacity of slow-response muscles. The muscles of the twin that runs the 100-meter dash will have a greater number of fast-twitch fibers (choice E).
