stem: A 24-year-old truck driver fractures the right humerus and cannot extend the wrist. He can flex the fingers but cannot make a tight fist. Which nerve was most likely injured?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The radial nerve lies in the musculospiral groove of the humerus and is subject to injury in association with a fracture of the midshaft of the humerus. The radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the forearm, including the muscles that extend the wrist; paralysis of these muscles results in a wrist drop. stem: A 3-year-old boy from a strictly vegan family has bilateral leg pain, abnormal gait, and bowed legs. Which bone change is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has the classic presentation of rickets, which is a childhood bone disorder characterized by poor mineralization of bone. Bone matrix consists of osteoid secreted by osteoblasts. This osteoid requires mineralization with calcium and phosphate to develop into mature bone.

When stores of these minerals are disrupted, as in vitamin D deficiency, either rickets or osteomalacia can occur. Rickets refers to mineralization deficiencies at the growth plate and can only occur while growth plates are open. Osteomalacia affects the rest of the bone and can occur at any age. In children, osteomalacia and rickets usually occur together, while in adults only osteomalacia occurs because growth plates are closed.

Hallmark signs of rickets include bow-legged deformities, chest wall deformities (pectus excavatum, pectus carinatum), bone pain, pathologic fractures, poor growth, and widened growth plates. Deposition of excess osteoid occurs in these patients as a compensatory mechanism for poor mineralization. Causes of rickets include dietary deficiency of vitamin D (as in vegans), dietary deficiency of calcium, issues with phosphate absorption (hypophosphatemic rickets), problems with vitamin D conversion to active metabolite (vitamin D-dependent rickets), or dysfunction of the vitamin D receptor (vitamin D-resistant rickets).

Laboratory findings in these patients are relatively nonspecific but can include increased alkaline phosphatase and decreased serum calcium and/or phosphate.

There are increased numbers of osteoblasts in rickets (compare with choice A), which lay down increased quantities of osteoid in an effort to strengthen the bone. Unfortunately, the increased osteoid is not mineralized and the bone remains soft and weak.

Osteoclast activity is normal in rickets. Unlike osteoblasts, osteoclasts break down and demineralize bone, releasing calcium and phosphate into the bloodstream. Osteoclast activity is dependent on both vitamin D and PTH. Deficiency of active vitamin D or defective vitamin D receptors limits osteoclastic activity. Increased osteoclast activity (choice C) is typical of hyperparathyroidism and Paget disease of bone because both PTH and vitamin D are present.

The bone marrow space is normal in rickets. The bone marrow is located in the interior bone space known as trabecular (or spongy) bone and is important for hematopoiesis. Marrow fibrosis (choice D) is more typical of hematopoietic disorders such as myeloproliferative syndrome with myelofibrosis, although hyperparathyroidism may also lead to bone marrow fibrosis.

Although poorly mineralized, the bony trabeculae are of normal abundance in rickets. Sparse trabeculae (choice E) are characteristic of osteoporosis. This may also give rise to bone deformation, pathologic fractures, and bowing of the legs.

stem: A 21-year-old man is bitten by a cat; the wound becomes inflamed, followed by fever and a tender popliteal lymph node. A bite at which site is most likely to drain to this node?

options.text: Lateral side ofthe dorsum of the foot

Medial side of the sole of the foot

explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient has cat scratch disease, which occurs as a result of a Bartonella henselae infection and is diagnosed with a Warthin-Starry stain. It can occur as a result of either a cat bite or a cat scratch. It typically presents with a primary cutaneous lesion within 3–10 days of primary injury before spreading to adjacent lymph nodes. The affected lymph nodes are usually tender and enlarged. There is also typically evidence of fever and sometimes there may be visceral organ involvement. Bartonella can also rarely produce hepatitis and affect the spleen, eye, or CNS.

Lymphatic drainage from skin of the lower limb generally follows the course of the superficial veins. Most of the venous drainage of the skin of the lower limb is to the great saphenous vein; the accompanying lymphatics drain into the superficial group of the inguinal lymph nodes. However, the skin drained by the small saphenous vein, including that of the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the foot, is an exception to this rule. Lymphatic fluid from this area drains into lymphatics accompanying the small saphenous vein, then drains into lymph nodes behind the knee in the popliteal fossa.

The lateral side of the thigh (choice B), the medial side of the leg below the knee (choice C), the medial side of the sole of the foot (choice D), and the medial side of the thigh (choice E) are all regions for which venous drainage is to the great saphenous vein and, therefore, the lymphatics from these regions all drain to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Superficial veins of the leg: the long saphenous vein drains and runs on the medial side of the leg and drains into inguinal lymph nodes; the short saphenous vein drains the lateral side of the dorsum of the foot and runs on the posterior side of the leg, and drains into lymph nodes in the popliteal fossa.

stem: A 46-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for hairy-cell leukemia has a very painful, warm, erythematous first toe and nodules on his ears. Which finding is most likely in joint fluid?

options.text: Large notched rectangular crystals with various birefringence
Mixed pleomorpnic crystals with various birefringence
Rnomboid crystals with weakly positive birefringence
pain in his large toe. He was recently diagnosed with hairy cell leukemia. He denies any trauma, but says that he has been exercising

explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has gout, which is characterized by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joint spaces and soft tissues. Patients often present with pain in the first toe (podagra). Late in the disease, patients may also present with tophi, most commonly found on the external ears. Tophi are the accumulation of the crystals in the soft tissues. Hyperuricemia leads to urate deposition. This can occur in several ways, secondary to enzyme deficiencies, lifestyle choice, or drug treatment, for example, chemotherapy drugs.

Our patient has leukemia and is undergoing treatment. Joint aspiration analysis with microscopy and polarization reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. In general, one needs to know two conditions that are associated with negative and positive birefringence (gout and pseudogout, respectively). “Negatively birefringent” refers to the crystals' yellow appearance when viewed parallel to the polarizer and blue when viewed perpendicular to the polarizer (as seen in gout). “Positively birefringent” refers to the crystals' blue appearance when viewed parallel to the polarizer and yellow when viewed perpendicular to the polarizer (as seen in pseudogout; calcium pyrophosphate).

Gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters (choice A) indicate a Staphylococcus arthritis and cellulitis. There is no history of trauma or open cut on the skin, and bacterial dissemination to the ear is less likely.

Large notched rectangular crystals with various birefringence (choice B) are seen with cholesterol crystals. Synovial fluid containing cholesterol crystals is not common, but can be seen sporadically with rheumatoid arthritis.

Mixed crystals with various birefringence (choice C) may be seen with corticosteroid injections. Our patient does not have a history of intra-articular injections.

Rhomboid crystals that are weakly positively birefringent (choice E) reflect calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition (pseudogout), which classically affects the knee or other large joints. Polarization microscopy reveals weak positive birefringence of crystals.

stem: An 82-year-old man has progressive posterior knee pain and stiffness. Examination shows a mildly fluctuant, tender popliteal mass limiting knee flexion; ultrasound shows a 1.6-cm fluid-filled space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The lesion is a popliteal cyst (also known as a Baker cyst) and anatomically represents an enlarged semimembranosus bursa. Baker cysts are more commonly seen at the extremes of age (older patients and children). They are completely benign and are thought to arise from the accumulation of bursal fluid that builds up secondary to motion at the joint. The fluid can be drained quite easily, providing patients with prompt relief. Unfortunately, the fluid can reaccumulate and sometimes surgery is needed to obliterate the space. The diagnosis is usually made on physical examination. Occasionally, a Baker cyst may rupture and produce pain behind the knee that extends down the calf muscles. Ultrasound is routinely used to ensure that the collection is arising from between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of the gastrocnemius.

Deep vein thrombosis (choice A) can present with pain, swelling, and redness in the lower extremity as a result of thrombosis of the femoral, popliteal, or deep veins of the pelvis. The most common risk factors are recent surgery, hospitalization, and/or immobility. Patients characteristically have identifiable risk factors and acute symptoms. Pain can occur with dorsiflexion of the ipsilateral foot (Homan's sign). The Virchow triad of abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulent blood flow), hypercoagulability, and endothelial damage rule the formation of thrombosis.

Hemophilic arthropathy (choice B) typically presents in the setting of recurrent intra-articular and periarticular hemorrhage associated with a congenital or acquired clotting factor disorder, i.e., hemophilia.

Myxoid liposarcoma (choice C) is a malignancy of fat cells and presents very differently from the well-circumscribed, tender mass seen in this patient, and not as a cystic mass on examination or ultrasound.

A popliteal artery aneurysm (choice D) is a localized dilation of the blood vessel caused by weakening of the vessel wall. These lesions present with lower-extremity ischemia as a result of thrombotic and embolic phenomena, as well as compression of adjacent structures. A popliteal artery aneurysm may present as a mass in the popliteal fossa, but it is usually pulsatile on examination. It can be diagnosed as a vascular structure by ultrasound.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with no past medical history comes to the physician for a routine physical examination. Physical examination shows a 1-cm, flat, white patch on the buccal mucosa. The lesion cannot be scraped off with a tongue depressor. The physician recommends a biopsy. Which diagnosis carries the greatest likelihood that this lesion will progress to an oral malignancy?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Leukoplakia is a white plaque on the oral mucosa for which a more specific diagnosis cannot be rendered. Leukoplakia is often associated with hyperkeratosis and may or may not show dysplastic squamous epithelium. On average, 5% of leukoplakias contain in situ or overt carcinoma; regardless, the lesion has a high probability of progressing to oral cancer.

White oral plaques can be due to a variety of causes. Frictional keratosis (choice A) of the oral mucosa most commonly occurs from persistent cheek and lip biting or from orthodontic prosthesis trauma. These white, keratotic lesions are a reactive process and have no malignant potential.

Lichen planus (choice C) may present with painful white, red, or ulcerated oral plaques. Microscopically, the lesion is characterized by intense lymphocytic infiltration of the dermoepidermal (or mucosal-submucosal) junction with destruction of the basal layer of cells. This inflammatory condition has not been shown to be premalignant.

Oral thrush (choice D) is a superficial candidal infection, typically occurring in the immunosuppressed or very young. Thrush is an infectious, non-neoplastic disease. The lesion can be easily scraped off.

Squamous papilloma (choice E) is a benign human papillomavirus (HPV) infection of the oral mucosa. Typically associated with HPV genotypes 6 and 11, squamous papilloma only rarely progresses to squamous carcinoma.

stem: A previously healthy 28-year-old primigravid woman at 34 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician because of swelling and deep, throbbing pain of her left thigh. Her pregnancy has been normal up to this 8 time. She has no signs or symptoms of labor. She had a 1-hour glucose tolerance test at 20 weeks’ gestation, which was normal. Screening anatomic ultrasound of the fetus at 20 weeks’ revealed mild bilateral 6 hydronephrosis. Physical examination of the mother shows the presence of a gravid uterus palpable near the xiphoid process. The abdomen is nontender and without guarding or rebound tenderness. Y Examination of the extremities shows swelling and warmth of the left thigh, and pain on left foot dorsifiexion. The superficial veins of the leg are prominent. Laboratory studies show a serum creatinine of 1.3 LL mg/dL, serum glucose of 109 mg/dL, and hematocrit of 39%. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This patient has clinical findings that are strongly suggestive of a deep venous thrombosis (DVT). Pain that increases upon dorsiflexion of the foot when the knee is extended is referred to as Homans sign. Pregnancy, particularly during the third trimester, induces a hypercoagulable blood state (possibly to limit the chance of fatal hemorrhage during delivery) that can manifest as DVT. The major complication of DVT is pulmonary embolism, which may be massive and can cause sudden death. Treatment of DVT in pregnant patients is with heparin (most commonly low-molecular-weight heparin); use of warfarin (Coumadin) is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. It is important to note that this patient has no signs or symptoms of active labor. If she is in active labor, temporary discontinuation of anticoagulation is for the purpose of securing regional anesthesia for the patient and to decrease the risk of epidural or spinal hematoma.

Amniotic fluid embolisms (choice A) are a rare but important cause of peripartum maternal mortality. During delivery, amniotic fluid is introduced into the maternal circulation, producing respiratory distress and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Arterial occlusion secondary to uterine compression (choice B) is a rare and unusual problem and would present with ischemic symptoms. The enlarged uterus most commonly compresses the inferior vena cava and contributes to lower-extremity edema of late pregnancy.

Although endothelial injury (choice C) is a component of Virchow’s triad (along with alteration in blood flow and hypercoagulability), it is not a likely mechanism in this patient.

The patient does not show the localized erythema that might suggest infection (choice E).

ReKaps: Deep vein thromboses can present with thigh pain that is characteristically exacerbated by extending the foot. Pregnant patients in the third trimester are in a hypercoagulable state that may predispose them to deep vein thrombosis and its risk of pulmonary embolism.

choice_explanations.B: Arterial occlusion causes ischemia with diminished perfusion; the swollen warm leg and venous prominence suggest venous thrombosis.
choice_explanations.C: Endothelial injury is one Virchow-triad component, but the vignette points to pregnancy-related hypercoagulability.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: late pregnancy is hypercoagulable and predisposes to DVT.
choice_explanations.E: Infection would more likely produce infectious signs and does not explain the classic DVT pattern.

stem: A 55-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension is brought to the emergency department because of right-sided hemiplegia. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and drinks 3–4 beers daily. He is in distress and has difficulty speaking. Examination shows right lower facial paralysis and paralysis of the right upper and lower extremities. Sensation is intact, and he can wrinkle his forehead bilaterally. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.text: Corticospinal tract in the upper cervical spinal cord
Medial portion of the left frontal lobe
Medial portion of the right frontal lobe

explanation: Contralateral face and arm/leg weakness with forehead sparing localizes above the facial nucleus to corticobulbar and corticospinal fibers. A compact lesion in the left internal capsule can affect both pathways and produce dense right hemiplegia. Severe hypertension makes hemorrhage plausible.

choice_explanations.A: An upper-cervical corticospinal lesion would not explain the ipsilateral cortical-pattern facial weakness.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: a left internal-capsule lesion interrupts compact descending motor fibers and causes right face/arm/leg weakness.
choice_explanations.C: The medial frontal motor cortex mainly represents the contralateral leg; this does not best explain combined face, arm, and leg findings.
choice_explanations.D: A right medial frontal lesion would affect the left leg, not the right face and limbs.
choice_explanations.E: A right internal-capsule lesion would produce left-sided weakness, the wrong side.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with diabetes comes to the physician because of ear pain 2 days after swimming in a local pool. Examination shows greenish discharge from the right external ear canal. Erythema is localized to the anterior half of the external ear canal, and manipulation of the tragus elicits extreme tenderness. Which nerve transmits this pain?

options.text: Auricular branch of the vagus nerve
Auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve

explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of V3, supplies the anterior portion of the external auditory canal. The clinical picture is otitis externa, and tragal manipulation commonly worsens pain. The vagal auricular branch supplies part of the posterior canal; greater auricular and lesser occipital nerves supply external auricular skin.

choice_explanations.A: The auricular branch of CN X supplies part of the external ear/canal, mainly posteriorly; the stem localizes pain to the anterior canal.
choice_explanations.B: Correct: the auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the anterior external auditory canal.
choice_explanations.C: The greater auricular nerve supplies skin over the lower auricle and adjacent parotid/mastoid region, not the anterior canal.
choice_explanations.D: The lesser occipital nerve supplies posterior auricular/occipital skin, not the anterior canal.
choice_explanations.E: CN VIII carries hearing and balance information, not external-canal pain.

stem: A 61-year-old man with a history of hypertension is brought to the emergency department because of left-sided hemiparesis. Neurologic examination shows dysarthria, and the tongue deviates to the right upon protrusion. There is also a loss of tactile and vibratory sensation over the trunk and over the left upper and lower extremities. An occlusion of which of the following vessels is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Rightward tongue deviation indicates right hypoglossal (CN XII) weakness from a right medial medullary lesion. Left hemiparesis reflects corticospinal-tract involvement before decussation, and left vibration/position loss reflects medial-lemniscus involvement. The medial medulla is supplied by paramedian branches of the anterior spinal and/or vertebral arteries (B).

choice_explanations.C: MCA strokes affect cerebral lateral hemispheric territories and do not explain an ipsilateral hypoglossal palsy.
choice_explanations.D: PCA stroke classically affects occipital/temporal territories, often causing visual deficits.
choice_explanations.E: PICA causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, typically with dysphagia/hoarseness and crossed pain-temperature deficits.

stem: A 25-year-old man who is otherwise healthy is admitted to the hospital with high fever, nausea, vomiting, severe headache, focal neurologic signs, and altered mental status. His symptoms have progressed over a period of five days. The family notes that the patient had just returned from a vacation at his lake house, where he participated in water-skiing. Physical examination reveals positive meningeal signs. CSF evaluation shows the presence of motile trophozoites. Serology reveals positive Toxoplasma IgG. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation: Naegleria fowleri enters through the nose during warm freshwater exposure and can cause rapidly progressive primary amebic meningoencephalitis. Motile trophozoites in CSF support the diagnosis. Positive Toxoplasma IgG indicates prior exposure and does not explain this acute syndrome. Answer D.

choice_explanations.C: Giardia causes intestinal malabsorption/diarrhea, not CNS infection.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressively worsening *uncoordinated* arm and leg movement and slurred speech. Physical examination shows preserved language ability but gross dysarthria. The boy has a staggering gait with a limited ability to walk unassisted. Motor examination shows normal bulk and tone, but strength is 3/5 in distal muscle groups and 4/5 in proximal groups in the upper and lower extremities. Patellar and ankle reflexes are absent; a plantar extensor response is present bilaterally. Vibration and position senses are impaired, but sensation of pinprick is intact. Which of the following is most likely a characteristic of this patient's illness?

options.text: Delayed muscle relaxation after strong contraction
Results from a trinucleotide repeat expansion

explanation: This is Friedreich ataxia: childhood-onset progressive ataxia, dysarthria, areflexia, extensor plantar responses, and impaired vibration/position sense. It is autosomal recessive and caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in FXN, reducing frataxin. Answer D.

choice_explanations.C: A post-viral acute neuropathy suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome, not a progressive inherited childhood ataxia.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: Friedreich ataxia is caused by a GAA trinucleotide-repeat expansion in FXN.
choice_explanations.E: Friedreich ataxia is inherited and is not a sexually transmitted infection.

stem: A 60-year-old woman comes to the physician because of discoloration of her toenails. Physical examination shows crumbling, friable nails with hyperkeratotic debris under the affected part of the nail. A photograph is shown. Treatment with which of the following is most appropriate oral medication for this patient?
explanation: The crumbly, discolored nails with subungual debris indicate onychomycosis, commonly caused by dermatophytes. Oral terbinafine inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase and is a standard systemic treatment for nail disease (E).

choice_explanations.D: Nystatin treats mucocutaneous Candida and is not effective for dermatophyte onychomycosis.

stem: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of diaphoresis, severe headache, and tachycardia. He was watching football and eating pizza at a friend's house. He has taken an antidepressant for 3 months. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse 105/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 200/110 mm Hg. Which drug is he most likely taking?
explanation: This is a tyramine-associated hypertensive crisis in a patient taking an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor. Tyramine-rich or fermented foods can cause excessive catecholamine release when MAO is inhibited. Phenelzine (C) is an MAOI.

choice_explanations.D: Trazodone is a serotonin antagonist/reuptake inhibitor, not an MAO inhibitor.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with a history of resistant depression is found unconscious and brought to the emergency department after ingesting an unknown quantity of amitriptyline. Her husband says that he does not know how long she had been lying unconscious at their home. Two hours after arrival, she dies, despite appropriate lifesaving measures. explanation: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose blocks fast cardiac sodium channels, widening QRS and predisposing to ventricular dysrhythmia, hypotension, and death. The most likely cause is lethal arrhythmia (C).

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty conceiving. She says that her periods are very light and irregular. Physical examination shows moderate acne. Laboratory studies of serum show elevated estrogen and androgen levels. Which of the following additional laboratory findings in serum will most likely be seen in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has polycystic ovarian disease, which is characterized by menstrual irregularity and androgen excess in women. The exact etiology is unknown but appears to result from abnormal function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis. There is elevated gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and an elevated ratio of LH to FSH. Increased testosterone is produced in the theca cells in response to LH stimulation. The increased levels of LH and subsequent androgen production result in the development of some male sex characteristics, such as the appearance of excessive body hair and acne. Elevated androgen production during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle results in the formation of several immature cystic follicles. Also, FSH secretion is typically suppressed (choice A is incorrect), often contributing to increased LH/FSH ratio. The combination of elevated androgens with an increased LH/FSH ratio stimulates development of multiple follicles, which do not, however, progress to maturity and ovulation. With low FSH, estrogen production by the ovaries is low, and the follicles cannot continue development. Total estrogen may or may not be elevated; the presentation of this disease is highly variable.

Elevated inhibin (choice B) is incorrect, because in polycystic ovarian disease the elevated androgens are converted to the estrogen estrone in the periphery. The ovaries do not produce as much estrogen and inhibin as normal. Reduced GnRH (choice D) is incorrect. Instead, GnRH is increased in this patient. Despite elevated estrogens, there is a defective feedback of estrogen, which normally suppresses GnRH secretion. The reduction in estrogen feedback causes an elevation in GnRH. Reduced insulin (choice E) is incorrect, because PCOS is strongly associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Not all patients with PCOS display this pattern, but it is very likely to occur, so the probability that insulin will be reduced is less than the probability that LH will be increased; therefore this is not the best answer.

choice_explanations.A: FSH is not the typically elevated gonadotropin in the classic PCOS pattern; LH is relatively increased.
choice_explanations.B: Elevated inhibin is not the characteristic additional finding used to identify PCOS here.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: increased GnRH pulse frequency can favor LH secretion, supporting ovarian androgen production in PCOS.
choice_explanations.D: PCOS is not characterized by reduced GnRH drive in the classic teaching pattern.
choice_explanations.E: Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia is common in PCOS; reduced insulin would not fit.

stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a blistering skin rash. She has no history of major medical illness, no known allergies, and is not taking medications. Physical examination shows flaccid bullae on her mouth, face, and trunk. Manual pressure on the lesion produces separation of the upper layer, followed by eventual sloughing of the skin. A biopsy specimen reveals acantholysis above the basal layer. Autoantibodies to which of the following are most likely present in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. This patient presents with a blistering skin rash and flaccid bullae, along with biopsy evidence of epithelial cell separation (acantholysis). This is most consistent with a diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vulgaris occurs typically in older patients (40–60 years of age) and can either occur spontaneously or with a trigger (drugs, malignancy, etc.). Oral involvement is common and often precedes the characteristic skin lesions.

The disease is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins known as desmogleins (specifically desmoglein 3), which normally form intercellular junctions between epidermal cells (keratinocytes). Disruption of desmosomes decreases the ability of the keratinocytes to adhere to one another, permitting formation of intraepidermal, flaccid vesicles and bullae. Suprabasal bullae occur since the basal keratinocytes adhere to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes. Clinically, breakdown of desmosomes also causes a positive Nikolsky sign, in which separation of the epidermis can occur upon manual stroking. This sign is present in other skin diseases including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (usually drug-induced) and epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

It is important to contrast pemphigus vulgaris with another bullae-forming disease known as bullous pemphigoid. In this disease, IgG autoantibodies are directed at hemidesmosomes (choice C) rather than desmosomes. Specifically, the hemidesmosomal protein antigens are the bullous pemphigoid antigens 1 and 2 (BPAG1 and BPAG2). Hemidesmosomes attach epidermal cells to the underlying basement membrane. Thus, when hemidesmosomes are disrupted, the epidermis remains intact and elevates off the basement membrane. This results in formation of subepidermal, tense blisters that do not easily rupture, and a negative Nikolsky sign. Additionally, there is usually no oral or mucosal involvement in these patients, unlike pemphigus vulgaris.

Antibodies against gliadin (choice B) are a feature of gluten intolerance and celiac disease. These patients can present with dermatitis herpetiformis, a rash usually distributed along extensor surfaces. IgA antibodies cross-react with components of the anchoring fibrils that anchor keratinocytes to the basement membrane, resulting in subepidermal blisters and microabscesses at the tips of the dermal papillae.

Antibodies against melanocytes (choice D) occur in patients with vitiligo. This results in patchy areas of depigmentation due to loss of melanin-producing cells, but not bullous lesions.

Antibodies against nuclear antigens (choice E) suggest systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The rash in this disease can have a malar (butterfly across cheeks) or discoid shape and is typically photosensitive. Histologically, there is degeneration of the basal epidermal cells with deposition of IgG and complement at the dermal-epidermal junction. These patients usually have a host of other symptoms including serositis, renal disease, intermittent fevers, and pericarditis.

choice_explanations.A: Correct: pemphigus vulgaris antibodies target desmogleins in desmosomes, causing suprabasal acantholysis and flaccid bullae.
choice_explanations.B: Anti-gliadin/tissue-transglutaminase antibodies are associated with celiac disease/dermatitis herpetiformis, which causes grouped pruritic vesicles, not flaccid oral bullae.
choice_explanations.C: Hemidesmosomes are targeted in bullous pemphigoid, which causes tense subepidermal bullae rather than suprabasal acantholysis.
choice_explanations.D: Melanocyte destruction is associated with vitiligo, not this blistering disorder.
choice_explanations.E: Nuclear antigens are targets in systemic autoimmune diseases such as lupus, not pemphigus vulgaris.

stem: A 26-year-old man with history of intravenous drug use comes to the emergency department after falling down a flight of stairs. explanation: Primary prevention prevents disease before it occurs; secondary prevention detects disease early; tertiary prevention treats established disease and limits complications. This patient already has HIV, so antiretroviral therapy is tertiary prevention (C).

stem: A physician treats a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Which clinical presentation is most likely?

options.text: A child with short stature, radial abnormalities, absent thumbs, and café-au-lait spots develops severe anemia
A child develops myoglobinuria after vigorous exercise
A neonate has splenomegaly and severe anemia
An adult develops anemia after taking an antimalarial drug
An adult develops severe shortness of breath during an airplane ride

explanation:
The correct answer is D. There are several variants of G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive) in Africa. The most common clinically significant variant is the so-called A-type, which produces an unstable G6PD enzyme. This variant is found in up to 11% of African-American males. In red cells, NADPH from the HMP shunt is essential for detoxifying reactive oxygen species that otherwise would damage proteins and lipids in the RBC. Glutathione reductase and glutathione peroxidase are involved in the normal detoxification process. The A-variant renders the individual's red cells susceptible to oxidative stresses, such as those that occur with administration of the antimalarial drug primaquine. Sulfonamides and dapsone are other agents that can trigger hemolytic episodes. Infections (bacterial or viral) are another important trigger for hemolysis in these individuals. Rarely, G6PD deficiency presents as neonatal jaundice or with chronic hemolysis. In Mediterranean populations, G6PD deficiency-associated hemolysis may occur in individuals who eat a meal of fava beans (Vicia fava) and several hours later develop hemoglobinuria and peripheral vascular collapse secondary to intravascular hemolysis as a result of the oxidant injury initiated by the fava beans.

Fanconi anemia (choice A) is caused by a mutation in one of several genes encoding a multiprotein nuclear complex that functions in the BRCA pathway, which repairs damage to DNA caused by cross-linking agents. All bone marrow elements are affected. In addition to the often-fatal leukemia, pigmentary changes in the skin and malformations of the heart, kidney, and limbs (aplasia of the radius, thumb deformity) are associated features.

Myoglobinuria following strenuous exercise, especially in the initial phase (choice B), is characteristic of myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease), a defect in muscle glycogenolysis.

A neonate with an enlarged spleen and chronic hemolysis (choice C) is consistent with pyruvate kinase deficiency, the neonatal form of which is often fatal. Transfusions coupled with splenectomy often lessen the symptoms.

An adult who suffers shortness of breath during an airplane ride (choice E) (or any activity at low pO2) is consistent with a person who is heterozygous or homozygous for the HbS allele of the hemoglobin beta-chain locus and is either a carrier (heterozygous) or a person with sickle cell anemia (homozygous).

choice_explanations.C: Not the best choice: Pyruvate kinase deficiency can cause neonatal hemolytic anemia and splenomegaly. The vignette/data instead support An adult develops anemia after taking an antimalarial drug. Oxidative stress from antimalarial drugs can precipitate hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
choice_explanations.D: Correct: G6PD deficiency: oxidant drugs including antimalarials can trigger hemolysis. Oxidative stress from antimalarial drugs can precipitate hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 40-year-old man has recurrent episodes of cough with hemoptysis. Oxygen saturation is 90%. Laboratory studies show anemia and elevated creatinine; urinalysis shows hematuria, and microscopy shows numerous red blood cell casts. Which serum antibody is most likely present?
explanation: The combination of pulmonary hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis is a pulmonary–renal syndrome. Anti–glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is caused by antibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen, shared by alveolar and glomerular basement membranes.

choice_explanations.A: Anti-dsDNA supports SLE; it does not explain the classic pulmonary–renal anti-GBM pattern.
choice_explanations.B: Antimitochondrial antibody is associated with primary biliary cholangitis.
choice_explanations.C: MPO-ANCA can occur in microscopic polyangiitis or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; the stem instead points to anti-GBM disease.
choice_explanations.D: PR3-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which can cause pulmonary and renal disease but is not the antibody classically tested by this presentation.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Anti-type IV collagen antibody targets alveolar and glomerular basement membranes.

A.text: Anti-dsDNA is listed with systemic lupus erythematosus.

B.text: Antimitochondrial antibody is associated with primary biliary cholangitis.

C.text: MPO-ANCA is associated with selected small-vessel vasculitides.

D.text: PR3-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent bacterial infections. Genetic testing shows an inherited defect in a component of NADPH oxidase. Which leukocyte process is most directly impaired?

options.text: Transfer of lysosomal enzymes to phagosomes

explanation: NADPH oxidase catalyzes the respiratory burst by generating superoxide, which is converted to hydrogen peroxide. Its deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease. Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to make hypochlorous acid, so that downstream reaction is impaired secondarily, but the direct defective process is H₂O₂ generation.

choice_explanations.A: Leukocyte adhesion and transmigration depend on adhesion molecules, not NADPH oxidase.
choice_explanations.B: Chemotaxis is not the primary defect in chronic granulomatous disease.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. NADPH oxidase initiates the respiratory burst and generates superoxide, leading to H₂O₂.
choice_explanations.D: HOCl production by myeloperoxidase is reduced downstream because NADPH oxidase supplies H₂O₂; it is not the direct enzyme defect asked for.
choice_explanations.E: Lysosomal-enzyme trafficking to phagosomes is not the NADPH-oxidase function.

A.text: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 impairs leukocyte migration/transmigration.

B.text: C5a is a potent chemotactic complement fragment.

C.text: The respiratory burst generates reactive oxygen species through NADPH oxidase.

D.text: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to form hypochlorous acid.

E.text: Chediak-Higashi syndrome impairs phagosome-lysosome fusion/trafficking; this is distinct from NADPH oxidase deficiency.

fa_summary: NADPH oxidase initiates the phagocyte respiratory burst; its defect reduces reactive oxygen species and causes chronic granulomatous disease.

stem: An investigator compares normally distributed systolic blood-pressure measurements among five independent age groups and wants to test whether their means are equal. Which statistical method is most appropriate?
explanation: A one-way ANOVA tests whether the means of three or more independent groups differ for a continuous outcome. It controls the family-wise type I error better than performing many pairwise t tests.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. ANOVA compares means across multiple independent groups.
choice_explanations.B: An odds ratio measures association between categorical exposure and outcome, not equality of continuous group means.
choice_explanations.C: Chi-square tests compare categorical counts or proportions.
choice_explanations.D: Pearson correlation measures linear association between two continuous variables.
choice_explanations.E: Repeated pairwise t tests inflate type I error when comparing five groups.

A.text: ANOVA compares means across three or more groups.

B.text: Odds ratio compares the odds of an outcome in exposed versus unexposed groups; First Aid gives the definition and formula.

C.text: Chi-square tests are used for categorical proportions or counts.

D.text: Pearson correlation quantifies linear association between continuous variables.

E.text: A t test compares two means; multiple pairwise testing increases type I error.

fa_summary: Use ANOVA to compare means among three or more groups; t tests compare two means.

stem: A four-year observational study finds more motor-vehicle collisions among current smokers than never-smokers. Current smokers are mostly assembly-line workers, whereas never-smokers are mostly managers. Which problem most threatens the validity of the association?
explanation: Occupation is associated with smoking group and may independently affect collision risk (for example, through different driving exposure). It is therefore a potential confounder that can create or distort the observed association. The study is observational, so the groups are not otherwise exchangeable.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. A third variable associated with exposure and outcome can distort the smoking–collision association.
choice_explanations.B: Expectancy bias occurs when expectations influence assessment or interpretation.
choice_explanations.C: Late-look bias arises from repeated interim analyses and stopping after a significant result.
choice_explanations.D: Measurement bias is systematic error in measuring exposure or outcome; the stated concern is group imbalance in occupation.
choice_explanations.E: Proficiency bias is not the principal epidemiologic threat described here.
choice_explanations.F: Recall bias is differential remembering of past exposures, generally in retrospective studies.

A.text: Confounding is distortion by a third variable associated with exposure and outcome.

B.text: Observer/expectancy effects can bias measurement or interpretation.

D.text: Measurement bias is systematic error in measuring study variables.

E.text: 已核对 First Aid 2026 相关章节，未找到可直接支持该选项的独立知识点。

stem: The diagnostic fasting-glucose threshold for diabetes is lowered from 140 to 126 mg/dL. Which change is most likely?
explanation: Lowering a positive-test threshold classifies more people as test-positive. Sensitivity rises and false negatives fall, while specificity falls and false positives rise. In the usual fixed-prevalence setting, the negative predictive value increases because fewer diseased patients remain among test-negative results.

choice_explanations.A: Sensitivity increases, rather than decreases, when the threshold is lowered.
choice_explanations.B: The false-negative rate decreases as more patients meet the positive criterion.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. With greater sensitivity and fewer false negatives, NPV generally increases at fixed prevalence.
choice_explanations.D: PPV generally decreases because specificity falls and false positives increase.
choice_explanations.E: Specificity decreases because more non-diseased people test positive.

A.text: Lowering a positive cutoff increases sensitivity.

B.text: A more sensitive test has fewer false negatives.

C.text: NPV is the probability that a negative result is truly disease-free; predictive values vary with prevalence (p. 262).

D.text: PPV depends on sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence; a lower cutoff tends to lower specificity.

E.text: Lowering a cutoff decreases specificity.

fa_summary: Changing the positive threshold trades sensitivity against specificity; predictive values also depend on prevalence.

stem: A city has 1,000,000 residents, including 10,000 people with AIDS. During one year, 1,000 new AIDS cases occur. Assuming no migration, which expression gives the annual incidence?
explanation: Incidence uses new cases during a specified period divided by the population at risk at the start of that period. People already living with AIDS are not at risk of becoming new cases, so the denominator is 1,000,000 − 10,000 = 990,000. Deaths are not subtracted from the incident case count.

choice_explanations.A: Uses net new cases after subtracting deaths; incidence counts new cases, not net prevalence change.
choice_explanations.B: Includes existing cases in the at-risk denominator and subtracts deaths from new cases.
choice_explanations.C: Correct: 1,000 new cases divided by 990,000 people initially free of AIDS.
choice_explanations.D: The denominator should exclude the 10,000 prevalent cases not at risk of a first AIDS diagnosis.
choice_explanations.E: All-cause deaths do not define incident AIDS cases.

A.text: Incidence counts new cases; it is not reduced by deaths.

B.text: The incidence denominator is the population at risk, excluding existing cases.

C.text: Incidence = new cases during the interval ÷ population at risk.

D.text: People with existing disease are excluded from the at-risk denominator.

E.text: 已核对 First Aid 2026 相关章节，未找到可直接支持该选项的独立知识点。

stem: Researchers compare patients who chose or were selected to receive a new drug with untreated patients using medical records. Hospitalizations are lower but all-cause mortality is higher in the treated group. Which possibility most undermines the conclusion that the drug should not be used?

options.text: Knowledge of treatment biased outcome measurement
Treated patients may have been less healthy at baseline

explanation: Because treatment was not randomly assigned, baseline differences may confound the comparison. If sicker patients preferentially received the drug, higher mortality may reflect their underlying illness rather than harm from treatment (confounding by indication).

choice_explanations.A: This is possible in an unblinded study but is not the strongest flaw given nonrandom treatment allocation.
choice_explanations.B: Observer bias can affect measurements, but it does not explain the explicit baseline-selection problem.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Confounding by indication can make treated patients less healthy before treatment.
choice_explanations.D: The outcomes were obtained from records, so recall bias is not the main concern.
choice_explanations.E: The Hawthorne effect is behavior change from knowing one is observed.
choice_explanations.F: Lead-time bias concerns earlier diagnosis making survival from diagnosis appear longer without changing time of death.

A.text: Expectancy/observer effects can influence outcome assessment.

B.text: Unblinded outcome assessment can produce measurement or observer bias.

C.text: Confounding arises from baseline differences linked to exposure and outcome.

D.text: Recall bias involves differential recollection of past exposures.

E.text: Hawthorne effect is behavior change from awareness of observation.

F.text: Lead-time bias creates apparent survival gain from earlier diagnosis.

fa_summary: Nonrandomized treatment groups can differ at baseline; confounding by indication distorts treatment effects.

stem: A neuronal cell line has normal morphology and axonal extension but defective fast anterograde transport of secretory vesicles from the Golgi toward the plasma membrane. Retrograde transport is normal. Which cytoskeletal motor is most likely deficient?
explanation: Kinesin generally carries cargo anterogradely toward the microtubule plus end, including movement toward axon terminals. Dynein supports retrograde transport toward the cell body. A selective anterograde transport defect therefore points to kinesin.

choice_explanations.A: Actin supports cortical structure and short-range transport but is not the principal long-range axonal track motor tested.
choice_explanations.B: Dynein is associated with retrograde transport, which is intact here.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Kinesin mediates plus-end-directed anterograde cargo transport.
choice_explanations.D: Myosin moves along actin filaments and is not the main long-distance axonal motor.
choice_explanations.E: Microtubules are the tracks, not the motor protein; the directional motor defect is kinesin.

A.text: Actin is listed as the component of microfilaments in the cytoskeleton table.

B.text: Dynein mediates retrograde transport along microtubules.

C.text: Kinesin mediates anterograde axonal transport.

D.text: 已核对 First Aid 2026 相关章节，未找到可直接支持该选项的独立知识点。

E.text: Microtubules provide tracks for kinesin- and dynein-dependent transport.

stem: A 5-year-old child has coarse facial features, hepatomegaly, and skeletal, cardiac, and neurologic abnormalities. Multiple lysosomal hydrolases are elevated in the blood. The disorder results from failure to phosphorylate mannose residues on lysosomal enzymes. In which organelle does this tagging step normally occur?
explanation: In I-cell disease, failure of Golgi N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase prevents formation of the mannose-6-phosphate targeting signal. Lysosomal enzymes are secreted rather than delivered to lysosomes.

choice_explanations.B: Correct. Golgi enzymes add the mannose-6-phosphate lysosomal targeting mark.
choice_explanations.C: Lysosomes receive the tagged enzymes; they do not create the targeting mark.
choice_explanations.D: Mitochondria are not involved in lysosomal enzyme sorting.
choice_explanations.E: Ribosomes translate proteins but do not perform M6P tagging.

stem: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks has fever, headache, and painful genital vesicles caused by herpes simplex virus. Which feature of axonal transport helps the virus reach sensory ganglia?

options.text: Transport moves proteins to the axon terminal
Transport moves vesicles to the axon terminal

explanation: After entering peripheral sensory nerve endings, HSV travels retrogradely toward the neuronal cell body in sensory ganglia. Retrograde movement along microtubules is mediated by dynein.

choice_explanations.A: The initial movement from peripheral nerve ending to ganglion is retrograde, not anterograde.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Dynein carries cargo toward the microtubule minus end and supports retrograde transport.
choice_explanations.C: Kinesin usually mediates anterograde transport toward the axon terminal.
choice_explanations.D: This describes anterograde movement away from the cell body.
choice_explanations.E: This also describes anterograde transport toward the terminal.

A.text: Anterograde transport proceeds toward the axon terminal.

B.text: Dynein mediates retrograde axonal transport.

C.text: Kinesin generally mediates anterograde transport.

D.text: Anterograde transport carries cargo toward the axon terminal.
