stem: A 34-year-old multigravid woman comes to the physician because of fever and a mass in her left breast. She gave birth without complications 2 months ago and has a history of mitral valve replacement complicated by endocarditis. Physical examination shows a fluctuant mass in the left breast. Her mother died from breast cancer at age 40. Breast ultrasound shows a fluid collection under the skin, and needle biopsy yields 15 mL of cloudy yellow fluid. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Acute mastitis, frequently complicated by breast abscess formation, typically develops in the postpartum period, when the nipples are first subjected to the physical stresses of breastfeeding. Bacteria enter the breast via cracks in the nipple, and flourish in the microenvironment of the lactating breast. Acute mastitis causes redness, pain, and swelling in the affected breast. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen, since it is the most abundant skin flora. Streptococcus is less likely but also possible. Treatment of simple cellulitis is with warm compresses and oral antibiotics, whereas an abscess requires drainage and sometimes IV antibiotics. During treatment, pumping of the milk from the affected breast should be done to facilitate recovery. As long as the antibiotics the mother is taking are not harmful, breastfeeding can continue on the affected breast if the mother can tolerate the irritation or pain. Some women breastfeed from the unaffected breast if it is too painful, then once the pain has subsided, the mother can breastfeed from the affected breast.

Although endocarditis (choice B) could send septic emboli to the breast, Staph. aureus endocarditis is more commonly associated with bacteremia, fever, proliferative glomerulonephritis, valvular dysfunction, and emboli to the brain, kidneys, heart, and gut. Fibrocystic changes of the breast (choice C) is a common condition characterized by noncancerous breast tissue proliferation and cyst formation that can cause discomfort or pain related to hormonal influences. There is no relationship to breast abscess development. Inflammatory breast carcinoma (choice D) does not provoke an inflammatory response and is not associated with an infection or abscess. Inflammatory breast carcinoma is characterized by tumor spread into the dermal lymphatics, producing diffuse induration, swelling, warmth, and skin tenderness with the typical peau d'orange (orange-peel) appearance. While the appearance of inflammatory carcinoma is similar to infection, the clinical symptoms are not. Additionally, the present patient is rather young for the development of breast cancer, although it is possible. Paget disease (choice E) presents as skin changes on the breast or nipple, in association with an invasive or in situ ductal carcinoma in the underlying breast that spreads along the large ducts and travels out into the epidermis. Paget disease produces an eczematous skin lesion that may be crusted, but it is not related to bacterial infection.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Lactation predisposes to nipple fissures and ascending bacterial infection; S. aureus is the most common cause of lactational mastitis and abscess.
choice_explanations.B: Endocarditis can cause bacteremia and embolic complications, but it is not the usual cause of a localized lactational breast abscess; the source explanation notes its typical systemic/embolic pattern.
choice_explanations.C: Fibrocystic change can cause hormonally related lumps or discomfort, but it is benign tissue proliferation/cyst formation and does not produce a purulent abscess.
choice_explanations.D: Inflammatory breast carcinoma can cause diffuse warmth, erythema, edema, and peau d’orange from dermal lymphatic involvement, but it does not account for cloudy purulent fluid in this postpartum presentation.
choice_explanations.E: Paget disease involves eczematous changes of the nipple associated with underlying ductal carcinoma; it is not a bacterial abscess.

A.text: Lactational mastitis occurs during breastfeeding; cracked nipples increase bacterial entry, and S. aureus is the most common pathogen.

B.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive chapter has no direct matching point for endocarditis as a cause of breast abscess.

C.text: Fibrocystic changes are common benign breast changes that may cause premenstrual pain or lumps.

D.text: Inflammatory breast cancer involves dermal lymphatic invasion and can produce warm, swollen, erythematous skin; it is a distinct malignant presentation.

E.text: Paget disease is extension of underlying DCIS/invasive breast cancer up the lactiferous ducts into the nipple epidermis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual bleeding. Biopsy of the endometrium shows a thick endometrium with long, coiled glands lined by columnar epithelium with prominent cytoplasmic vacuoles adjacent to the gland lumen. Earlier in the menstrual cycle, the glands were much smaller and lined by cells without vacuoles. Which hormone is primarily responsible for initiating glandular secretion in endometrial tissue?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Progesterone initiates a transition from the proliferative phase of the endometrial cycle to the secretory phase, characterized by greatly increased glandular activity. The proliferative phase is characterized by endometrial thickening and differentiation over a period of about ten days immediately following menstruation. These changes are stimulated by estrogen released from developing follicles. After ovulation, progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum inhibits estrogen-induced proliferation and initiates glandular secretory activity, preparing the endometrium for fertilization and implantation.

The mineralocorticoid aldosterone (choice A) is secreted by the adrenal glands. It regulates Na+ and K+ handling by the renal tubule. It does not produce the endometrial changes described. Estrogen (choice B) is responsible for the proliferative phase of the endometrial cycle and prepares the endometrium for rising progesterone levels and transition to the secretory phase. LH (choice C) and FSH (choice D) are secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. During the secretory phase, the levels of FSH and LH are decreased due to negative feedback by the corpus luteum. These hormones are not directly responsible for secretory endometrium.

choice_explanations.A: Aldosterone regulates renal sodium and potassium handling; it does not initiate endometrial secretory activity.
choice_explanations.B: Estrogen stimulates endometrial proliferation and straight, narrow glands before ovulation; it is not the primary trigger for the secretory transformation.
choice_explanations.C: LH supports ovulation and corpus-luteum formation, but progesterone is the hormone that directly stimulates the secretory endometrial phase.
choice_explanations.D: FSH supports follicular development in the ovary; it does not directly initiate uterine gland secretion.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Corpus-luteum progesterone induces secretory transformation, including tortuous, dilated glands.

A.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive chapter has no direct matching point for aldosterone in endometrial cycling.

B.text: Estrogen stimulates the proliferative phase and endometrial development before ovulation.

C.text: LH stimulates the luteal phase after ovulation; the reproductive-cycle diagram places LH in ovarian-cycle regulation rather than as the endometrial secretory stimulus.

D.text: FSH stimulates follicular development in the ovarian cycle; it is not the uterine-cycle signal for glandular secretion.

E.text: Progesterone stimulates the secretory phase, producing tortuous, dilated endometrial glands and preparing the endometrium for implantation.

stem: A 29-year-old woman consults her physician because of difficulty becoming pregnant. She has kept records of her menstrual periods for 6 months; they show menses at 28-day intervals. Her most recent menses began 12 days before the office visit. Which cellular event is most likely occurring at the present time?

options.text: Granulosa cells begin to express aromatase
Granulosa cells begin to express FSH receptors
Granulosa cells begin to express LH receptors
Theca cells begin to express LH receptors
Theca cells begin to express side-chain cleavage enzyme

explanation:
The correct answer is C. Development of granulosa cells is critical to ovulation. During the early follicular phase, FSH dominates the control of follicular development. However, in the late follicular phase, granulosa cells increase expression of receptors for LH. In the absence of LH receptors, follicular development is arrested in the early antral stage. Women who have inactivating mutations of LH receptors have normal primary and secondary sexual characteristics, but have amenorrhea, do not develop preovulatory follicles, and do not ovulate. Estrogen synthesis requires LH stimulation of theca cells to produce androgens, which are converted to estrogen by granulosa cells stimulated by FSH. The secretion of estrogen by the developing follicle can best be explained using the two-cell-two-gonadotropin hypothesis. Theca cells have LH receptors during the early follicular phase and are stimulated by LH to secrete the androgens androstenedione and testosterone. The androgens then diffuse into the granulosa cells, where they are aromatized to estrogens; this conversion is stimulated by FSH action on granulosa cells. Only as the follicle approaches ovulation do LH receptors begin to be expressed by the granulosa cells. Response of granulosa cells to LH, which favors progesterone production, is apparently required for maturation of the dominant follicle, ovulation, and then luteinization.

Choice A is incorrect because granulosa cells have aromatase activity prior to the preovulatory phase; this is demonstrated by their ability to produce estrogens when stimulated by FSH. Aromatase activity does increase greatly after the LH surge, but it is nevertheless significant also during early stages of follicular development. Choice B is incorrect because, as discussed above, granulosa cells are responsive to FSH throughout the follicular phase; it does not begin only as ovulation approaches. Choice D is incorrect because theca cells express LH receptors early in the follicular phase. LH is key to stimulation of thecal cell production of the androgen precursors that granulosa cells convert to estrogens, and after ovulation, convert largely to progesterone. Choice E is incorrect because activity of the side-chain cleavage enzyme, P450scc, is the first step in ovarian steroidogenesis. P450scc converts cholesterol to pregnenolone. Without activity of this enzyme throughout the ovarian cycle, steroids could not be produced. Therefore, it does not begin only as ovulation approaches, but throughout the follicular and luteal phases.

choice_explanations.A: Aromatase is already active in granulosa cells earlier in follicular development: FSH stimulates conversion of theca-derived androgens to estrogens.
choice_explanations.B: Granulosa cells respond to FSH throughout the follicular phase; FSH-receptor expression does not first begin near ovulation.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. As the dominant follicle approaches ovulation, granulosa cells acquire LH receptors, enabling LH-mediated maturation and luteinization.
choice_explanations.D: Theca cells express LH receptors early in the follicular phase and produce androgen precursors under LH stimulation; this is not the late-cycle event asked about.
choice_explanations.E: Side-chain cleavage is an early steroidogenic step, not an event that begins only as ovulation approaches.

A.text: The follicular diagram shows aromatase in granulosa cells converting theca-derived androstenedione to estrogen.

B.text: The ovarian follicle diagram identifies FSH receptors on granulosa cells; First Aid does not state that their expression begins only near ovulation.

C.text: The ovarian follicle diagram shows LH receptors on granulosa cells and theca cells; the source explanation supplies the timing—granulosa LH-receptor expression rises in the late follicular phase.

D.text: The follicular diagram shows LH receptors on theca cells, which provide androgen substrate for granulosa-cell estrogen synthesis.

E.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive chapter does not directly discuss side-chain cleavage enzyme timing in this follicular transition.

stem: A healthy 24-year-old woman has regular menstrual cycles, each lasting about 28 days. Daily serum samples have been obtained for 4 weeks. Over the past 3 days, progesterone and 17β-estradiol levels have decreased; serum LH and FSH levels are low but beginning to increase, and basal body temperature is falling. Which event is most likely to occur within 3 days?
explanation: This is the end of the luteal phase. Regression of the corpus luteum causes progesterone and estrogen to fall, removing support for the secretory endometrium and triggering its shedding. FSH begins to rise as the next follicular phase starts. The temperature decline reflects falling progesterone; ovulation and the LH surge occurred roughly 2 weeks earlier.

choice_explanations.A: Inhibin is not markedly rising just before menses; luteal inhibin falls along with corpus-luteum activity.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Withdrawal of corpus-luteum progesterone and estrogen triggers menstrual shedding.
choice_explanations.C: Ovulation occurs near midcycle, before the luteal-phase hormone decline described here.
choice_explanations.D: LH peaks before ovulation and is not expected to undergo a new rapid decrease immediately before menstruation.
choice_explanations.E: Basal temperature rises after ovulation under progesterone; it falls as the corpus luteum regresses.

A.text: First Aid 2026 identifies the fixed 14-day luteal phase but does not give a direct premenstrual inhibin trend.

B.text: The cycle diagram shows menstruation following the luteal phase; endometrial support changes across the ovarian and uterine cycle.

C.text: Ovulation is the midcycle release of the secondary oocyte following the LH surge.

D.text: The cycle diagram places the LH surge around midcycle, before the luteal phase; the option’s premenstrual timing is inconsistent.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss basal body temperature changes across the cycle.

stem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician after noticing a lump in her left breast. She denies a family history of breast cancer, tobacco smoking, or alcohol use. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. After further evaluation, she undergoes lumpectomy. Microscopic examination shows small infiltrating glandular structures lined by poorly differentiated cells, surrounded by desmoplastic stroma with minimal lymphocytic infiltrate. Which cancer type is most likely?
explanation: This is invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common invasive breast carcinoma. It forms infiltrating malignant glands and typically elicits a desmoplastic stromal response. The source describes the same pattern and contrasts it with mucin-rich colloid carcinoma and the less gland-forming patterns of other choices.

choice_explanations.A: Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma has abundant extracellular mucin and is more common in older women; that feature is not described.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Invasive ductal carcinoma forms infiltrating glands surrounded by reactive desmoplastic stroma.
choice_explanations.C: Invasive lobular carcinoma classically infiltrates as single-file cells and loses E-cadherin rather than forming the described glands.
choice_explanations.D: Medullary carcinoma typically forms sheets/syncytial growth with prominent lymphocytic infiltrates, unlike this specimen’s minimal lymphocytes.
choice_explanations.E: A metastatic lung carcinoma would require evidence of a lung primary and would not be identified by this characteristic primary breast glandular/desmoplastic pattern.

A.text: Mucinous carcinoma is a malignant breast-tumor subtype; First Aid distinguishes its mucin-rich pattern from other breast cancers.

B.text: Invasive breast carcinomas commonly arise from the terminal duct lobular unit; the page summarizes invasive ductal carcinoma as the most common type.

C.text: Invasive lobular carcinoma is associated with decreased E-cadherin and orderly rows of cells.

D.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive breast-pathology pages do not directly describe medullary carcinoma in this differential.

E.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive breast-pathology pages do not directly cover metastatic lung cancer to the breast.

stem: An autopsy of an 83-year-old man who died suddenly at a nursing home shows a small amount of abnormal protein deposited in the heart. When stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light, the protein demonstrates apple-green birefringence. This finding is absent from other organs. His only medical problem was hypertension, and there was no evidence of systemic inflammation at the time of death. Misfolding of which protein is most likely responsible for these findings?
explanation: This is age-related, localized cardiac amyloidosis. Congo-red positivity with apple-green birefringence confirms amyloid. In an older adult with cardiac deposition and no evidence of systemic inflammatory disease or another involved organ, wild-type transthyretin is the most likely precursor. Transthyretin amyloid can accumulate in the heart with aging; hereditary variants may also cause cardiomyopathy and neuropathy.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Amyloid A (AA) is produced from serum amyloid A during chronic inflammatory disease; no chronic inflammatory condition is described.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. AL amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains and is associated with plasma-cell dyscrasias such as multiple myeloma.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. β-amyloid is derived from amyloid precursor protein and is associated with Alzheimer disease, not isolated senile cardiac deposits.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. β2-microglobulin amyloid is associated with long-term dialysis and commonly affects osteoarticular tissues.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Wild-type transthyretin can deposit in the heart with aging, producing senile cardiac amyloidosis.

A.text: AA (serum amyloid A) is associated with chronic inflammatory conditions.

B.text: AL amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains and is seen in plasma-cell dyscrasias.

C.text: β-amyloid is derived from amyloid precursor protein and is associated with Alzheimer disease.

D.text: β2-microglobulin amyloid is associated with end-stage renal disease on long-term dialysis.

E.text: Wild-type transthyretin amyloid is associated with aging and predominantly affects the heart; mutant transthyretin may cause familial polyneuropathy or cardiomyopathy.

fa_summary: Amyloidosis is extracellular deposition of misfolded fibrillar protein. First Aid lists AL with plasma-cell dyscrasias, AA with chronic inflammation, β2-microglobulin with long-term dialysis, β-amyloid with Alzheimer disease, and transthyretin with age-related cardiac or hereditary cardiac/neurologic disease.

stem: An 82-year-old woman is found unconscious in her apartment by her son. A gas oven is on, with its door open. She is revived and placed on 100% oxygen by face mask. She reports a severe frontal headache and dizziness while baking cookies, with no memory of what happened afterward. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Her cheeks, lips, and fingers are red. Which mechanism most likely underlies her condition?

options.text: Right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve

explanation: The open gas oven, headache, dizziness, altered consciousness, and flushed appearance point to carbon monoxide poisoning. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity to form carboxyhemoglobin, reducing the amount of oxygen that can be carried. It also shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, making oxygen harder to unload to tissues.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Plasma-membrane damage is a general mechanism of irreversible cell injury; it does not explain the exposure history or carboxyhemoglobin formation.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Calcium dysregulation and mitochondrial injury can occur in cell damage but are not the primary mechanism of carbon monoxide poisoning.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Carbon monoxide causes a left shift, not a right shift, and reduces oxygen content by occupying hemoglobin-binding sites.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysosomal rupture can contribute to cellular autolysis but does not explain this inhalational poisoning syndrome.

A.text: Irreversible cell injury includes plasma-membrane breakdown and leakage of intracellular contents.

B.text: Carbon monoxide produces carboxyhemoglobin and reduces oxygen delivery; see the carbon monoxide poisoning comparison.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not provide a direct standalone match for calcium transport into mitochondria as the cause of this presentation.

D.text: Carbon monoxide shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve left; the proposed right shift is the opposite direction.

E.text: Lysosomal rupture causes autolysis as part of irreversible cell injury.

fa_summary: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache, confusion or coma, possible cherry-red skin, elevated carboxyhemoglobin, and reduced oxygen delivery. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve left.

stem: An investigator is studying bone healing in experimentally induced fractures in an animal model. Decalcified bone sections at different stages of healing are examined. An electron micrograph shows two different cells in one section. Which choice best describes the cell identified by the arrow?
explanation: The indicated cell shows cytoplasmic and nuclear blebbing with fragmentation into apoptotic bodies, the organized morphology of apoptosis. In bone remodeling, apoptosis can remove osteoblasts that are no longer needed. Necrosis instead involves membrane failure, enzymatic degradation, and inflammation.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Membrane blebbing and apoptotic bodies are characteristic of programmed cell death.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. A bone-lining macrophage would not show the nuclear fragmentation and apoptotic-body pattern indicated in the source micrograph.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. A dividing osteoblast would show mitotic chromatin condensation and an intact dividing-cell configuration, not apoptotic fragmentation.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Necrosis is disorganized cell death with membrane damage and inflammation; the source describes apoptotic bodies without that pattern.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. The typical osteoblast is the adjacent functional bone-forming cell, not the blebbing cell indicated by the arrow.

A.text: Apoptosis involves membrane blebbing and formation of apoptotic bodies, typically without significant inflammation.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe bone-lining macrophages as a distinct cell type in this context.

C.text: Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells; the source figure distinguishes the typical osteoblast from the apoptotic cell.

D.text: Necrosis causes enzymatic degradation and a local inflammatory reaction, unlike apoptosis.

E.text: Osteoblasts build bone by secreting collagen and catalyzing mineralization.

fa_summary: Apoptosis is programmed cell death with cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, and apoptotic-body formation, typically without inflammation. Necrosis involves cell injury and inflammation. Osteoblasts build bone.
question_figure_description: 局部电子显微镜图像，仅含题目所需细胞及箭头；无题干、选项、答案或解析。

stem: A 76-year-old woman dies from lung cancer after a prolonged hospital stay complicated by pneumonia. She smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years. At autopsy, histologic examination of the lung shows islands of mitotically active squamous cell carcinoma with central areas of coagulative necrosis. Which mechanism underlies this tumor necrosis?
explanation: A rapidly growing tumor can outgrow its vascular supply. The poorly perfused central region becomes ischemic and undergoes coagulative necrosis. Tumor cells may secrete antiangiogenic factors, but these are not the immediate mechanism described by this pattern.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Antiangiogenic factors can limit vascular growth, but the source explains the central necrosis as a mismatch between rapid tumor growth and its available blood supply.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Apoptosis is programmed single-cell death and does not produce the central region of coagulative tumor necrosis described.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Granulomatous infections such as tuberculosis produce caseous necrosis, not central coagulative necrosis in a squamous carcinoma.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Antitumor immunity can damage individual tumor cells, but it does not explain the central ischemic necrosis from inadequate vascular supply.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Tumor growth can outstrip vascular supply, causing central ischemia and coagulative necrosis.

A.text: Cancer can sustain angiogenesis through increased pro-angiogenic factors or decreased inhibitory factors.

B.text: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, distinct from necrosis.

C.text: Caseous necrosis is associated with tuberculosis and some systemic fungal infections.

D.text: Tumor cells may evade immune recognition; this is distinct from ischemic tumor necrosis.

E.text: Ischemia is inadequate blood supply; ischemic injury causes coagulative necrosis in most tissues.

fa_summary: Necrosis follows irreversible cell injury; coagulative necrosis is caused by ischemia in most tissues. Malignant tumors may show erratic growth and necrosis, and cancer-related angiogenesis is covered separately.

stem: A 27-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and undergoes an appendectomy. The next day, he is febrile and continues to have a large volume of urine output. He complains of severe thirst despite persistent fluid intake. His serum sodium concentration is 175 mEq/L, and urinalysis reveals a low urine specific gravity. Diagrams A–E show the relative osmolarity (y-axis) and volume (x-axis) of the intracellular and extracellular fluid compartments during normal conditions (solid lines) and after various disturbances (dashed lines). Which diagram best represents this patient's body-fluid balance after surgery?
explanation: The severe hypernatremia and dilute urine indicate diabetes insipidus with inadequate renal water reabsorption. When water loss is not replaced, more water than sodium is lost. Extracellular-fluid osmolarity rises, drawing water out of cells; both extracellular and intracellular volumes fall. This is hypertonic contraction (diagram D).

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Isotonic contraction follows loss of fluid with approximately the same osmolality as plasma, such as hemorrhage or diarrhea; serum osmolarity does not rise substantially.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypertonic expansion reflects net gain or retention of hypertonic solute, expanding extracellular volume while increasing osmolarity.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypotonic contraction follows proportionally greater sodium loss than water loss, as with mineralocorticoid deficiency; it does not fit marked hypernatremia.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Diabetes insipidus causes loss of hypotonic urine; un-replaced water loss contracts both compartments and raises osmolarity.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Hypotonic expansion occurs with excess free-water retention or intake, typically lowering serum sodium and osmolarity.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for the isotonic-contraction/Darrow–Yannet label was found in the checked fluid-balance and endocrine sections.

B.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for the hypertonic-expansion/Darrow–Yannet label was found in the checked fluid-balance and endocrine sections.

C.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for the hypotonic-contraction/Darrow–Yannet label was found in the checked fluid-balance and endocrine sections.

D.text: Diabetes insipidus causes large amounts of dilute urine, with increased serum osmolality; this supports water-loss hypertonicity, though the Darrow–Yannet label itself is not shown.

E.text: SIADH causes free-water retention and euvolemic hyponatremia; this is the opposite direction from hypernatremic water loss.

fa_summary: First Aid p.342 describes central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus as causes of large-volume dilute urine, often with thirst and increased serum osmolality; SIADH is characterized by free-water retention and euvolemic hyponatremia. Page 599 reviews the 60–40–20 total-body-water distribution and fluid compartments. First Aid does not directly present the Darrow–Yannet disturbance labels in the answer choices.

stem: A 51-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for hematemesis and acute loss of consciousness. His wife says that he had not been vomiting before the blood appeared. He has a long history of alcohol abuse but no prior hematemesis or recent illness. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. This is a classic presentation of life-threatening bleeding from esophageal varices (tortuous, dilated submucosal esophageal vessels). Sclerotherapy of the vessels and pressure on the bleeding site with an esophageal balloon may temporarily control the problem, but bleeding unfortunately often recurs and exsanguination is a frequent cause of death. Esophageal varices develop secondary to portal hypertension, a complication of cirrhosis. In the United States, the most common causes of cirrhosis are chronic alcoholism and hepatitis C virus infection. Portal hypertension tends to back up into the systemic venous circulation at sites of portosystemic anastomoses. These include the lower rectum (hemorrhoids), paraumbilical veins (caput medusae), and esophagus (varices). A TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) procedure can help reduce varices, but can cause worsening of hepatic encephalopathy (high ammonia).

Achalasia (choice A) is a motor dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter that causes difficulty with swallowing. Food builds up before the esophageal sphincter and causes esophageal dilation and megaesophagus. Radiographic studies of a barium swallow reveal a “bird-beak” appearance. Bleeding is less common.

Esophageal carcinoma (choice C), either adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, tends to present as progressive dysphagia, not acute bleeding episodes.

Mallory-Weiss tears (choice E) are lesions in the esophageal mucosa caused by pressure related to retching. Boerhaave syndrome (choice B) is a related condition, but the tear extends through all esophageal layers and causes fluid or air in the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum). Both syndromes cause upper GI bleeding. There is some difficulty distinguishing esophageal tears from varices, especially since prolonged retching can be caused by excessive alcohol consumption, a significant risk factor for cirrhosis. Esophageal tears usually happen after heavy emesis, which occurs before the blood. A history of chronic alcoholism or liver disease helps point toward varices.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome (choice F) consists of hypochromic, microcytic anemia; atrophic glossitis; and esophageal webs. Bleeding is uncommon.

Schatzki rings (choice G) are benign mucosal rings found at the squamocolumnar junction of the esophagus, below the aortic arch. These usually form as a result of chronic GERD.

Zenker diverticulum (choice H) is an esophageal evagination at the junction of the pharynx and esophagus. Symptoms include dysphagia and halitosis, but usually not bleeding.

choice_explanations.A: Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids from impaired lower-esophageal-sphincter relaxation; it does not typically cause acute hematemesis.
choice_explanations.B: Boerhaave syndrome is a transmural esophageal rupture, usually after forceful vomiting, often with severe chest pain and pneumomediastinum. No preceding emesis is reported here.
choice_explanations.C: Esophageal cancer commonly presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss, not abrupt massive bleeding as the initial event.
choice_explanations.D: Portal hypertension from alcohol-associated cirrhosis dilates lower-esophageal submucosal veins; variceal rupture can cause sudden massive hematemesis and hemodynamic compromise.
choice_explanations.E: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal/submucosal longitudinal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, classically following repeated retching or vomiting before hematemesis.
choice_explanations.F: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is iron-deficiency anemia with glossitis and esophageal webs, causing dysphagia; it does not explain acute variceal-type bleeding.
choice_explanations.G: A Schatzki ring is a benign mucosal ring near the gastroesophageal junction that causes intermittent solid-food dysphagia, not acute hematemesis.
choice_explanations.H: Zenker diverticulum causes oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation, and halitosis; it rarely presents with bleeding.

A.text: Achalasia: impaired LES relaxation, progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, and a dilated esophagus with distal ‘bird’s-beak’ narrowing.

B.text: Boerhaave syndrome is a transmural esophageal rupture caused by violent retching; may cause pneumomediastinum.

C.text: Esophageal cancer risk and presentation; usually progressive dysphagia rather than an abrupt first episode of hematemesis.

D.text: Portal hypertension creates portosystemic collaterals including esophageal varices; varices in the lower esophagus may cause life-threatening hematemesis.

E.text: Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a partial-thickness longitudinal mucosal/submucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after severe vomiting.

F.text: Plummer-Vinson syndrome: dysphagia, iron-deficiency anemia, and esophageal webs; increased risk of esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma.

G.text: No direct Schatzki-ring entry found in First Aid 2026; the esophageal pathology page covers related strictures/rings but does not identify this specific benign mucosal ring.

H.text: Zenker diverticulum is an acquired false diverticulum of the esophagus; false diverticula contain mucosa and submucosa only.

fa_summary: Portal hypertension causes portosystemic collateralization and lower-esophageal varices; rupture can cause sudden life-threatening hematemesis. Distinguish from post-retching esophageal tears.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with hereditary spherocytosis comes to the physician because of intermittent right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Ultrasonography shows multiple stones in the gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely composition of these stones?
explanation:
The correct answer is B. Calcium bilirubinate gallstones (black pigmented stones) are derived from degradation of heme. They are seen in patients with chronic hemolytic disorders, such as this patient's hereditary spherocytosis. Brown pigment gallstones, which are associated with bile tract infections, are also comprised of calcium bilirubinate.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a condition caused by a membrane protein defect of red blood cells. The most common defect is in the cytoskeletal protein ankyrin or spectrin, which causes spherocyte formation. These abnormal red cells are removed from the circulation in the spleen (extravascular hemolysis). Heme will subsequently be broken down into unconjugated bilirubin. Treatment is splenectomy and cholecystectomy.

choice_explanations.A: Ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones form in alkaline urine in the setting of urease-producing urinary pathogens such as Proteus; they are urinary calculi, not gallstones.
choice_explanations.B: Calcium bilirubinate forms black pigment gallstones in chronic hemolysis, as occurs in hereditary spherocytosis.
choice_explanations.C: Calcium carbonate is not a typical major gallstone composition; the principal classes are cholesterol and bilirubinate pigment stones.
choice_explanations.D: Cholesterol is the most common gallstone composition overall, but chronic hemolysis specifically favors calcium-bilirubinate pigment stones.
choice_explanations.E: Palmitate is a fatty acid and is not the characteristic composition of hemolysis-associated black pigment gallstones.

A.text: Urease-producing Proteus alkalinizes urine and can promote struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) urinary stones; this is distinct from gallstones.

B.text: Pigment stones: black stones are calcium bilirubinate and are associated with chronic hemolysis.

C.text: No direct First Aid 2026 gallstone entry for calcium carbonate; the gallstone page identifies cholesterol and calcium-bilirubinate pigment stones.

D.text: Cholesterol stones are the most common gallstone type (about 80%); supersaturation with cholesterol and reduced bile salts/stasis contribute.

E.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry for palmitate as a gallstone component; the gallstone page identifies cholesterol and calcium-bilirubinate pigment stones.

fa_summary: Chronic hemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin and predisposes to black calcium-bilirubinate pigment stones; cholesterol stones are most common overall.

stem: A 34-year-old multigravid woman gives birth to a boy at 37 weeks’ gestation. Newborn examination shows a firm right testicular mass, which is resected. The mass is homogeneous and yellow-white. Histology shows epithelial-lined spaces with flattened-to-cuboidal cells containing vacuolated cytoplasm and eosinophilic, hyaline-like globules; scattered structures resemble primitive glomeruli. The eosinophilic cytoplasmic globules would most likely stain positive for which of the following?
explanation: This is a yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor. Schiller-Duval bodies resemble primitive glomeruli, and the hyaline cytoplasmic globules contain AFP (and α1-antitrypsin). AFP is also a useful serum marker for recurrence. PLAP instead points toward seminoma; hCG is associated with syncytiotrophoblastic cells and choriocarcinoma.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Yolk sac tumor cells produce AFP, which is present in the hyaline cytoplasmic globules and can also serve as a serum marker.
choice_explanations.B: Estrogen receptors are relevant to hormone-responsive breast tumors and some sex-cord stromal tumors, not the characteristic hyaline globules of a yolk sac tumor.
choice_explanations.C: hCG is produced by syncytiotrophoblastic cells, including choriocarcinoma; it is not the marker of yolk-sac differentiation described here.
choice_explanations.D: HPV is associated with epithelial lesions such as anogenital warts and some carcinomas, not this germ-cell tumor.
choice_explanations.E: PLAP is associated with seminoma; the primitive-glomerulus-like structures and hyaline globules instead identify a yolk sac tumor.

A.text: Yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor) has Schiller-Duval bodies resembling glomeruli; AFP is its characteristic tumor marker.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify estrogen receptors as a marker of testicular yolk sac tumor.

C.text: First Aid lists increased hCG with choriocarcinoma and sometimes other germ-cell tumors, not as the defining yolk sac marker.

D.text: First Aid 2026 testicular-tumor discussion has no direct HPV association for yolk sac tumors.

E.text: PLAP is increased in seminoma, distinguishing it from the AFP-associated yolk sac tumor.

stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of urinary urgency and pelvic pain. Pelvic examination shows masses in both adnexae. Ultrasound confirms cystic masses in both ovaries. After surgical resection, each mass is found to be a unilocular cyst containing clear fluid; the entire cyst wall is covered with papillary outgrowths. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A bilateral epithelial ovarian tumor that is a unilocular, clear-fluid cyst with papillary projections is a serous cystadenocarcinoma. Serous tumors resemble fallopian-tube epithelium and are often bilateral. Mucinous tumors are mucin-producing and usually more multiloculated; granulosa tumors arise from sex-cord stroma, while mature teratomas arise from germ cells.

choice_explanations.A: Endometrioid ovarian tumors resemble endometrial epithelium; the clear fluid and papillary architecture are more characteristic of a serous epithelial tumor.
choice_explanations.B: Granulosa cell tumors are sex-cord stromal tumors, often estrogen-producing and associated with Call-Exner bodies or endometrial effects; they are not the classic clear-fluid papillary cyst described.
choice_explanations.C: Mature cystic teratomas are germ-cell tumors containing tissues from all three germ layers, often including hair, teeth, or sebum.
choice_explanations.D: Mucinous cystadenocarcinomas contain mucin-producing epithelium and commonly have solid/cystic or multiloculated features, unlike the clear unilocular cyst here.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Serous cystadenocarcinoma is an epithelial ovarian malignancy commonly presenting as a clear-fluid cyst with papillary projections and often bilateral disease.

A.text: First Aid 2026 p. 664 does not directly discuss endometrioid ovarian tumors; its endometrioid-carcinoma entry elsewhere refers to endometrial carcinoma, not this ovarian differential.

B.text: Granulosa cell tumor is a malignant sex-cord stromal tumor that may produce estrogen and has Call-Exner bodies; see the tumor classification and features.

C.text: Mature cystic teratoma is a benign germ-cell tumor containing derivatives of all three germ layers.

D.text: Mucinous ovarian tumors arise from mucin-secreting epithelium; malignant mucinous tumors are uncommon and may be multiloculated.

E.text: Serous ovarian epithelial tumors resemble fallopian-tube epithelium and are often bilateral; serous carcinoma is the most common malignant ovarian neoplasm.

stem: A 48-year-old woman undergoes radical mastectomy with axillary dissection because of a breast carcinoma measuring 2.5 cm in diameter. Pathologic examination shows metastatic involvement of 3 of 12 axillary lymph nodes. Immunohistochemistry for estrogen receptors is shown. Estrogen receptor status of breast carcinoma is most likely associated with which of the following clinicopathologic parameters?

options.text: Likelihood of spread to distant organs

explanation:
The correct answer is D. Breast carcinoma arises from mammary glandular tissue, which is estrogen/progesterone-dependent. Some breast cancers retain their dependence on hormonal stimulation by expressing receptors for estrogen or progesterone, or both. Such a feature can be assessed on tissue section by immunohistochemical staining with antibodies against estrogen and progesterone receptors. Positive staining manifests as brown, nuclear precipitate in the cells that express the antigen tested (in this case, receptors for estrogen). Assessing receptor status by immunohistochemistry has become standard procedure in the diagnostic evaluation of breast carcinoma.

Carcinomas that are ER/PR-positive will be more likely to respond to hormonal therapy with tamoxifen. ER/PR-positive cancer has a better prognosis than ER/PR-negative cases. Human growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) testing is another predictive test that should be performed in all cases of invasive breast carcinoma. HER2 testing is done to decide which patients will receive trastuzumab therapy; HER2-positive tumors respond to this monoclonal antibody therapy, but they are aggressive tumors. Both markers have prognostic value (regarding the natural history of the disease) and predictive value (regarding the likelihood of response to a certain therapy).

The diagnostic subtype of a neoplasm (choice A) can be determined by H&E staining. Receptor status has no bearing on histopathologic classification. Remember that ductal and lobular carcinomas are the most frequent subtypes, with invasive ductal carcinoma being more commonly diagnosed than invasive lobular carcinoma. Grading of breast carcinoma (choice B) is based on histologic and cytologic features such as nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic activity, and nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio. Likelihood of spread to distant organs (choice C) is not related in any manner to expression of estrogen/progesterone receptors by tumor cells. Staging of breast carcinoma (choice E) is dependent on combined pathologic and clinical investigations aimed at establishing the extent of spread of the primary neoplasm to regional lymph nodes and distant organs.

choice_explanations.A: Histologic subtype is determined by morphology (for example, ductal versus lobular pattern), not by estrogen-receptor status.
choice_explanations.B: Grade is assessed from histologic/cytologic features such as nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic activity, not receptor expression.
choice_explanations.C: ER status is not a measure of whether tumor cells have spread to distant organs; that requires evidence of metastasis.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. ER status informs prognosis and predicts benefit from endocrine treatment such as tamoxifen for ER-positive disease.
choice_explanations.E: Staging describes anatomic extent of disease, including tumor size and regional/distant spread, not receptor expression.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not state that estrogen-receptor status determines histologic subtype.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly link estrogen-receptor status to tumor grade.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly link receptor status to distant-organ spread.

D.text: Breast cancer commonly overexpresses estrogen/progesterone receptors; triple-negative tumors are more aggressive. Tamoxifen is used for ER/PR-positive breast cancer, supporting both prognostic and treatment relevance.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify receptor status as a staging criterion.

question_figure_description: Localized estrogen-receptor immunohistochemistry micrograph from the Word/PDF source; the full page and answer choices are excluded.

stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total hysterectomy for uterine leiomyomas. Histologic examination of an ovary shows multiple primary follicles, each containing an oocyte. At which stage of meiosis are these oocytes most likely arrested?
explanation: Primary oocytes enter meiosis I during fetal life and remain arrested in prophase I until the relevant follicle matures and ovulation approaches. After completing meiosis I, the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II until fertilization. The question specifies primary follicles, so prophase I is the appropriate arrest point.

choice_explanations.A: Anaphase is not the prolonged arrest stage of a primary oocyte.
choice_explanations.B: Interphase is the interval between divisions; it is not the characteristic meiotic arrest stage asked about.
choice_explanations.C: Metaphase II is the arrest point for the secondary oocyte after ovulation, not the primary oocyte in a follicle.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I from fetal life until ovulation-related maturation.
choice_explanations.E: Telophase is not the prolonged meiotic arrest stage of an oocyte.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not identify anaphase as an oocyte arrest point.

B.text: The oogenesis diagram labels interphase as the DNA-replication interval, distinct from meiotic arrest in prophase I.

C.text: First Aid distinguishes the secondary oocyte’s metaphase-II arrest until fertilization from the primary oocyte’s prophase-I arrest.

D.text: Primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for years until ovulation.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not identify telophase as an oocyte arrest point.

stem: A 55-year-old woman reports episodic intense heat and flushing over her trunk and face, occurring more often over the past 3 months. Episodes last a few minutes and then subside. She also has reduced vaginal lubrication and dyspareunia. Which hormonal pattern is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Decreased FSH, decreased LH, increased estrogen
Increased FSH, unchanged LH, decreased estrogen
Increased hCG, increased estrogen, increased progesterone
Increased LH, increased FSH, increased GnRH
Increased LH, increased progesterone, increased estrogen

explanation: The vasomotor episodes and vaginal dryness/dyspareunia are menopausal symptoms. As the ovarian follicle pool declines, estrogen falls and negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost; GnRH, FSH, and LH rise. Menopause is diagnosed after 12 months without menses, but the hormonal pattern and symptoms can appear during the transition.

choice_explanations.A: This is inconsistent with menopause: estrogen falls and gonadotropins rise as ovarian follicles are depleted.
choice_explanations.B: FSH and LH both rise with loss of ovarian negative feedback; LH is not expected to remain unchanged.
choice_explanations.C: This is a pregnancy pattern, not the pattern associated with hot flashes and genitourinary symptoms of menopause.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Reduced ovarian estrogen feedback causes increased GnRH, LH, and FSH.
choice_explanations.E: Estrogen and progesterone do not rise in menopause; reduced follicular activity lowers estrogen, while progesterone is not elevated.

A.text: Menopause features decreased estrogen and markedly increased FSH (with increased LH and GnRH), the opposite of this option.

B.text: First Aid lists increased FSH and increased LH after loss of ovarian feedback; both change, not FSH alone.

C.text: Placental hCG and pregnancy-associated estrogen/progesterone are described separately from menopause.

D.text: Menopause: decreased estrogen removes negative feedback, increasing GnRH, LH, and especially FSH.

E.text: Menopause is characterized by decreased estrogen, not increased estrogen or progesterone.

stem: A 43-year-old woman at 14 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. She is concerned about intermittent vaginal spotting and has not felt fetal movement. She denies abdominal pain or contractions. The uterus is larger than expected for gestational age, and fetal heart tones are absent. Serum hCG is markedly elevated. Ultrasound shows no gestational sac or fetus, but multiple echoes with small anechoic spaces. After dilation and evacuation, the products of conception consist of thin-walled translucent vesicles without fetal parts. Which of the following is the most serious complication of this condition?
explanation: The absent fetus, markedly elevated hCG, uterus larger than dates, and grape-like hydropic chorionic villi identify a complete hydatidiform mole. Its most serious complication is malignant transformation to choriocarcinoma, which can spread hematogenously, especially to the lungs and brain. Complete moles carry a greater risk of choriocarcinoma than partial moles.

choice_explanations.A: Endometrial carcinoma arises from the uterine lining and is not the characteristic malignant sequel of a hydatidiform mole.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Rapid trophoblastic proliferation in a complete mole can progress to choriocarcinoma, with potential hematogenous metastases.
choice_explanations.C: Dysgerminoma is a malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor, not a complication of molar pregnancy.
choice_explanations.D: Sarcoma botryoides is an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma variant that presents as a grapelike vaginal mass in young children; it is unrelated to a molar pregnancy.
choice_explanations.E: Yolk sac tumor is a germ-cell tumor associated with AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies, not a molar-pregnancy complication.

A.text: Endometrial carcinoma is an endometrial malignancy and is distinct from gestational trophoblastic disease.

B.text: Complete hydatidiform mole has a 2% risk of choriocarcinoma; choriocarcinoma is a malignant trophoblastic tumor that can follow an abnormal pregnancy.

C.text: Dysgerminoma is an ovarian germ-cell tumor; it is a separate category from trophoblastic disease.

D.text: Sarcoma botryoides is an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma variant presenting as a vaginal grapelike mass in young girls.

E.text: Yolk sac tumors are germ-cell tumors associated with Schiller-Duval bodies and increased AFP.

stem: A 60-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an itchy white patch on her vulva. Biopsy shows a squamous epithelial lesion without koilocytes. The lesion has papillary projections composed of disordered, well-differentiated squamous cells. The basement membrane at the dermal-epidermal junction is disrupted by groups of squamous cells extending deep into the dermis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Disruption of the basement membrane with squamous-cell groups invading the dermis establishes invasive vulvar squamous cell carcinoma. The patient's age and pruritic white lesion are compatible. Absence of koilocytes argues against condyloma, while Paget disease is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma and lichen sclerosus is a non-neoplastic inflammatory disorder.

choice_explanations.A: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign HPV-associated lesion; koilocytes are expected and invasion through the basement membrane is absent.
choice_explanations.B: Extramammary Paget disease is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, not an invasive squamous-cell lesion.
choice_explanations.C: Lichen sclerosus causes chronic porcelain-white inflammatory plaques and increases SCC risk, but it does not itself show invasive squamous-cell nests.
choice_explanations.D: Vulvar melanoma is a melanocytic malignancy; the biopsy is described as a squamous epithelial lesion.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Invasion of atypical squamous cells through the basement membrane into dermis indicates vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.

A.text: First Aid 2026 p. 661 does not directly describe condyloma acuminatum in its vulvar-pathology section.

B.text: Extramammary Paget disease is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma (carcinoma in situ) and usually has low risk of an underlying carcinoma.

C.text: Lichen sclerosus causes pruritic porcelain-white plaques and slightly increases SCC risk.

D.text: First Aid 2026 p. 661 does not directly cover vulvar melanoma.

E.text: Vulvar carcinoma arises from squamous epithelium and may be associated with high-risk HPV or long-standing lichen sclerosus.

stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a lump in her breast. She has occasional breast pain but no other symptoms and takes oral contraceptives. Examination shows a 1.5-cm, firm-to-rubbery, freely movable nodule in the left breast. Core-needle biopsy is performed. Which finding in the biopsy specimen implies an increased risk of subsequently developing invasive carcinoma?

options.text: Dilated large ducts with inflammation and fibrosis
Proliferation of both fibrous and glandular components without atypia

explanation:
The correct answer is E. A palpable, freely mobile breast mass in a young woman is usually benign, though examining a biopsy specimen can aid in diagnosis. Of the answer choices, the only biopsy result that increases risk of invasive carcinoma is a variant of fibrocystic breast disease known as sclerosing adenosis. As with other types of fibrocystic disease, clinical features include pain, fluctuating size, and palpable breast lump(s), classically in the upper lateral quadrant. It usually presents in women over the age of 30. Pathologically, sclerosing adenosis is characterized by fibrosis that distorts the glands and lobules into a whorled pattern. This may be accompanied by proliferation of small ducts and myoepithelial cells near the terminal duct lobular unit. When sclerosing adenosis shows these hyperplastic changes or cellular atypia, there is an increased risk for subsequent invasive breast cancer.

Apocrine metaplasia (choice A) is the term used to describe the transformation of ductal epithelial cells to eosinophilic cells resembling apocrine sweat gland epithelium. This is a benign, common, non-proliferative change found in other types of fibrocystic breast disease, but is not associated with increased cancer risk. As a caveat, it is important to note that certain types of metaplasia (such as Barrett's esophagus) can produce increased risk of malignancy. A blue-domed cyst (choice B) is a fluid-filled cyst, sometimes up to 5 cm in size, which appears blue grossly before it is incised. When incised, the fluid is serous and dark-colored. These cysts are part of benign nonproliferative fibrocystic disease and do not carry increased cancer risk. Duct ectasia (choice C) is characterized by large, dilated ducts with foamy macrophages within the lumen. This results when lactiferous ducts become clogged, inciting periductal inflammation and fibrosis. Clinical features include pain, periareolar erythema, green-brown nipple discharge, and subareolar mass. It is found in elderly women with a smoking history, although the cause is not clear. Though this disease can mimic cancer, there is no increased risk of malignancy. Proliferation of both fibrous and glandular components with no atypia is consistent with fibroadenoma (choice D). These benign tumors classically occur in women under 25 years of age. They appear as small, rubbery, mobile, well-delineated masses that may or may not be painful. These lesions can increase in size during pregnancy or menstruation (increased estrogen states). They do not increase risk of malignancy.

choice_explanations.A: Apocrine metaplasia is a common benign, nonproliferative fibrocystic change and is not associated with increased cancer risk.
choice_explanations.B: Blue-domed cysts are fluid-filled benign cysts in nonproliferative fibrocystic disease and do not increase cancer risk.
choice_explanations.C: Duct ectasia causes dilated ducts with inflammation and fibrosis; it can mimic cancer clinically but does not increase malignancy risk.
choice_explanations.D: Fibroadenoma is a benign proliferation of fibrous and glandular tissue without atypia; it is not the proliferative lesion identified as increasing risk here.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Sclerosing adenosis with ductal hyperplasia is a proliferative fibrocystic lesion associated with increased risk of subsequent invasive carcinoma.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss apocrine metaplasia as a benign breast-biopsy finding.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss blue-domed breast cysts.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss mammary duct ectasia or its benign biopsy pattern.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss fibroadenoma histology in the breast-cancer section.

E.text: First Aid 2026 p. 668 discusses breast carcinoma and risk context, but does not directly identify sclerosing adenosis with ductal hyperplasia or its risk. No direct FA match for this option.

stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 0, at 10 weeks’ gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. Her pregnancy has been uneventful, but she has a history of 3 clinical spontaneous abortions. Serum progesterone is substantially below the usual range for this stage of pregnancy. Deficiency of which of the following most likely is responsible for the low progesterone production?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. One of the most common causes of first trimester spontaneous abortion is human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) deficiency. The corpus luteum secretes estrogens, progesterone, and relaxin. hCG, secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast lining the placental villi, maintains the corpus luteum during the first trimester of pregnancy. Deficiency of hCG would allow progesterone to drop, leading potentially to increased risk of miscarriage.

Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin; choice A) does not play a significant role during pregnancy. FSH (choice B) acts on granulosa cells to promote the conversion of androstenedione to estradiol. LH (choice D) acts on theca cells to promote androstenedione secretion. Progesterone (choice E) is important for maintaining the pregnancy; however, it does not act to maintain the corpus luteum.

choice_explanations.A: ADH regulates water balance and does not maintain the corpus luteum or drive progesterone production in early pregnancy.
choice_explanations.B: FSH stimulates granulosa-cell development and estrogen production; it is not the signal that rescues the corpus luteum in the first trimester.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Syncytiotrophoblast-derived hCG maintains the corpus luteum, preserving early-pregnancy progesterone secretion.
choice_explanations.D: LH supports theca-cell steroid production and is not the placental luteotropic signal responsible for corpus-luteum maintenance in early pregnancy.
choice_explanations.E: Progesterone is the deficient product, not the upstream hormone whose deficiency explains reduced luteal progesterone output.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly connect ADH with corpus-luteum function or early-pregnancy progesterone.

B.text: FSH supports follicular/granulosa-cell function; it is distinct from hCG's first-trimester rescue of the corpus luteum.

C.text: hCG is secreted by syncytiotrophoblast and maintains the corpus luteum, increasing progesterone during the first trimester.

D.text: LH participates in the ovarian cycle and acts on theca cells; First Aid distinguishes this from hCG maintenance of the corpus luteum in early pregnancy.

E.text: Progesterone is mainly secreted by the corpus luteum during the first 10 weeks and later by the placenta; it is the product, not the deficient regulatory hormone.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is being evaluated for infertility. She has had four spontaneous abortions and chronic pelvic pain. Ultrasound shows a smoothly marginated, rounded 5-cm submucosal mass in the uterine fundus and several smaller, well-circumscribed subserosal and submucosal masses measuring 2–4 cm. Hysterosalpingography shows patent fallopian tubes but an irregular endometrial cavity. Which finding is most likely on microscopic examination of the uterine masses?

options.text: Heterogeneous cells with components of endoderm and ectoderm
Increased number of columnar cells with preservation of the basement membrane
Moderately differentiated cells with a striated pattern
Poorly differentiated cells with abundant atypical mitoses

explanation:
The correct answer is E. The lesions are the very common leiomyomas (fibroids) of the uterus, which are well-circumscribed, rubbery, white-tan masses. Leiomyomas, if numerous or large, may cause chronic pelvic pain and infertility or pregnancy complications (if they intrude on the uterine cavity). Histologically, they are characterized by whorls of spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells. There is continued debate over whether there is malignant potential associated with fibroids or whether leiomyosarcomas arise de novo.

Heterogeneous cells with components of endoderm and ectoderm (choice A) describes a teratoma, which is unlikely to be multiple or intrauterine. They tend to arise in the ovary. Increased number of columnar cells with preservation of the basement membrane (choice B) describes endometrial hyperplasia, which would not present with subserosal masses. Moderately differentiated cells with a striated pattern (choice C) describes rhabdomyomas, which are benign tumors of skeletal muscle and would not arise in the uterus. Poorly differentiated cells with abundant atypical mitoses (choice D) describes a malignant neoplasm, which would not be so well defined in its borders.

choice_explanations.A: Heterogeneous derivatives of endoderm and ectoderm suggest a teratoma, which is generally ovarian rather than a set of uterine masses.
choice_explanations.B: Increased endometrial glands with preserved basement membrane describes endometrial hyperplasia, not smooth-muscle uterine masses.
choice_explanations.C: A striated pattern suggests skeletal-muscle differentiation such as rhabdomyosarcoma, not a benign myometrial tumor.
choice_explanations.D: Poor differentiation and abundant atypical mitoses suggest malignancy; these well-circumscribed masses are characteristic of benign leiomyomas.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Leiomyomas show whorled bundles of well-differentiated smooth-muscle cells.

A.text: Ovarian mature cystic teratomas contain tissues derived from all three germ layers; this is a distinct ovarian germ-cell tumor, not a uterine mass.

B.text: Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal endometrial-gland proliferation, distinct from a myometrial smooth-muscle tumor.

C.text: Sarcoma botryoides is an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma variant; it presents as a vaginal grapelike mass in young children, not as uterine fibroids.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe leiomyosarcoma histology or atypical mitoses for this differential.

E.text: Leiomyomas are benign myometrial tumors, commonly multiple and submucosal/intramural/subserosal; histology shows whorled smooth-muscle bundles.

stem: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of sexual dysfunction for the last 7 years. He has sexual desire and can achieve an erection but cannot maintain it long enough to ejaculate. He recently began a sexual relationship with a new girlfriend; before this relationship, he had not been sexually active for about 7 years. He has non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and hypertension and takes an oral hypoglycemic agent and a calcium-channel blocker. His 60-year-old girlfriend is sexually healthy but has mild postmenopausal vaginal dryness. They have attempted intercourse four times in the past week without success. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's disorder?

options.text: Increased blood flow into the corpora cavernosa
Increased guanylate cyclase activity in penile smooth muscle

explanation:
The correct answer is A. Erectile dysfunction (ED) is diagnosed in men who cannot achieve or maintain an erection. It is estimated that 70% of men age 70 and above experience some degree of ED. Because erection is complex and involves psychologic and physiologic systems, the potential causes are numerous. This patient is experiencing ED due to a physiologic disorder. Sexually related psychic and/or physical stimuli are integrated in the limbic system and stimulate motor impulses in the spinal cord. The parasympathetic nervous system is responsible for impulses that enter the sacral region of the spinal cord before entering the penis. These impulses cause the vasodilation of the arterioles and corpora cavernosa. Nitric oxide is released from nonadrenergic, noncholinergic nerves and endothelial cells and stimulates guanylate cyclase in penile smooth muscle. This stimulation results in increased levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and ultimately in smooth muscle relaxation, which allows engorgement of the blood vessels. Once the vessels are engorged, the penis is erect and the blood-filled arterioles and cavernosa occlude the veins. This occlusion restricts blood flow, trapping blood in the erectile tissue and reducing blood outflow. A decrease in nitric oxide release would prevent smooth muscle relaxation, thus preventing engorgement.

Increased blood flow to the cavernosum is required for erection and would not result in ED. When penile smooth muscle relaxes, the penile arteries dilate, allowing blood to flow into the corpora cavernosum. The cavernosum becomes engorged with blood, expanding and lengthening the penis. The expanding tissue compresses the veins that normally empty the blood from the penis, thereby maintaining the blood in the penile tissue. Therefore, choice B is incorrect. Increased guanylate cyclase in penile smooth muscle (choice C) would not cause ED, but would increase smooth muscle relaxation to facilitate blood flow into the penis. Increased parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) action (choice D) is incorrect because parasympathetic activity is responsible for vasodilation of vessels in the penis. This action is essential for increased penile blood flow. Penile smooth muscle relaxation (choice E) is required for erection and would not result in ED. Smooth muscle of the cavernosa must relax to facilitate penile engorgement. Once the penile arterioles have engorged, the swelling causes the occlusion of veins that prevents blood outflow. This blood trapping is required to maintain rigidity.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Less nitric oxide means less cGMP-mediated cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation and reduced arterial engorgement.
choice_explanations.B: Increased cavernosal blood flow supports erection; it does not explain erectile failure.
choice_explanations.C: Increased guanylate-cyclase activity raises cGMP and promotes smooth-muscle relaxation, favoring erection rather than causing dysfunction.
choice_explanations.D: Parasympathetic activity mediates erection through nitric oxide and vasodilation; increased activity is not the cause described.
choice_explanations.E: Cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation is required for erection, so increased relaxation would not cause this disorder.

A.text: Erection depends on parasympathetic NO release, increased cGMP, and cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation; reduced NO interrupts this proerectile sequence.

B.text: NO/cGMP-mediated relaxation causes vasodilation and increased blood inflow during erection.

C.text: First Aid links NO to increased cGMP and smooth-muscle relaxation, which promotes erection.

D.text: Erection is mediated by parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).

E.text: Penile smooth-muscle relaxation is part of the NO/cGMP proerectile pathway.

stem: A 25-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a routine prenatal examination. She is in the second trimester and has had no complications. Urinalysis shows glucose, and her blood glucose is 210 mg/dL. She has no history of diabetes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Placental growth hormone (PGH), a placental variant of growth hormone, has anti-insulin effects and reduces maternal insulin sensitivity. Increased PGH can therefore raise maternal glucose and contribute to gestational diabetes. Human placental lactogen also promotes maternal insulin resistance, but the hormone identified in the question's answer choices and source explanation is increased PGH.

choice_explanations.A: Reduced hCG would threaten early corpus-luteum support and does not cause second-trimester maternal hyperglycemia.
choice_explanations.B: hPL promotes maternal insulin resistance; a decrease would not explain hyperglycemia.
choice_explanations.C: PGH has anti-insulin activity, so decreased rather than increased PGH would not cause this glucose elevation.
choice_explanations.D: hCG supports the corpus luteum in early pregnancy; increased hCG is not the source's explanation for gestational diabetes in the second trimester.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Placental GH is anti-insulin and can reduce maternal insulin sensitivity, raising glucose.

A.text: hCG maintains the corpus luteum and increases progesterone in the first trimester; it is not the source of second-trimester insulin resistance.

B.text: Human placental lactogen is GH/PRL-like and increases maternal insulin resistance; the decrease in this option points away from hyperglycemia.

C.text: First Aid 2026 describes hPL-related maternal insulin resistance but does not directly discuss placental growth hormone (PGH).

D.text: hCG supports the corpus luteum and progesterone production; First Aid does not associate increased hCG with gestational hyperglycemia.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify placental growth hormone as a cause of gestational diabetes; the related hPL insulin-resistance concept is on p. 651.

stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual bleeding and recurrent spotting between periods. She has regular menstrual cycles and takes no medications. Vital signs are normal. Pelvic examination shows an enlarged, nontender uterus. Ultrasound shows a large, round, well-circumscribed 4-cm submucosal mass on the anterior uterine wall. A day-14 endometrial biopsy shows normal secretory endometrium without inflammation. Which is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: This is a uterine leiomyoma (fibroid), a benign smooth-muscle tumor of the myometrium. Leiomyomas are typically well-circumscribed and may be submucosal, intramural, or subserosal. A submucosal lesion can distort the endometrial cavity and cause heavy or intermenstrual bleeding; chronic blood loss can produce anemia. Normal secretory endometrium and absence of inflammation support a structural myometrial lesion rather than endometrial hyperplasia or infection.

choice_explanations.A: Endometrial carcinoma is not supported by the benign, well-circumscribed uterine mass and normal secretory endometrial biopsy.
choice_explanations.B: Endometrial hyperplasia is an endometrial gland-proliferation disorder; the biopsy is normal and the discrete mass is myometrial.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. A round, well-circumscribed submucosal myometrial mass with abnormal uterine bleeding is characteristic of leiomyoma.
choice_explanations.D: Leiomyosarcoma is malignant and is not the typical explanation for a well-circumscribed uterine mass with this presentation; the source identifies the lesion as benign leiomyoma.
choice_explanations.E: PID causes pelvic infection/inflammation, not an isolated well-circumscribed submucosal uterine mass; the endometrial biopsy shows no inflammation.

A.text: Endometrial carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the endometrium, distinct from the myometrial fibroid described.

B.text: Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal gland proliferation, usually from excess estrogen unopposed by progesterone.

C.text: Leiomyoma is a benign, often multiple myometrial tumor that may be submucosal and cause bleeding, pelvic pain, or reproductive dysfunction; histology is whorled smooth muscle.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe leiomyosarcoma in this uterine-conditions section.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss PID as a differential for a discrete submucosal uterine mass.

stem: A 29-year-old primigravid woman is brought to the emergency department because of headache and dizziness at 34 weeks’ gestation. Prenatal care has been up to date. Her blood pressure has ranged from 140–170/90–105 mm Hg since 30 weeks. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Examination shows edema of the lower extremities. AST is 40 U/L and ALT is 45 U/L. Which is the most appropriate definitive therapy?
explanation: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria and elevated liver enzymes indicates preeclampsia with severe features. Antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate reduce immediate maternal risks, but delivery is the definitive treatment because the disease is driven by the pregnancy/placenta. At 34 weeks, delivery should not be delayed solely to prolong gestation.

choice_explanations.A: Antihypertensives control blood pressure and reduce complications but do not remove the placental cause; they are not definitive treatment.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Delivery is definitive therapy for preeclampsia, particularly with severe features at 34 weeks.
choice_explanations.C: Low-dose aspirin is used for prophylaxis in patients at risk, not as treatment for established severe preeclampsia.
choice_explanations.D: Oxygen does not treat the underlying preeclampsia or resolve its maternal-fetal risks.
choice_explanations.E: Renal dialysis is not indicated by the presented findings and does not treat the pregnancy-related cause.

A.text: First Aid lists antihypertensives for blood-pressure control in preeclampsia, but delivery is definitive.

B.text: Preeclampsia treatment includes antihypertensives and IV magnesium; delivery is definitive. At 34 weeks, the question's timing supports delivery.

C.text: Aspirin is prophylaxis for preeclampsia, not definitive therapy after disease is established.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not recommend oxygen supplementation as preeclampsia therapy.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not identify dialysis as treatment for preeclampsia.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because she has not yet begun menstruating. Examination shows a very shallow vagina without a palpable uterus and palpable masses in the labia majora. Karyotype is 46,XY. Which of the following was most likely present during early fetal life?
explanation: The 46,XY karyotype, female external phenotype, shallow vagina, absent uterus, and testes palpable in the labia majora indicate androgen insensitivity syndrome from an androgen-receptor defect. Testicular Sertoli cells produce anti-Müllerian hormone (Müllerian inhibitory factor), which causes regression of the Müllerian ducts, so a uterus and oviducts do not develop. Androgen levels are typically increased, not decreased; the gonads are testes, not streak ovaries.

choice_explanations.A: A uterus is absent in androgen insensitivity because anti-Müllerian hormone causes regression of the Müllerian ducts.
choice_explanations.B: Oviducts derive from Müllerian ducts and are likewise absent after anti-Müllerian hormone exposure.
choice_explanations.C: Androgen levels are not decreased; the disorder is impaired androgen-receptor response despite testicular androgen production.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Sertoli-cell anti-Müllerian hormone (Müllerian inhibitory factor) is present and causes Müllerian-duct regression.
choice_explanations.E: Streak ovaries occur in other disorders of sexual development; this patient has testes, suggested by palpable labial masses and AMH exposure.

A.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome has absent uterus and fallopian tubes because anti-Müllerian hormone persists from the testes.

B.text: Müllerian structures, including fallopian tubes, regress in androgen insensitivity syndrome due to anti-Müllerian hormone.

C.text: Androgen insensitivity is associated with increased testosterone, estrogen, and LH; the problem is receptor resistance, not low androgen production.

D.text: Anti-Müllerian hormone from testes causes absence of uterus and fallopian tubes in androgen insensitivity syndrome.

E.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is a genotypic male condition with testes; First Aid contrasts it with disorders involving streak gonads.

stem: Diagrams A–E show the relative osmolarity (y-axis) and volume (x-axis) of the intracellular and extracellular fluid compartments during normal conditions (solid lines) and after various disturbances in body fluids (shaded areas). Which diagram best depicts an individual who runs a marathon on a hot summer day and replaces all volume lost in sweat by drinking pure (solute-free) water during the race?
explanation: Sweat contains sodium chloride and is hypotonic relative to plasma. Replacing the lost sweat volume entirely with solute-free water replaces the water but not the lost salt, so total body water remains approximately unchanged while body-fluid osmolarity falls.
