The extracellular fluid loses solute and contracts; water shifts into cells, increasing intracellular volume. This is hypotonic contraction, shown in diagram C.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Isotonic contraction occurs when isotonic fluid is lost, as in diarrhea; water and solute decrease proportionally, with little change in osmolarity or cell volume.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypertonic expansion follows net gain or retention of sodium chloride relative to water; extracellular osmolarity and volume rise and water shifts out of cells.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Sodium chloride lost in sweat is replaced by water alone, lowering extracellular osmolarity and volume while water shifts into and expands cells; total body water is restored.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypertonic contraction occurs when hypotonic fluid is lost without adequate water replacement; both compartments contract and osmolarity rises.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Hypotonic expansion follows excess free-water retention or intake; extracellular osmolarity falls while extracellular volume expands.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for isotonic contraction/Darrow–Yannet diagram A was identified in the reviewed fluid-compartment material.

B.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism is listed with Conn syndrome; the source explanation also notes mineralocorticoid excess as a possible cause of hypertonic expansion. The diagram label itself is not shown.

C.text: First Aid reviews total-body-water, intracellular-fluid, and extracellular-fluid compartments; it does not directly depict hypotonic contraction or sweat replacement.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for hypertonic contraction after hypotonic sweat loss without water replacement was identified in the reviewed fluid-compartment material.

E.text: SIADH causes free-water retention with euvolemic hyponatremia, a related source example of hypotonic water retention; the Darrow–Yannet label is not shown.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 p.599 gives the 60–40–20 total-body-water distribution, relative intracellular and extracellular compartments, and normal serum osmolality. It does not include the Darrow–Yannet labels or the specific sweat-replacement shift. Related alternative mechanisms appear separately: SIADH/free-water retention on p.342 and hyperaldosteronism on p.354.
question_figure_description: 仅含A–E流体隔室示意图与重新标注字母，不含原始radio控件、选中状态、正确答案标记、题干或解析。

stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menstrual cycles. She menstruates each month but cannot predict when. Review of her last 5 cycle dates shows a regular 35-day cycle. She wants to become pregnant but cannot predict when ovulation occurs. On which day of the cycle is ovulation most likely to occur?
explanation: The luteal phase is relatively fixed at about 14 days because of the lifespan of the corpus luteum; most variability in cycle length occurs during the follicular phase. In a 35-day cycle, ovulation therefore occurs about 14 days before the next menses: around day 21.

choice_explanations.A: Day 10 would be too early for a 35-day cycle; the follicular phase is longer than in a 28-day cycle.
choice_explanations.B: Day 17 is earlier than expected because ovulation is timed about 14 days before the next period.
choice_explanations.C: Day 20 is close but does not match the source's 14-day luteal-phase calculation for a 35-day cycle.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. A 35-day cycle minus the approximately 14-day luteal phase gives ovulation around day 21.
choice_explanations.E: Day 25 would leave only about 10 days before the next period, shorter than the usual luteal phase.

A.text: The menstrual-cycle diagram shows ovulation near midcycle in a typical 28-day cycle; a longer cycle mainly lengthens the follicular phase.

B.text: The luteal phase after ovulation lasts a fixed 14 days, so this timing is early for a 35-day cycle.

C.text: A 35-day cycle with a fixed 14-day luteal phase places ovulation around day 21, not day 20.

D.text: The luteal phase lasts a fixed 14 days; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation is approximately day 21.

E.text: The fixed 14-day luteal phase means ovulation is earlier than day 25 in this 35-day cycle.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not begun menstruating. Examination shows Tanner stage I breasts and genitalia with sparse pubic hair. Further evaluation shows weak pulses in the lower extremities, markedly elevated LH and FSH, and decreased free T3 and T4. Which is the best explanation for her abnormal sexual development?
explanation: Primary amenorrhea, absent secondary sexual development, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (high LH/FSH), weak lower-extremity pulses from coarctation, and hypothyroidism are characteristic of Turner syndrome. Ovarian dysgenesis with streak ovaries leads to low estrogen and loss of negative feedback, so LH and FSH rise.

choice_explanations.A: Excess TRH can affect prolactin and ovarian cycling but does not explain the Turner phenotype, coarctation clue, and markedly elevated gonadotropins.
choice_explanations.B: Progesterone is reduced, not excessive, when ovarian dysgenesis prevents normal ovarian steroid production.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Streak ovaries in Turner syndrome cause ovarian dysgenesis, low sex steroids, and elevated LH/FSH.
choice_explanations.D: GnRH deficiency causes low or inappropriately normal LH/FSH, not the markedly elevated gonadotropins in this patient.
choice_explanations.E: Primary pituitary failure would not produce postmenopausal-range gonadotropins; elevated LH/FSH indicate primary gonadal failure.

A.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly link elevated TRH to this Turner-syndrome presentation.

B.text: Turner syndrome causes ovarian dysgenesis and loss of normal ovarian sex-steroid production; excess progesterone is not expected.

C.text: Turner syndrome is associated with ovarian dysgenesis (streak ovaries) and is a common cause of primary amenorrhea.

D.text: First Aid distinguishes hypergonadotropic primary gonadal failure from hypogonadotropic disorders; Turner syndrome is the former.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify primary hypopituitarism as a cause in this Turner-syndrome differential.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a congenital abnormality of her reproductive system undergoes hysterectomy. The surgical specimen is shown. Which is the most likely complication of this condition?
explanation: The specimen shows a bicornuate (bifid) uterus, caused by incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts and producing a Y-shaped uterine cavity. The abnormal cavity can impair implantation and reduce available space for fetal growth, increasing the risk of recurrent pregnancy loss, often in the second trimester, as well as prematurity and malpresentation.

choice_explanations.A: Dyspareunia is pain with intercourse and can have many causes, but it is not the characteristic complication of a bicornuate uterus.
choice_explanations.B: A bicornuate uterus is not a recognized predisposing condition for endometrial carcinoma.
choice_explanations.C: Endometriosis involves ectopic endometrial tissue and is not the characteristic complication of incomplete Müllerian-duct fusion.
choice_explanations.D: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection, not a congenital consequence of a bicornuate uterus.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. A bicornuate uterine cavity can impair implantation and is associated with recurrent spontaneous abortion and other obstetric complications.

A.text: First Aid 2026 p. 640 does not identify dyspareunia as a direct complication of bicornuate uterus.

B.text: Endometrial carcinoma is described as a separate endometrial malignancy; uterine anomalies are not identified as its risk factor.

C.text: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial tissue and has a separate pathophysiology from Müllerian-duct fusion anomalies.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly link PID to bicornuate uterus.

E.text: Müllerian uterine anomalies decrease fertility and increase risk of complicated pregnancy, including spontaneous abortion.

question_figure_description: Tight crop of the bicornuate uterine specimen only, retaining its photographic background and excluding all interface, question, options, and key.

stem: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for follow-up because she has never menstruated. She has sparse downy hair in the axillae and pubic region. Pelvic examination shows a vagina but no palpable uterus. Karyotype is 46,XY, and laboratory studies show elevated testosterone and LH. Which is the most likely underlying condition?

options.text: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development (true hermaphroditism)

explanation: A 46,XY individual with female external genitalia, a short/blind-ending vagina, absent uterus, elevated testosterone and LH, and sparse androgen-dependent hair has androgen insensitivity syndrome. An androgen-receptor defect prevents target tissues from responding to testosterone. Testicular Sertoli-cell anti-Müllerian hormone causes regression of the uterus and fallopian tubes.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Androgen-receptor resistance in a 46,XY patient explains the female phenotype despite high testosterone; anti-Müllerian hormone explains absent Müllerian organs.
choice_explanations.B: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically causes androgen excess with virilization in a 46,XX patient and does not explain the 46,XY phenotype with absent uterus and elevated LH/testosterone.
choice_explanations.C: Klinefelter syndrome is typically 47,XXY with testicular failure and low testosterone, not this phenotype.
choice_explanations.D: Ovotesticular DSD is not supported by the characteristic 46,XY androgen-receptor resistance pattern and elevated testosterone/LH.
choice_explanations.E: Turner syndrome is 45,X with ovarian dysgenesis and low sex steroids, unlike this 46,XY patient.

A.text: Androgen insensitivity is a defect in the androgen receptor causing a female-appearing 46,XY individual with absent uterus/fallopian tubes and increased testosterone, estrogen, and LH.

B.text: First Aid 2026 p. 656 does not directly cover congenital adrenal hyperplasia in this androgen-insensitivity comparison.

C.text: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome disorder with seminiferous-tubule dysgenesis and low testosterone, distinct from 46,XY androgen insensitivity.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe ovotesticular DSD in this differential.

E.text: Turner syndrome is 45,X and associated with ovarian dysgenesis and primary amenorrhea, unlike this 46,XY presentation.

stem: A 15-month-old boy develops a testicular mass. Examination shows a 5-cm nontender, firm left testicular mass that does not transilluminate. After orchiectomy, the cut surface has a heterogeneous appearance. Histology shows cartilage, thyroid tissue, and neural tissue, as well as a small focus of squamous cell carcinoma. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The tumor contains mature derivatives of multiple germ layers, establishing a teratoma. The focus of squamous cell carcinoma is evidence of malignant transformation within the teratoma. Embryonal carcinoma is a distinct malignant germ-cell tumor and is not identified by this collection of differentiated tissues plus a squamous carcinoma focus.

choice_explanations.A: A dermoid cyst is a mature cystic teratoma, but the carcinoma focus means this lesion has undergone malignant transformation.
choice_explanations.B: Embryonal carcinoma is a separate malignant germ-cell tumor; it does not account for the multiple differentiated tissues and squamous carcinoma arising within them.
choice_explanations.C: An immature teratoma contains immature/fetal tissue, especially immature neuroectoderm; the decisive finding here is a distinct squamous carcinoma focus.
choice_explanations.D: A mature teratoma alone does not account for the malignant squamous-cell component.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. A teratoma containing a focus of squamous cell carcinoma is a teratoma with malignant transformation.

A.text: Ovarian mature cystic teratoma is also called a dermoid cyst and contains tissues from all three germ layers; this is a related germ-cell-tumor concept.

B.text: Embryonal carcinoma is a distinct malignant testicular germ-cell tumor and may be associated with hCG; it is separate from teratoma with somatic tissue.

C.text: First Aid describes immature teratoma as malignant/aggressive and containing fetal or neuroectodermal tissue; it does not match the squamous carcinoma focus as directly as malignant transformation.

D.text: First Aid notes testicular teratoma may be malignant in adult males but is benign in children; the infant's carcinoma focus requires malignant transformation rather than mature teratoma alone.

E.text: First Aid notes malignant transformation of mature ovarian teratoma is rare and usually to squamous cell carcinoma; it does not directly state the same behavior for pediatric testicular teratoma, so this is a related rather than exact match.

stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician with a 3-month sensation of heaviness in his right scrotum. Examination shows painless testicular enlargement. Serum human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein levels are normal, but placental alkaline phosphatase is elevated. The cut surface of the orchiectomy specimen is shown. Histology shows lobules and nests of large malignant cells with prominent nucleoli surrounded by abundant lymphocytes. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is a seminoma: a painless, homogeneous testicular enlargement in a young adult with lobules of large tumor cells and a lymphocytic infiltrate. Seminomas commonly express placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP), while AFP is typically normal. The gross specimen shows a solid, pale, fleshy mass. Pure seminoma is highly radiosensitive and generally has a favorable prognosis.

choice_explanations.A: Choriocarcinoma typically has markedly elevated β-hCG, hemorrhage/necrosis, and early hematogenous spread; it does not fit the PLAP-positive, AFP-normal pattern.
choice_explanations.B: Embryonal carcinoma is usually an aggressive, hemorrhagic and necrotic mass; AFP and/or β-hCG may rise, especially in mixed tumors.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Painless homogeneous enlargement, PLAP elevation, and large cells in lobules with lymphocytes are characteristic of seminoma.
choice_explanations.D: Teratomas contain tissues derived from multiple germ layers and have no characteristic PLAP elevation.
choice_explanations.E: Yolk sac tumors characteristically elevate AFP and may show Schiller-Duval bodies; this patient's AFP is normal.

A.text: Choriocarcinoma is a distinct testicular germ-cell tumor associated with elevated hCG and hematogenous metastases.

B.text: Embryonal carcinoma is typically hemorrhagic/necrotic and may be associated with elevated hCG or AFP when mixed.

C.text: Seminoma causes painless homogeneous enlargement, lobulated large cells, and increased PLAP.

D.text: Mature teratoma can be malignant in adult males; it is not the PLAP-associated tumor described here.

E.text: Yolk sac tumor is associated with elevated AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies.

question_figure_description: 题目所需的局部图像。

stem: A 40-year-old man comes to the physician because of breast enlargement. Examination shows bilateral gynecomastia and an enlarged right testicle. Palpation reveals a 3.5-cm nontender mass that does not transilluminate. Orchiectomy shows a well-circumscribed, golden-brown, homogeneous mass. Microscopically, it consists of uniform large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell borders, and round central nuclei. Rod-shaped crystals are scattered among the cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The golden-brown tumor, gynecomastia, and Reinke crystals identify a Leydig (interstitial) cell tumor. Leydig cells can produce estrogen as well as androgens, explaining the breast enlargement. Most Leydig cell tumors are benign; a minority are malignant.

choice_explanations.A: An immature teratoma contains immature tissues from germ layers, often including embryonal/neural tissue; it does not produce Reinke crystals.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Reinke crystals are highly characteristic of a Leydig cell tumor, which can secrete estrogen and cause gynecomastia.
choice_explanations.C: Sertoli cell tumors arise from sex-cord stroma but do not have the defining Reinke crystals or typical golden-brown appearance.
choice_explanations.D: Spermatocytic seminoma is a germ-cell tumor, not a steroid-producing sex-cord stromal tumor; the characteristic Reinke crystals point to Leydig cells.
choice_explanations.E: Yolk sac tumor is an AFP-producing germ-cell tumor, often with Schiller-Duval bodies, rather than a Reinke-crystal-containing tumor.

A.text: First Aid notes that testicular teratomas may be malignant in adult males; it does not associate them with Reinke crystals.

B.text: Leydig cell tumors are usually benign, golden-brown, contain Reinke crystals, and may produce estrogen or androgens.

C.text: Sertoli cell tumor is listed separately as a mostly benign non-germ-cell tumor; the stated Reinke crystals identify Leydig origin.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss spermatocytic seminoma as a separate subtype.

E.text: Yolk sac tumor is an AFP-associated germ-cell tumor; it is distinct from the hormone-producing Leydig tumor.

stem: A double-blind study of fertility-enhancing drugs is conducted. A 28-year-old woman receives sequential doses of a hormone, causing its plasma concentration to rise progressively over several days. Initially, her FSH and LH levels decline, but later both hormones suddenly and dramatically increase. Which hormone is she most likely receiving?
explanation: Estrogen exerts concentration-dependent feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. At low-to-moderate concentrations it suppresses FSH and LH; when a high estrogen level is sustained, feedback becomes positive, producing the midcycle gonadotropin surge, especially the LH surge that triggers ovulation.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Sustained high estrogen switches from negative to positive feedback and causes the FSH/LH surge.
choice_explanations.B: Continuous GnRH can initially stimulate and then desensitize pituitary receptors; it does not produce the described estrogen-level-dependent switch to positive feedback.
choice_explanations.C: Inhibin selectively suppresses FSH and would not cause a simultaneous dramatic FSH and LH surge.
choice_explanations.D: Progesterone supports the secretory endometrium after ovulation and does not produce the preovulatory gonadotropin surge.
choice_explanations.E: Testosterone does not produce the characteristic sustained-estrogen positive-feedback switch responsible for ovulation.

A.text: Estrogen inhibits FSH/LH and, at the appropriate sustained level, upregulates receptors and leads to the LH surge.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly compare constant GnRH administration with the dose sequence described here.

C.text: Sertoli-cell inhibin B inhibits FSH; it does not cause a joint FSH/LH surge.

D.text: Progesterone stimulates the uterine secretory phase after ovulation, rather than causing the preovulatory surge.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly connect testosterone to this female gonadotropin-feedback pattern.

stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician with 6 months of fatigue, bloating, and a 9.1-kg (20-lb) weight loss. Examination shows a protuberant abdomen with a mild fluid wave and bilateral adnexal masses. Ultrasound shows multiloculated cystic masses involving both ovaries. After hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pathology shows bilateral papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma. Which serum marker is most useful for monitoring tumor recurrence?
explanation: CA 125 is useful for monitoring response to treatment and recurrence of epithelial ovarian carcinoma, including serous cystadenocarcinoma. It is not recommended as a screening test in the general population. The bilateral serous epithelial tumors in this case make CA 125 the best choice.

choice_explanations.A: AFP is associated with yolk sac tumors and some other germ-cell tumors, not routine surveillance of serous epithelial ovarian carcinoma.
choice_explanations.B: CA 19-9 is more closely associated with pancreaticobiliary and some mucinous tumors; it is not the preferred marker here.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. CA 125 is used to monitor epithelial ovarian cancer response and recurrence.
choice_explanations.D: CEA is used in other adenocarcinomas and can be elevated in some mucinous tumors, but it is not the preferred marker for serous ovarian carcinoma.
choice_explanations.E: S-100 is not the standard serum recurrence marker for epithelial ovarian carcinoma.

A.text: First Aid associates AFP with ovarian yolk sac tumors, a germ-cell tumor distinct from this epithelial serous carcinoma.

B.text: First Aid 2026 ovarian-tumor pages do not directly identify CA 19-9 as a marker for this differential.

C.text: For epithelial ovarian tumors, monitor treatment response/relapse with CA 125; it is not a screening test.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss CEA for monitoring serous ovarian carcinoma.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss S-100 as an ovarian epithelial tumor marker.

stem: An 83-year-old woman comes to the physician with a 1-month history of an erythematous, pruritic, ulcerating lesion of the left nipple and serosanguineous discharge. Topical creams have not helped. Biopsy shows scattered large cells with clear, abundant cytoplasm within the nipple epidermis; these cells stain positive for cytokeratin. Which underlying condition is most likely?
explanation: This is Paget disease of the breast: malignant glandular (Paget) cells extend through the lactiferous ducts into the nipple epidermis, producing an eczematous, pruritic or ulcerating nipple lesion. Paget disease is strongly associated with an underlying breast carcinoma. In the absence of a palpable mass, the associated lesion is most likely ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS); a palpable mass would favor invasive ductal carcinoma.

choice_explanations.A: Acute mastitis causes an inflammatory, often painful and erythematous breast process, not malignant cytokeratin-positive cells in the nipple epidermis.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Paget disease without a palpable mass is commonly associated with underlying DCIS.
choice_explanations.C: An intraductal papilloma can cause serous or bloody nipple discharge, but it does not explain Paget cells in the epidermis.
choice_explanations.D: Invasive lobular carcinoma is an underlying invasive cancer subtype, but the source explanation identifies DCIS as the likely cause when no mass is palpable.
choice_explanations.E: Phyllodes tumor is a fibroepithelial stromal mass and does not produce intraepidermal Paget cells.

A.text: Mastitis/abscess is a benign inflammatory breast disease, distinct from intraepidermal Paget cells.

B.text: Paget disease is extension of underlying DCIS or invasive breast cancer into nipple skin; without a mass, DCIS is the likely underlying lesion.

C.text: Intraductal papilloma is a separate benign breast lesion associated with nipple discharge, not Paget cells.

D.text: First Aid describes invasive lobular carcinoma among breast cancer subtypes; the no-mass Paget association in this case favors DCIS.

E.text: Phyllodes tumor is a distinct fibroepithelial breast tumor, not the ductal source of Paget disease.

stem: An autopsy is performed on a 52-year-old man who died of an acute myocardial infarction. He had a history of rheumatoid arthritis. Premortem laboratory tests showed elevated troponin I, serum cholesterol of 300 mg/dL, and creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL. The left anterior descending artery had 80% occlusion with a superimposed thrombus. The left and right ventricles appear thicker, paler, and firmer than normal; the kidneys and liver are also firm and pale. Microscopy of the kidneys, liver, and myocardium shows abundant amorphous proteinaceous material that stains with Congo red. A heart photomicrograph is shown. Which amyloid protein is most likely responsible?
explanation: This is secondary systemic amyloidosis. Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis provides chronic inflammation, which increases serum amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant. AA fibrils derived from SAA can deposit systemically, including in the kidneys, liver, and heart. Amyloid appears as extracellular amorphous eosinophilic material on H&E and stains red with Congo red, with apple-green birefringence under polarized light. The multi-organ distribution and inflammatory history favor AA over localized or other systemic amyloid types.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. AA amyloid is derived from SAA and is associated with chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis; it can deposit in multiple organs.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Aβ is derived from amyloid precursor protein and is associated with Alzheimer disease; it does not explain systemic deposits in a patient with chronic inflammatory disease.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. β₂-microglobulin amyloid is associated with long-term hemodialysis, which is not described.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. AL amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains and is associated with plasma-cell dyscrasias; no such disorder is suggested, and the rheumatoid arthritis points to AA.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Transthyretin amyloid is associated with age-related wild-type cardiac amyloidosis or hereditary amyloidosis; it does not account as well for the systemic multi-organ deposits in the setting of rheumatoid arthritis.

A.text: Secondary amyloidosis is AA derived from serum amyloid A and is associated with chronic inflammatory conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

B.text: Alzheimer disease amyloid is Aβ, cleaved from amyloid precursor protein.

C.text: Dialysis-related amyloidosis is due to β₂-microglobulin and is associated with long-term dialysis.

D.text: Primary systemic amyloidosis is AL from immunoglobulin light chains and is associated with plasma-cell dyscrasias such as multiple myeloma.

E.text: Transthyretin amyloidosis can be sporadic (wild-type, slowly progressive, mainly cardiac in older adults) or hereditary (polyneuropathy and/or cardiomyopathy).

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 p.208 describes amyloidosis, Congo-red staining, and systemic types: secondary AA derived from serum amyloid A is associated with chronic inflammatory conditions including rheumatoid arthritis; AL is associated with plasma-cell dyscrasias; transthyretin amyloidosis may be age-related and mainly cardiac; β₂-microglobulin is associated with long-term dialysis; Aβ is associated with Alzheimer disease.
question_figure_description: Cardiac amyloid histology micrograph only; the original page, stem, choices, answer state, and UI are excluded.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with sudden right lower-quadrant abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She had untreated pelvic inflammatory disease 3 years ago. Examination shows right lower-quadrant tenderness, serum β-hCG is positive, and pelvic ultrasound confirms an ectopic tubal pregnancy. Which underlying mechanism most likely caused this condition?

options.text: Lack of adherence of the embryo to surface epithelial cells
Separation of the inner and outer cell masses of the embryo

explanation: Prior pelvic inflammatory disease can scar the fallopian tube and damage its cilia, delaying blastocyst transport to the uterine cavity. The blastocyst may then implant in the tube, most commonly the ampulla. First-trimester pain and vaginal bleeding with a positive β-hCG are classic clues to ectopic pregnancy.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. PID-related tubal scarring and ciliary injury delay blastocyst transit, allowing implantation in the tube.
choice_explanations.B: Failure of the blastocyst to adhere to uterine epithelium prevents normal implantation; it does not explain tubal implantation after PID.
choice_explanations.C: Loss of the zona pellucida is a normal prerequisite for implantation, not the cause of ectopic implantation.
choice_explanations.D: Preimplantation loss is an early pregnancy loss before clinical recognition, not implantation in the tube.
choice_explanations.E: The inner and outer cell masses normally differentiate into the embryo and trophoblast; their separation is not the mechanism of ectopic pregnancy.

A.text: Ectopic implantation most often occurs in the tubal ampulla; tubal scarring from salpingitis/PID is a risk factor.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss blastocyst adhesion failure in this ectopic-pregnancy differential.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss zona-pellucida loss in this ectopic-pregnancy differential.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss preimplantation loss in this ectopic-pregnancy differential.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss separation of the inner and outer cell masses as a cause of ectopic pregnancy.

stem: A couple is being evaluated for infertility. The husband has gynecomastia, sparse body hair, a normal penis, and small testes. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Testicular biopsy shows sparse, completely hyalinized seminiferous tubules. He is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: The combination of small, atrophic testes, azoospermia, gynecomastia, and hyalinized seminiferous tubules is characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). Testicular failure causes infertility and reduced inhibin B, while impaired Leydig-cell function can lower testosterone and raise LH.

choice_explanations.A: Alcohol use can impair reproductive function but does not characteristically cause the XXY phenotype and hyalinized seminiferous tubules described.
choice_explanations.B: 5α-reductase deficiency impairs conversion of testosterone to DHT and causes undervirilized external genitalia, not primary testicular failure with gynecomastia.
choice_explanations.C: Kartagener syndrome causes impaired sperm motility from ciliary dysfunction; it does not cause testicular atrophy or hyalinized tubules.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Klinefelter syndrome causes small firm testes, azoospermia, gynecomastia, and seminiferous-tubule hyalinization.
choice_explanations.E: Androgen insensitivity usually presents with a phenotypic female appearance and absent uterus, not a normally formed penis with small testes and azoospermia.

A.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly link alcoholism to the biopsy pattern in this question.

B.text: 5α-reductase deficiency is a separate disorder of DHT-dependent sexual differentiation, unlike this hypergonadotropic testicular failure.

C.text: Kartagener syndrome is associated with impaired sperm-tail motility, not seminiferous-tubule hyalinization.

D.text: Klinefelter syndrome features small firm testes, infertility/azoospermia, gynecomastia, and seminiferous-tubule dysfunction.

E.text: Androgen insensitivity is associated with a phenotypic female, absent uterus, and testes; it does not match this male phenotype.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks’ gestation comes to the emergency department because of vaginal bleeding. She has no abdominal cramping or pain. She begins bleeding profusely and passes several large fragments of tissue and clot. Which underlying cause is most likely?
explanation: This is a spontaneous abortion in the first trimester. Most early pregnancy losses are caused by fetal chromosomal abnormalities, commonly trisomies, triploidy, or monosomy X (45,X). Placental abruption and placenta previa are later-pregnancy causes of bleeding; infection or trauma is not suggested by the presentation.

choice_explanations.A: Placental abruption usually occurs later in pregnancy and is classically associated with painful bleeding and uterine tenderness.
choice_explanations.B: Chorioamnionitis is an intra-amniotic infection, usually with fever, uterine tenderness, or fetal/membrane findings; it is not the common cause of this early loss.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Most first-trimester spontaneous abortions are due to fetal chromosomal abnormalities, especially trisomies, triploidy, and monosomy X.
choice_explanations.D: Placenta previa typically causes painless bleeding in the second half of pregnancy, not tissue passage at 10 weeks.
choice_explanations.E: There is no history of trauma, and trauma is not the common underlying cause of first-trimester spontaneous abortion.

A.text: First Aid 2026 discusses placental abruption as a later-pregnancy placental disorder, not as the cause of this 10-week loss.

B.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly discuss chorioamnionitis in the context of first-trimester spontaneous abortion.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly specify chromosomal abnormalities as the usual cause of first-trimester spontaneous abortion; this point is established in the supplied source explanation.

D.text: Placenta previa is a separate placental bleeding disorder of later pregnancy, not an explanation for first-trimester tissue passage.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly identify trauma as a common cause of first-trimester spontaneous abortion.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of blood-tinged serous discharge from one nipple. Examination shows a small palpable subareolar tumor, which is resected. Which histologic feature is most helpful in establishing that this tumor is benign?

options.text: Presence of both epithelial and myoepithelial cells

explanation: The presentation suggests an intraductal papilloma. Benign papillomas retain a myoepithelial cell layer beneath the luminal epithelial cells; invasive ductal carcinoma lacks this layer. The other listed features can occur in both benign and malignant papillary lesions and therefore do not establish benignity.

choice_explanations.A: High mitotic activity favors a high-grade malignancy rather than a benign papilloma.
choice_explanations.B: Both benign papillomas and malignant papillary tumors can be intraductal, so location alone is not decisive.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. A preserved myoepithelial layer supports a benign intraductal papilloma and is absent in invasive carcinoma.
choice_explanations.D: Papillary fronds can be present in both benign and malignant papillary lesions.
choice_explanations.E: Both benign and malignant papillary tumors may be small; size alone does not establish benignity.

A.text: First Aid 2026 breast pages do not specify mitotic count as the discriminating feature for papilloma versus carcinoma.

B.text: Intraductal papilloma is a small fibroepithelial tumor within lactiferous ducts, usually beneath the areola; this location alone does not prove benignity.

C.text: The supplied source explanation directly states that benign papilloma retains myoepithelial cells while invasive ductal carcinoma lacks them; First Aid 2026 does not detail this histologic discriminator.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly use papillary fronds to distinguish benign papilloma from malignant papillary carcinoma.

E.text: First Aid describes intraductal papilloma as small, but size alone is not diagnostic because malignant papillary tumors can also be small.

stem: During an investigational study, estradiol secretion is measured daily over a 28-day menstrual cycle. The graph shows the results. Which structure is the most likely source of the estrogen surge around days 10–14?
explanation: During the follicular phase, granulosa cells in the developing ovarian follicle aromatize theca-derived androgens into estradiol. Estradiol rises before ovulation, peaks around days 10–14, and then falls after ovulation; the corpus luteum contributes to a smaller second rise later in the cycle.

choice_explanations.A: The adrenal cortex produces some sex-steroid precursors, but it is not the source of the large preovulatory estradiol surge.
choice_explanations.B: The anterior pituitary secretes FSH and LH, which stimulate ovarian follicular development; it does not synthesize the estradiol surge.
choice_explanations.C: The corpus luteum forms after ovulation and contributes to the later, smaller estradiol rise, not the days 10–14 preovulatory peak.
choice_explanations.D: The hypothalamus secretes GnRH, which regulates pituitary gonadotropins; it does not produce ovarian-cycle estradiol.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Granulosa cells of the growing ovarian follicle produce estradiol during the follicular phase.

A.text: Estrogen is produced by the ovaries, placenta, and adipose tissue; the adrenal cortex is not the principal source of the preovulatory surge.

B.text: FSH and LH stimulate follicular growth and steroidogenesis, but the anterior pituitary does not itself secrete the ovarian estradiol surge.

C.text: The corpus luteum forms after ovulation and is associated with the luteal phase, rather than the preovulatory follicular estrogen peak.

D.text: GnRH from the hypothalamus regulates the reproductive axis but is not the source of estradiol.

E.text: The ovarian follicle’s granulosa cells produce estradiol through aromatization during follicular development.

stem: A 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. She has lacerations on her arms but insignificant blood loss. While waiting, she becomes anxious and hyperventilates, then feels faint and has blurred vision. Which of the following is most likely decreased?
explanation: Anxiety-related hyperventilation lowers arterial PCO₂ by blowing off CO₂. Low PCO₂ causes cerebral vasoconstriction, increasing cerebrovascular resistance and reducing cerebral blood flow. The transient reduction in cerebral perfusion explains her presyncope and blurred vision. Hyperventilation also causes respiratory alkalosis, so pH and PaO₂ rise rather than fall; oxygen content changes very little because hemoglobin is already nearly saturated.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Arterial oxygen content rises very slightly, at most, when hemoglobin is already nearly saturated; it is not the decreased variable causing symptoms.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperventilation lowers alveolar PCO₂ and raises alveolar/arterial PO₂, assuming normal pulmonary function.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Loss of CO₂ raises pH, producing acute respiratory alkalosis.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction, increased cerebrovascular resistance, and decreased cerebral blood flow.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Cerebrovascular resistance increases in response to low PCO₂; it is cerebral blood flow that decreases.

A.text: Blood oxygen content is predominantly oxygen bound to hemoglobin, with only a small dissolved component; when hemoglobin is already nearly saturated, a rise in PaO₂ changes total content only slightly.

B.text: Hyperventilation reduces alveolar PCO₂ and increases alveolar/arterial PO₂; First Aid describes this in respiratory physiology.

C.text: Respiratory alkalosis is caused by decreased PCO₂; the resulting pH increases.

D.text: Cerebral perfusion is driven primarily by PCO₂; lower PCO₂ causes vasoconstriction and decreased cerebral blood flow.

E.text: Low PCO₂ causes cerebral vasoconstriction, increasing cerebrovascular resistance.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 p.512 explains cerebral perfusion: PCO₂ is a primary driver, and hyperventilation lowers PCO₂, causing cerebral vasoconstriction and reduced cerebral blood flow. Page 609 covers respiratory acid-base disorders; p.687 explains oxygen content as primarily hemoglobin-bound oxygen, with dissolved oxygen contributing minimally.

stem: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because she has not experienced menarche. She has trained in ballet since age 6 and has followed a strict low-calorie, low-fat, high-protein diet since age 11. She is 160 cm tall and weighs 46 kg (BMI 17.9 kg/m²), exercises more than 4 hours daily, and is very muscular. Her sexual maturity rating is Tanner stage 2. Abdominal ultrasound shows a uterus and ovaries of a size consistent with her Tanner stage. Which serum findings are most likely?

options.text: Decreased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency, and decreased estrogen
Decreased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency, and increased estrogen
Increased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency, and decreased estrogen
Increased FSH and LH pulse amplitude and frequency, and increased estrogen

explanation: Intense exercise, low energy availability, and dietary restriction suppress pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH release, producing low or infrequent LH/FSH pulses and reduced ovarian estrogen. This functional hypothalamic amenorrhea delays menarche and is part of the female athlete triad, with risk of low bone density and stress fractures.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Hypothalamic suppression lowers GnRH pulsatility, reducing LH/FSH pulses and ovarian estrogen.
choice_explanations.B: Low gonadotropin pulses would reduce ovarian estrogen; increased estrogen does not fit this patient's delayed sexual development.
choice_explanations.C: Low TSH with high thyroxine suggests primary hyperthyroidism, which is not supported by her presentation and does not explain the exercise/diet history as well.
choice_explanations.D: High gonadotropins with low estrogen suggests primary ovarian failure; her exercise restriction and appropriately immature uterus/ovaries favor hypothalamic suppression.
choice_explanations.E: High gonadotropins and estrogen would indicate active ovarian steroid production and would not explain absent menarche with delayed maturation.
choice_explanations.F: High TSH and high thyroxine is not the expected gonadotropin pattern and is inconsistent with the absence of thyroid symptoms.

A.text: Stress can disrupt pulsatile GnRH secretion, lowering LH, FSH, and estrogen; this is the closest First Aid physiology link for hypothalamic amenorrhea.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not describe decreased gonadotropin pulses with increased estrogen as a typical amenorrhea pattern.

C.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly map this thyroid-hormone pattern to exercise-associated amenorrhea.

D.text: Hypergonadotropic primary gonadal failure is a distinct low-estrogen state; First Aid discusses this pattern in sex-chromosome/gonadal disorders.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not describe increased FSH/LH together with increased estrogen as the expected pattern in this case.

F.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly map this thyroid-hormone pattern to amenorrhea.

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of persistent swelling and tenderness in her left breast. Despite antibiotic treatment 4 weeks ago, the breast has become more affected. She recalls no trauma. Her temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F). Examination shows a swollen, tender, erythematous, warm, indurated area adjacent to the areola without axillary lymphadenopathy. The breast photograph is shown. A superficial biopsy is obtained. Which histologic feature is most likely?

options.text: Atypical ductal epithelial cell proliferation without obvious invasion
Cancer cells within the epidermis of the areola
Dermal lymphatic channel invasion by cancer cells
Invasive cancer cells surrounded by abundant lymphocytes

explanation: This is inflammatory breast cancer. Tumor emboli obstruct dermal lymphatic channels, causing edema, warmth, erythema, induration, and peau d’orange. The inflammatory appearance is due to lymphatic obstruction, not a primary inflammatory-cell infiltrate; persistence despite antibiotics and lack of infectious risk factors are important warning signs.

choice_explanations.A: Atypical ductal proliferation without invasion describes DCIS, which generally does not cause this diffuse inflammatory skin change.
choice_explanations.B: Paget disease involves malignant ductal cells spreading into the nipple/areolar epidermis and usually causes eczematous nipple changes.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Inflammatory carcinoma spreads through dermal lymphatics, producing edema and peau d’orange.
choice_explanations.D: Fat necrosis is often associated with prior trauma and is not the cause of this persistent diffuse inflammatory presentation.
choice_explanations.E: Tumor-associated lymphocytes may surround medullary carcinoma cells, but they do not explain the peau d’orange pattern.

A.text: DCIS is a noninvasive breast carcinoma, distinct from the dermal lymphatic invasion responsible for inflammatory cancer.

B.text: Paget disease extends underlying DCIS/invasive carcinoma into nipple skin; this differs from diffuse inflammatory skin changes.

C.text: Inflammatory breast cancer invades dermal lymphatic spaces, causing breast pain, erythema, edema, and peau d’orange.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss dermal fat necrosis as a breast-cancer mimic.

E.text: Medullary carcinoma is an invasive carcinoma subtype associated with a lymphocytic response; that is not the dermal-lymphatic process described.

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of gynecomastia, low libido, and erectile dysfunction. Examination shows abnormally small, firm testes. Biopsy reveals fibrosis and hyalinization of seminiferous tubules with clumped, hyperplastic Leydig cells. Karyotype is 47,XXY. Which laboratory finding is most likely?
explanation: Klinefelter syndrome causes primary testicular failure. Seminiferous-tubule dysgenesis impairs spermatogenesis and lowers inhibin B, increasing FSH; Leydig-cell dysfunction lowers testosterone, increasing LH. Thus decreased plasma testosterone is the expected finding despite Leydig-cell hyperplasia on histology.

choice_explanations.A: Estrogen is not the expected decreased hormone; gynecomastia reflects a relative increase in estrogenic effect compared with androgen activity.
choice_explanations.B: FSH rises because damaged seminiferous tubules produce less inhibin B and provide less negative feedback.
choice_explanations.C: LH rises in response to low testosterone from primary testicular failure.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Klinefelter syndrome causes testicular failure and reduced testosterone, with compensatory LH elevation.
choice_explanations.E: Inhibin B is decreased because Sertoli-cell/seminiferous-tubule function is impaired.

A.text: First Aid 2026 notes gynecomastia in Klinefelter syndrome but does not specify reduced plasma estrogen as the expected laboratory pattern.

B.text: Seminiferous-tubule dysgenesis lowers inhibin B, resulting in increased FSH, not decreased FSH.

C.text: Abnormal Leydig-cell function in Klinefelter syndrome lowers testosterone and raises LH.

D.text: Klinefelter syndrome produces primary hypogonadism with decreased testosterone and compensatory increased LH.

E.text: Sertoli-cell dysfunction lowers inhibin B, which normally inhibits FSH.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a routine examination. He has a history of one undescended testis, which has not descended spontaneously. What is the most serious complication of this condition?
explanation: Cryptorchidism increases the risk of testicular germ-cell cancer, including in the normally descended contralateral testis. It can also impair spermatogenesis and cause infertility, but malignancy is the most serious complication because it can be fatal, particularly after spread beyond the testis.

choice_explanations.A: Testicular atrophy and impaired spermatogenesis can occur because the warmer abdominal/inguinal environment damages germ cells, but it is not the most serious complication.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Cryptorchidism substantially increases testicular cancer risk, including seminoma and other germ-cell tumors.
choice_explanations.C: A patent processus vaginalis can accompany cryptorchidism and predispose to inguinal hernia, but this is less serious than malignancy.
choice_explanations.D: Infarction can result from torsion, which is more common with cryptorchidism, but is less serious than the cancer risk.
choice_explanations.E: Subfertility or sterility may occur from impaired spermatogenesis; unilateral cryptorchidism may leave the other testis functional.

A.text: Undescended testes impair spermatogenesis because sperm develop best below core body temperature.

B.text: Cryptorchidism increases the risk of germ-cell tumors; this is the serious long-term complication.

C.text: Cryptorchidism is associated with a patent processus vaginalis, which can allow inguinal hernia.

D.text: Testicular torsion can compromise blood flow and cause infarction; cryptorchidism is a risk factor for torsion.

E.text: Cryptorchidism impairs spermatogenesis and may cause subfertility, though unilateral cases may retain fertility.

stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of breast development. She was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has met developmental milestones. Examination shows Tanner stage III breast and pubic-hair development and a nontender mass in the right lower abdomen. CT shows an ovarian mass. Which neoplasm is most likely?
explanation: A granulosa cell tumor is an estrogen-producing ovarian sex-cord stromal tumor. In a preadolescent girl, estrogen secretion can cause precocious sexual development. The Word OCR reads Tanner stage I, but the source PDF question image clearly says Tanner stage III, consistent with the clinical presentation and answer explanation; the PDF visual was used to resolve that source-text OCR error.

choice_explanations.A: Ovarian choriocarcinoma is a germ-cell tumor that produces hCG; it does not best explain estrogen-mediated precocious puberty.
choice_explanations.B: Dysgerminoma is an ovarian germ-cell tumor and is not the typical estrogen-secreting tumor causing this presentation.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Granulosa cell tumors can secrete estrogen and cause precocious puberty in preadolescent girls.
choice_explanations.D: Serous cystadenoma is an epithelial ovarian tumor and does not cause estrogen-driven sexual precocity.
choice_explanations.E: Teratoma is a germ-cell tumor containing differentiated tissues; it is not typically estrogen-secreting.

A.text: Choriocarcinoma is a malignant germ-cell tumor associated with hCG-mediated effects, distinct from estrogen-secreting sex-cord stromal tumors.

B.text: Dysgerminoma is a malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor and is distinct from the hormone-producing granulosa tumor.

C.text: Granulosa cell tumor may secrete estrogen and cause sexual precocity in preadolescent girls.

D.text: Serous tumors are epithelial ovarian tumors; they are distinct from sex-cord stromal estrogen-producing tumors.

E.text: Teratomas are ovarian germ-cell tumors that differentiate into somatic structures; they are not the estrogen-secreting cause described.

stem: A photograph shows a 5-year-old boy with an inherited disorder affecting the growth plates of long bones. He is brought to the pediatrician for recent-onset sleep apnea. He has normal intelligence, and both parents have features of short-limbed dwarfism. Which protein or biochemical pathway is most likely altered?
explanation: The findings indicate achondroplasia, an autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia caused by a gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation. Constitutively active FGFR3 inhibits chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate and impairs endochondral ossification, producing short limbs. Intramembranous ossification is relatively spared, so the head and axial skeleton are relatively preserved; normal intelligence and sleep-disordered breathing can occur.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Constitutive FGFR3 signaling inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and longitudinal growth of long bones in achondroplasia.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Defective lysosomal degradation of mucopolysaccharides causes mucopolysaccharidoses, often with coarse facies, organ involvement, and developmental findings, rather than the classic familial short-limb phenotype of achondroplasia.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, typically with tall stature, long limbs, aortic-root disease, and lens abnormalities.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Homeobox (HOX) transcription-factor defects can cause developmental patterning abnormalities, such as syndactyly or urogenital anomalies; they do not produce the characteristic FGFR3-mediated achondroplasia pattern.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, characterized by bone fragility and recurrent fractures, often with blue sclerae or dentin abnormalities.

A.text: Achondroplasia is caused by constitutive FGFR3 activation, which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, producing short limbs.

B.text: Lysosomal enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of abnormal substrates; mucopolysaccharidoses reflect impaired degradation of glycosaminoglycans. Hunter syndrome is listed among X-linked recessive diseases on p.59.

C.text: Marfan syndrome is caused by FBN1 mutation, resulting in defective fibrillin-1.

D.text: Homeobox (HOX) genes regulate neural-tube segmentation and cranial-caudal differentiation; mutations can cause limb syndactyly and urogenital abnormalities.

E.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta commonly results from COL1A1/COL1A2 defects affecting type I collagen and causes brittle bones, fractures, and often blue sclerae.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 p.467 describes achondroplasia: constitutively active FGFR3 inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, causing short limbs while membranous ossification is spared. The printed page places this topic in the Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue chapter. Additional per-choice links: type I collagen/OI p.49; fibrillin/Marfan p.50; mucopolysaccharidosis and lysosomal disease p.86; Hunter syndrome p.59; HOX/homeobox genes p.500.
question_figure_description: Photo-only crop of the child with achondroplasia; excludes question text, choices, answer state, and interface.

stem: A 51-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She is concerned about a recent history of abnormal periods, fatigue, and weight loss. Pelvic examination shows an adnexal mass. Resection of the mass confirms a malignant ovarian tumor. She reports a family history of breast cancer in her mother and aunt, both in their 40s; her grandmother had ovarian cancer. This patient most likely has a genetic abnormality in a tumor-suppressor gene located on which chromosome arm?
explanation: The early-onset breast cancers in two close relatives together with ovarian cancer in the family suggest hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome from a germline BRCA1 tumor-suppressor mutation. BRCA1 is on chromosome 17q; BRCA2 is on 13q. Tumor-suppressor syndromes follow the two-hit model: one defective allele may be inherited, and somatic inactivation of the remaining functional allele permits tumor development. The stem's menstrual symptoms and weight loss are nonspecific; the decisive clue is the family pattern of breast and ovarian cancer.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. VHL is on 3p. Its loss is associated with von Hippel–Lindau syndrome, including clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastomas, and pheochromocytoma.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. APC is on 5q. Germline loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis and markedly increases colorectal-cancer risk.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. WT1 is on 11p and is associated with Wilms tumor and the WAGR spectrum.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. BRCA1 is a tumor-suppressor gene on 17q and is associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. BRCA2 is on 13q.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. The source explanation associates 18q with DPC and DCC tumor-suppressor genes, linked respectively with pancreatic and colorectal cancer; this is not the characteristic familial breast/ovarian cancer locus.

A.text: VHL is listed at 3p. First Aid associates VHL loss with von Hippel–Lindau disease; renal tumors are discussed in the renal chapter (p.623).

B.text: APC is listed at 5q. First Aid's neoplasia section (p.220) associates APC with familial adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer.

C.text: WT1 is listed at 11p; First Aid's renal tumor discussion (p.623) links WT1 with Wilms tumor.

D.text: BRCA1 is listed at 17q and BRCA2 at 13q. First Aid p.220 connects BRCA1/2 tumor-suppressor genes with breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility.

E.text: Chromosome 18 is represented in the First Aid chromosome-gene table; the source explanation specifies DCC/DPC tumor-suppressor associations on 18q. First Aid p.220 covers tumor-suppressor genes in neoplasia but does not directly state the DCC/DPC chromosome-arm pairing.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.62 lists the chromosome-to-gene associations, including BRCA1 on 17q, BRCA2 on 13q, VHL on 3p, APC on 5q, WT1 on 11p, and genes associated with chromosome 18. Printed p.220 discusses tumor-suppressor genes in neoplasia, including BRCA1/2 and their cancer associations. Together these support the keyed BRCA1/17q link and the two-hit tumor-suppressor framework.

stem: A 37-year-old man with follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma returns for follow-up. The lymphoma cells do not appear to be actively dividing, but the number of malignant cells continues to increase. Overexpression of which of the following best accounts for the inhibited apoptosis of these abnormal cells?
explanation: Follicular lymphoma classically carries t(14;18), which places BCL2 near the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus and increases BCL-2 expression. BCL-2 is antiapoptotic: it stabilizes the mitochondrial outer membrane and prevents cytochrome-c release, reducing caspase activation. The malignant lymphocytes therefore accumulate because they avoid programmed cell death, not because they are proliferating rapidly.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. BCL-2 inhibits the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic pathway; its overexpression in follicular lymphoma is associated with t(14;18).
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Caspases are executioner proteases activated during apoptosis. They promote cell death rather than inhibit it.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Fas (CD95) is an extrinsic death receptor; Fas-ligand binding activates apoptosis. Loss of Fas signaling can cause lymphoproliferation, but overexpression would not explain inhibited apoptosis here.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Perforin enables cytotoxic lymphocytes to deliver granzymes into target cells and trigger apoptosis; it is pro-death, not an antiapoptotic lymphoma protein.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. p53 is a tumor suppressor that can arrest the cell cycle or induce apoptosis after DNA damage. Loss/inactivation, not overexpression, is oncogenic in this setting.

A.text: BCL-2 is antiapoptotic and prevents mitochondrial cytochrome-c release/caspase activation; p.435 directly links follicular lymphoma to t(14;18) and BCL-2.

B.text: Caspases are cytosolic proteases activated by intrinsic, extrinsic, and perforin/granzyme apoptotic pathways; they execute cellular breakdown.

C.text: Fas (CD95) is an extrinsic death receptor; FasL binding triggers apoptosis. Defective Fas-FasL signaling can cause autoimmune lymphoproliferation.

D.text: The perforin/granzyme B pathway activates caspases and apoptosis; perforin is a cytotoxic mechanism, not an apoptosis inhibitor.

E.text: TP53 is a tumor-suppressor pathway in neoplasia; loss of p53 function promotes cancer. Printed p.217 lists TP53 among mutations involved in evasion of apoptosis.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.204 explains intrinsic mitochondrial apoptosis: BCL-2 is antiapoptotic, prevents cytochrome-c release and caspase activation, while Fas and perforin/granzyme are proapoptotic pathways and caspases are executioners. Printed p.435 directly links follicular lymphoma with t(14;18), BCL-2, and inhibition of apoptosis. Pages 217 and 220 provide the cancer hallmarks and tumor-suppressor context, including p53.

stem:
A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of erectile dysfunction. Physical examination shows darkened skin and limited range of motion in the small joints of both hands. Fasting serum glucose is 170 mg/dL. Imaging studies show a small, nodular liver and splenomegaly. A liver-biopsy photomicrograph is shown. Which combination of serum laboratory values is most likely?

Test | A | B | C | D | E
Serum iron | Low | Low | Normal | High | High
Ferritin | Low | High | Normal | Low | High
Transferrin | High | Low | High | High | Low
Transferrin saturation | Low | Low | Low | Low | High

options.text: Low serum iron, low ferritin, high transferrin, low transferrin saturation
Low serum iron, high ferritin, low transferrin, low transferrin saturation
Normal serum iron, normal ferritin, high transferrin, low transferrin saturation
High serum iron, low ferritin, high transferrin, low transferrin saturation
High serum iron, high ferritin, low transferrin, high transferrin saturation

explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient is suffering from hemochromatosis, a disease of excess iron. You must remember these key facts about serum iron studies: iron is stored bound to the soluble protein ferritin; transferrin is the transport protein for iron; serum transferrin is synthesized in the liver; transferrin synthesis increases when ferritin is low and decreases when ferritin is high; total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) reflects transferrin; and percent transferrin saturation is the amount of iron bound to transferrin. In hemochromatosis, serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation are increased, while transferrin and TIBC are decreased.

Normally, iron is absorbed from the intestine. Excess iron is stored in mucosal epithelial cells as insoluble ferritin and excreted in feces when the mucosal epithelium sloughs off as part of its life cycle. Iron is not significantly excreted in the urine or metabolized by the liver.

Hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive hereditary disease tightly linked to the HLA-A3 locus. More males are symptomatic because the excess iron in female patients is lost in menses. As a result, male patients tend to present in their 50s while female patients present many years after menopause. Secondary hemochromatosis can arise from conditions that require multiple transfusions (e.g., thalassemia). In either case, excess iron is deposited in tissues primarily as ferritin, which has a golden-yellow color. The excess iron causes oxidative cell damage.

Hemochromatosis has sometimes been called “bronze diabetes” because the iron deposition in blood vessels discolors the skin and damages the pancreas, liver, and heart. Diabetes mellitus may ensue from pancreatic damage. The excess iron also produces arthropathy, hypogonadism, cirrhosis, and cardiomyopathy. Patients may complain of weakness, fatigue, loss of libido, weight loss, or abdominal pain. A small and nodular liver, splenomegaly, and signs of cirrhosis or congestive heart failure may be present in advanced cases. Prussian blue staining of a liver specimen shows positive staining for iron deposition.

Iron deficiency (choice A), due to low dietary iron or slow iron loss (e.g., chronic gastrointestinal bleeding), causes low serum iron. Less iron is bound in ferritin. This stimulates an increase in transferrin synthesis. TIBC is high. Percent saturation is low.

Anemia of chronic disease (choice B) is likely due to chronic inflammation. In this case, hepcidin (an acute-phase reactant, as is ferritin) prevents iron release to transferrin. Ferritin levels will be high, followed by a decrease in transferrin (and TIBC), decrease in serum iron, and decrease in iron saturation.

Oral contraceptive pills (choice C) cause an increase in transferrin production, but do not affect iron stores directly. Thus, serum iron and ferritin are normal. Increasing transferrin without increasing iron causes a decrease in the ratio of iron to transferrin, so percent transferrin saturation decreases.

Choice D does not correspond with hemochromatosis.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. This is iron deficiency: low serum iron and ferritin lead to compensatory increased transferrin/TIBC and low saturation.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. This pattern is anemia of chronic inflammation: hepcidin sequesters iron, raising ferritin while lowering serum iron and transferrin/TIBC; saturation is low.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased transferrin with normal iron stores and low saturation is compatible with pregnancy or oral contraceptive use, not systemic iron overload.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. The combination is internally inconsistent with hemochromatosis: iron overload should increase ferritin and suppress transferrin, with increased—not low—transferrin saturation.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Hemochromatosis produces high serum iron and ferritin, low transferrin/TIBC, and high transferrin saturation.

A.text: Iron-deficiency anemia: low serum iron and ferritin, increased transferrin/TIBC, and markedly low transferrin saturation.

B.text: Anemia of chronic disease: low serum iron and transferrin/TIBC, high ferritin, and low or decreased transferrin saturation.

C.text: Pregnancy/OCP use: increased transferrin/TIBC with no direct change in iron stores; percent saturation decreases.

D.text: No First Aid iron-study pattern matches this combination. First Aid p.423 shows that hemochromatosis instead has high ferritin, low transferrin/TIBC, and high transferrin saturation.

E.text: Hemochromatosis: increased serum iron, low transferrin/TIBC, increased ferritin, and markedly increased transferrin saturation.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.423 directly compares iron-study patterns. Hemochromatosis is the column with increased serum iron, decreased transferrin/TIBC, increased ferritin, and increased transferrin saturation. This matches the clinical iron-overload syndrome in the stem.
question_figure_description: Liver-biopsy photomicrograph with coarse golden-brown iron pigment in hepatocytes, consistent with iron deposition.

stem: An autopsy is performed on a 12-year-old boy who died of multi-organ failure. He had a history of chronic anemia and required frequent hospitalizations and transfusions. On autopsy, he is found to have short stature, hepatosplenomegaly, and expansion of the calvarium. Histologic examination shows the presence of abundant pigment in macrophages of the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes, as well as in parenchymal cells of the heart, liver, endocrine organs, and kidney. The photomicrograph shows a section of kidney. The pigment seen histologically in this patient is most likely which of the following?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Any prolonged systemic overload of iron results in a condition called hemosiderosis. This may result from hemolytic anemias (intracellular release of iron), repeated blood transfusions as with our patient, or increased iron absorption in conditions such as congenital hemochromatosis. Due to elevated serum iron (along with increased ferritin, decreased TIBC, and increased transferrin saturation), hemosiderin accumulates within macrophages of the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, lung, and kidneys. The pigment appears as coarse, golden-brown granules within the cytoplasm, which can be identified with Prussian blue stain.

Patients with severe forms of sickle-cell anemia or thalassemia are especially prone to this complication. In these diseases, anemia results from mutated hemoglobin chains rather than a deficiency of iron. Providing iron transfusions to these patients temporarily relieves their anemia, but precipitates iron overload. Each unit of packed red blood cells contains 250 mg of iron. Signs of extramedullary hematopoiesis, including calvarial expansion and splenomegaly, suggest that our patient likely presents with one of the hereditary hemoglobinopathies described above.

With sufficient iron overload, patients may have symptoms of hemochromatosis. Features of this disease include restrictive cardiomyopathy, hepatic disease, diabetes mellitus (due to pancreatic involvement), and skin pigmentation (“bronze-diabetes”). Treatments include deferoxamine (iron chelator) and phlebotomy.

Bilirubin (choice A) is the normal pigment of bile. Bilirubin is responsible for coloration of stool and urine. In cases of obstructive jaundice or liver disease, excess serum conjugated bilirubin accumulates as yellow-green pigment within Kupffer cells and bile ducts, and can produce darker urine, while lack of excretion in the intestines results in pale stools.

Inhalation of carbon particles (choice B) is an inevitable consequence of living in polluted urban areas and of cigarette smoking. Carbon particles are taken up by alveolar macrophages and transported to the regional lymph nodes, causing a dark discoloration of hilar lymph nodes and lung interstitium known as anthracosis.

Homogentisic acid (choice D) is a black pigment occurring in alkaptonuria. It is an autosomal recessive deficiency in homogentisic acid oxidase, an enzyme in the tyrosine metabolism pathway. Findings include dark connective tissue, pigmented sclera, and dark urine. Sequelae include arthritis and kidney stones.

Lipofuscin (choice E) is a golden-brown pigment that accumulates in aging postmitotic cells such as cardiac myocytes, hepatocytes, skin, and neurons. It represents an epiphenomenon of free-radical injury, but as far as we know, lipofuscin is harmless.

Melanin (choice F) may appear remarkably similar to hemosiderin on H&E tissue sections. It is the brown pigment synthesized by melanocytes from the tyrosinase-catalyzed oxidation of tyrosine to melanin. Metastatic melanoma cells can be present in the brain and liver; some cells will retain their pigmentation.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Bilirubin is a bile pigment that accumulates particularly in hepatocytes/Kupffer cells and bile ducts in cholestasis or jaundice; it does not explain widespread iron-overload pigment after repeated transfusions.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Carbon particles are inhaled and accumulate in pulmonary macrophages and hilar lymph nodes (anthracosis), not throughout the reticuloendothelial system and parenchymal organs in this transfused patient.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Hemosiderin is an intracellular iron-storage pigment. Repeated transfusions and hemolysis can cause systemic iron overload, with deposits in macrophages and, when severe, parenchymal organs.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Homogentisic acid pigment occurs in alkaptonuria, causing dark connective tissue, sclera, and urine with ochronosis/arthritis; it is not caused by transfusional iron overload.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown wear-and-tear pigment that accumulates in aging or chronically stressed postmitotic cells; it does not cause this systemic iron-deposition pattern.
choice_explanations.F: Incorrect. Melanin is synthesized by melanocytes and may be present in melanocytic lesions or metastases; it does not explain iron-loading distribution or the transfusion history.

A.text: No directly matching First Aid passage was verified for bilirubin as a tissue-pigment distractor in this context.

B.text: No directly matching First Aid passage was verified for anthracotic carbon pigment as a distractor in this context.

C.text: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages are identified on First Aid p.316; the iron-overload pattern and hemochromatosis iron studies are summarized on p.423.

D.text: No direct First Aid printed-page match for homogentisic-acid pigment as a tissue differential was verified in this audit.

E.text: No direct First Aid printed-page match for lipofuscin as a tissue-pigment differential was verified in this audit.

F.text: No direct First Aid printed-page match for melanin as a tissue-pigment differential was verified in this audit.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.316 identifies hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Printed p.423 covers ferritin/iron storage and hemochromatosis iron-study patterns. Together these pages support hemosiderin as an iron-storage pigment, although the exact renal photomicrograph and transfusion-associated distribution are not reproduced in First Aid.
question_figure_description: Kidney histology photomicrograph showing coarse golden-brown cytoplasmic pigment granules in renal tissue.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of severe acid reflux is admitted to the hospital for biopsies of the antral and duodenal mucosa. Samples are prepared for light microscopy as well as fluorescence immunohistochemistry. Which of the following hormones is most likely to be detected in tissue from both biopsy samples?
explanation: Gastrin is produced by G cells in both the gastric antrum and the duodenum, so it can be detected in both biopsy samples. The severe reflux is contextual: gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion, but the decisive clue is its distribution in both sampled regions.

choice_explanations.A: Cholecystokinin is produced by I cells in the duodenum and jejunum, not by the gastric antrum; it therefore would not be present in both sampled tissues.
choice_explanations.B: GIP is produced by K cells in the duodenum and jejunum, not the gastric antrum.
choice_explanations.C: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum, matching both biopsy sites.
choice_explanations.D: Motilin is produced in the small intestine; it is not a hormone of both the gastric antrum and duodenum.
choice_explanations.E: Secretin is produced by S cells in the duodenum, not the gastric antrum.

A.text: Cholecystokinin is produced by I cells in the duodenum and jejunum.

B.text: GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) is produced by K cells in the duodenum and jejunum.

C.text: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum; it increases gastric acid secretion.

D.text: Motilin is produced in the small intestine and stimulates migrating motor complexes.

E.text: Secretin is produced by S cells in the duodenum.

fa_summary: Gastrointestinal regulatory hormones are produced by region-specific enteroendocrine cells. Gastrin is the listed hormone found in both gastric antrum and duodenum.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child checkup. A large, palpable, nontender, right intra-abdominal mass that crosses the midline is found on physical examination. CT shows a mass in the right retroperitoneum and abdominal cavity. The tumor is resected. Microscopic examination shows ganglion cells and primitive small, round cells, occasionally organized in rosettes and embedded in a fibrillary pink matrix. Which of the following features is most likely associated with this tumor?
explanation: This is neuroblastoma, a neural-crest tumor that commonly arises from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain. Neuroblastoma can form a large abdominal mass that crosses the midline; histology may show small round cells, Homer Wright rosettes, and a fibrillary neuropil matrix. Amplification of N-MYC (MYCN) is associated with aggressive disease and a worse prognosis. By contrast, Wilms tumor arises from renal nephroblasts, often does not cross the midline, and is associated with WT1 loss. Neuroblastoma may also produce catecholamine metabolites such as homovanillic acid.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. C-MYC amplification/translocation is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, not neuroblastoma.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. N-MYC (MYCN) amplification is associated with neuroblastoma and a poorer prognosis.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. WT1 loss is associated with Wilms tumor, a renal nephroblastoma; it does not explain this neural-crest tumor's histology.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Multiple renal cysts suggest polycystic kidney disease, not a solid tumor composed of ganglion cells and primitive neuroblastic cells.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Nephroblasts are the cells of origin of Wilms tumor. Neuroblastoma arises from neural-crest-derived sympathetic tissue.

A.text: MYCC (C-MYC) is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, not neuroblastoma.

B.text: MYCN (N-MYC) amplification is associated with neuroblastoma.

C.text: No direct First Aid p.220 pairing of WT1 deletion with this tumor is given; WT1 loss is a Wilms tumor association, unlike the neuroblastoma association tested here.

D.text: No direct First Aid p.220 association for renal cysts; this option points to polycystic kidney disease, not neuroblastoma.

E.text: No direct First Aid p.220 association for nephroblasts; nephroblasts are the contrasting cell of origin in Wilms tumor.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.220 lists MYCN (N-MYC) amplification as associated with neuroblastoma and MYCC (C-MYC) with Burkitt lymphoma. It also identifies WT1 as a tumor-suppressor gene; this supports the keyed distinction from Wilms tumor.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of abdominal fullness and pain. She reports early satiety and fewer bowel movements than usual, and has noticed decreased stool caliber. A radiographic bowel series shows a circumferential lesion narrowing the sigmoid-colon lumen and more than 100 polyps. Her carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level is 100 times the upper limit of normal. Further investigation reveals a genetic disease that predisposes her to this condition. The genetic defect most likely involves which chromosome site?
explanation: More than 100 colorectal adenomatous polyps strongly indicates familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). FAP is caused by a germline loss-of-function mutation in the APC tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21–q22. The sigmoid lesion and reduced stool caliber reflect an obstructing colorectal cancer; the markedly elevated CEA supports tumor burden but is not the genetic clue.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. APC on chromosome 5q21–q22 is mutated in FAP, which causes numerous adenomatous colorectal polyps and a very high risk of colorectal cancer.
choice_explanations.B: 11p13 contains WT1; loss-of-function is associated with Wilms tumor, not FAP.
choice_explanations.C: 13q14 contains RB1; loss of both RB1 alleles causes retinoblastoma and is not the FAP locus.
choice_explanations.D: 17p13 contains TP53; germline TP53 variants cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, whereas APC is the classic polyposis gene.
choice_explanations.E: 22q12 contains NF2 (merlin); NF2 loss causes neurofibromatosis type 2, not FAP.

A.text: First Aid lists familial adenomatous polyposis under chromosome 5 (p. 62) and specifies an autosomal-dominant APC tumor-suppressor mutation at 5q21–q22 with thousands of adenomatous polyps (p. 394).

B.text: First Aid associates chromosome 11 and WT1 with Wilms tumor. The precise 11p13 band is not printed in these entries; this is the relevant competing chromosome/gene association, not FAP.

C.text: First Aid associates chromosome 13 and RB1 with retinoblastoma; the exact 13q14 band is not printed in these entries.

D.text: First Aid lists TP53 with chromosome 17 and Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and describes p53 as a tumor suppressor; the exact 17p13 band is not printed in these entries.

E.text: First Aid associates chromosome 22/NF2 (merlin) with neurofibromatosis type 2; the exact 22q12 band is not printed in these entries.
